Fill in each blank unshaded cell with a positive integer less than 100, such that every consecutive group of unshaded cells within a row or column is an arithmetic sequence.

You do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible; you merely need to find an answer that satisfies the constraints above.

solutions.title: Start from the forced runs
solutions.body:
A run of unshaded cells is determined by its first term and common difference, so start where two entries of one run are given.

* **Bottom row, left run.** The run in columns 1–6 contains $31, 26$ in columns 5–6, so its difference is $-5$: $51, 46, 41, 36, 31, 26$.
* **Left part.** Let $t$ be the entry in row 3, column 1. Column 1 (rows 3–5) is $t, \frac{t + 51}{2}, 51$, so $t$ is odd. Row 3 (columns 1–4) is $t, 10, 20 - t, 30 - 2t$. Column 4 (all five rows, ending in 36) has $30 - 2t$ in row 3, so its difference is $t + 3$ and its top entry is $24 - 4t > 0$, so $t \le 5$. Row 1 (columns 1–6) starts with 3 and has $24 - 4t$ in column 4, so $3 \mid 21 - 4t$, i.e. $3 \mid t$. Hence $t = 3$: row 3 is $3, 10, 17, 24$, column 1 is $3, 27, 51$, column 4 is $12, 18, 24, 30, 36$, and row 1 is $3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18$. Column 6 runs from 18 to 26: $18, 20, 22, 24, 26$. Column 3 (rows 1–3) is $9, 13, 17$, so row 2 (columns 3–4) is $13, 18$ ✓.
* **Right part.** Let $h$ be the difference of column 8 ($59, 59 + h, \dots, 59 + 4h$). Row 2 (columns 6–9) starts at 20 and has $59 + h$ in column 8, so $h$ is odd; the bottom-right run goes from $59 + 4h$ to 59 in three steps, so $3 \mid h$. Then row 1 (from 59), column 9 (rows 1–3), row 3 (columns 8–11) and column 11 (rows 3–5, ending in 59) must all stay between 1 and 99. Checking the few remaining cases leaves only $h = -9$, with row 2 difference 15 and row 1 difference 12. This gives row 2 $= 20, 35, 50, 65$, column 8 $= 59, 50, 41, 32, 23$, row 1 right $= 59, 71, 83, 95$, row 3 right $= 41, 59, 77, 95$, bottom-right $= 23, 35, 47, 59$, and column 11 (rows 3–5) $= 95, 77, 59$.

The completed grid:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 3 & 6 & 9 & 12 & 15 & 18 & \blacksquare & 59 & 71 & 83 & 95\\\hline \blacksquare & \blacksquare & 13 & 18 & \blacksquare & 20 & 35 & 50 & 65 & \blacksquare & \blacksquare\\\hline 3 & 10 & 17 & 24 & \blacksquare & 22 & \blacksquare & 41 & 59 & 77 & 95\\\hline 27 & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & 30 & \blacksquare & 24 & \blacksquare & 32 & \blacksquare & \blacksquare & 77\\\hline 51 & 46 & 41 & 36 & 31 & 26 & \blacksquare & 23 & 35 & 47 & 59\\\hline\end{array}$$
($\blacksquare$ = shaded cell)

**Check.** Every maximal run of unshaded cells is arithmetic: for example column 8 is $59, 50, 41, 32, 23$ (difference $-9$) and column 9 is $71, 65, 59$; all entries are positive and less than 100.

prompt: Let $A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5$ be a regular pentagon with side length 1. The sides of the pentagon are extended to form the 10-sided polygon shown in bold in the picture. Find the ratio of the area of quadrilateral $A_2A_5B_2B_5$ (shaded in the picture) to the area of the entire 10-sided polygon.

solutions.title: Compare congruent triangles
solutions.body:
The 10-sided polygon is the pentagon plus five "tip" triangles, one on each side. Each tip triangle has base 1 and base angles equal to the exterior angle of the pentagon, $72^\circ$; call its area $T$.

Cut the pentagon along the diagonals $A_2A_5$ and $A_3A_5$ into:
* the triangle $A_5A_1A_2$, area $y$ (two sides 1 with a $108^\circ$ angle);
* the triangle $A_3A_4A_5$, also area $y$ (congruent to the first);
* the triangle $A_2A_3A_5$, area $z$.

**Shaded part:** trapezoid $A_2A_3A_4A_5$ plus the tips on $A_2A_3$ and $A_4A_5$ (points $B_5$, $B_2$ lie on line $A_3A_4$), area $y + z + 2T$.

**Unshaded part:** triangle $A_5A_1A_2$ plus the other three tips, area $y + 3T$.

Now $\angle A_4A_3A_5 = \frac12(180^\circ - 108^\circ) = 36^\circ$, so $\angle A_2A_3A_5 = 108^\circ - 36^\circ = 72^\circ$, and likewise at $A_2$. So triangle $A_2A_3A_5$ is isosceles with base $A_2A_3 = 1$ and base angles $72^\circ$, the same as the tip triangle on $A_2A_3$. Two triangles on the same base with the same base angles are congruent: $z = T$.

Hence shaded $= y + 3T =$ unshaded, and the ratio is $\frac12$.

**Answer: $\frac12$**

solutions.title: Coordinates check
solutions.body:
Place the pentagon with circumradius 1 and $A_1$ at the bottom. The tips $B_5$ and $B_2$ lie on line $A_3A_4$ at height $\cos 36^\circ$, and computing the two areas with the shoelace formula (for example numerically) gives
$$\frac{[A_2A_5B_2B_5]}{[\text{star}]} = 0.5000\ldots,$$
in agreement with the exact answer $\frac12$ found above (the ratio does not depend on the size of the pentagon).

prompt:
Let $a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots$ be a sequence of positive real numbers such that:

(i) For all positive integers $m$ and $n$, we have $a_{mn} = a_ma_n$, and

(ii) There exists a positive real number $B$ such that for all positive integers $m$ and $n$ with $m < n$, we have $a_m < Ba_n$.

Find all possible values of $\log_{2015}(a_{2015}) - \log_{2014}(a_{2014})$.

solutions.title: Monotone and multiplicative means a power
solutions.body:
**The sequence is non-decreasing.** From (i), $a_{n^k} = a_n^k$. For any $n$ and $k$, $n^k < (n+1)^k$, so by (ii)
$$a_n^k = a_{n^k} < Ba_{(n+1)^k} = Ba_{n+1}^k,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad\left(\frac{a_n}{a_{n+1}}\right)^k < B$$
for every $k$; hence $a_n \le a_{n+1}$. Also (i) with $m = 1$ gives $a_1 = 1$.

**Case $a_2 = 1$.** Then $a_{2^k} = 1$ for all $k$, and monotonicity squeezes every $a_n$ between $a_1 = 1$ and $a_{2^k} = 1$, so $a_n = 1$ and both logarithms are 0.

**Case $a_2 = \lambda > 1$.** Fix $n \ge 2$ (so $a_n \ge a_2 > 1$). For large $p$ choose $q$ with $n^q < 2^p \le n^{q+1}$. Monotonicity gives $a_n^q \le \lambda^p \le a_n^{q+1}$. Taking $\log_2$:
$$q\log_2 n < p \le (q+1)\log_2 n,\qquad q\log_2 a_n \le p\log_2\lambda \le (q+1)\log_2 a_n.$$
Dividing (all quantities positive),
$$\frac{q}{q+1}\log_n a_n \le \log_2\lambda \le \frac{q+1}{q}\log_n a_n.$$
As $p \to \infty$, $q \to \infty$, so $\log_n a_n = \log_2\lambda$ for every $n \ge 2$ (i.e. $a_n = n^c$ with $c = \log_2\lambda$).

In both cases $\log_{2015}a_{2015} = \log_{2014}a_{2014}$, so the difference is 0 (and the value 0 does occur, e.g. for $a_n = n$).

**Answer: 0**

prompt: Nine distinct positive integers are arranged in a circle such that the product of any two non-adjacent numbers in the circle is a multiple of $n$ and the product of any two adjacent numbers in the circle is not a multiple of $n$, where $n$ is a fixed positive integer. Find the smallest possible value for $n$.

solutions.title: A prime witness for each adjacent pair
solutions.body:
Write $\nu_p(m)$ for the exponent of the prime $p$ in $m$. Let the numbers be $x_1, \dots, x_9$ around the circle (indices mod 9). For each $i$, $n \nmid x_ix_{i+1}$, so there is a prime $p_i$ with
$$\nu_{p_i}(x_i) + \nu_{p_i}(x_{i+1}) < \nu_{p_i}(n).$$

**No prime witnesses two non-consecutive pairs.** Suppose $p = p_i = p_j$ where the pairs $\{x_i, x_{i+1}\}$ and $\{x_j, x_{j+1}\}$ are disjoint, and let $k = \nu_p(n)$. Adding the two witness inequalities: $\nu_p(x_i) + \nu_p(x_{i+1}) + \nu_p(x_j) + \nu_p(x_{j+1}) < 2k$. But $x_i, x_j$ are non-adjacent and so are $x_{i+1}, x_{j+1}$ (in a 9-cycle with disjoint, non-consecutive pairs), so $\nu_p(x_i) + \nu_p(x_j) \ge k$ and $\nu_p(x_{i+1}) + \nu_p(x_{j+1}) \ge k$ — contradiction.

So each prime is a witness for at most two pairs, and then they are consecutive pairs $i, i+1$ (three pairs would include two disjoint ones).

**A prime used twice divides $n$ squared.** If $p = p_i = p_{i+1}$ and $\nu_p(n) = 1$, then none of $x_i, x_{i+1}, x_{i+2}$ is divisible by $p$; but $x_i, x_{i+2}$ are non-adjacent, so $p \mid n \mid x_ix_{i+2}$ — contradiction. So $p^2 \mid n$.

**Lower bound.** Every witness divides $n$, and the nine pairs use primes with multiplicity at most 2, each prime used twice dividing $n$ to at least the second power. So $n$ is divisible by a product of nine primes, each appearing at most twice. The smallest such product takes the nine smallest entries of $2, 2, 3, 3, 5, 5, 7, 7, 11, 11, \dots$:
$$n \ge 2^2\cdot3^2\cdot5^2\cdot7^2\cdot11 = 485100.$$

**Construction.** With $n = 485100$ take, in order around the circle,
$$\frac{n}{2\cdot11},\ \frac{n}{2^2},\ \frac{n}{2\cdot3},\ \frac{n}{3^2},\ \frac{n}{3\cdot5},\ \frac{n}{5^2},\ \frac{n}{5\cdot7},\ \frac{n}{7^2},\ \frac{n}{7\cdot11}.$$
The product of two of these is $n^2$ divided by the product of their two denominators. For adjacent numbers the denominators share a prime $p$ whose total exponent exceeds $\nu_p(n)$ (e.g. $2\cdot11$ and $2^2$ give $2^3 > 2^2$), so the product is not a multiple of $n$. For non-adjacent numbers the denominators multiply to a divisor of $n$, so the product is a multiple of $n$. The nine numbers are distinct.

**Answer: 485100** ($= 2^2\cdot3^2\cdot5^2\cdot7^2\cdot11$)

prompt: A finite set $S$ of unit squares is chosen out of a large grid of unit squares. The squares of $S$ are tiled with isosceles right triangles of hypotenuse 2 so that the triangles do not overlap each other, do not extend past $S$, and all of $S$ is fully covered by the triangles. Additionally, the hypotenuse of each triangle lies along a grid line, and the vertices of the triangles lie at the corners of the squares. Show that the number of triangles must be a multiple of 4.
answer: Treat each hypotenuse as a mirror and shoot a laser through the tiles diagonally; it travels in a closed loop through whole squares. Counting the squares by direction (NW, NE, SW, SE) gives $a = b = c = d$, so each loop covers $4a$ squares ($= 4a$ triangles, as each triangle has area 1). Remove loops one by one.

solutions.title: Laser loops
solutions.body:
Each triangle has legs $\sqrt2$ and area 1, so the number of triangles equals the number of unit squares in $S$. Each triangle consists of two half-squares (cut by a diagonal), each having its right angle at the midpoint $M$ of the triangle's hypotenuse, which is a grid point.

**The laser.** Treat every hypotenuse as a two-sided mirror and every leg as glass. Start a laser at the midpoint $M$ of some hypotenuse, heading into one half of its triangle along the diagonal of that unit square perpendicular to the cut. It crosses the square through its centre and arrives at the opposite corner of the square. The other half of this square belongs to a tile whose hypotenuse midpoint is exactly that corner, so the laser hits that tile's mirror at $45^\circ$, reflects, and crosses the next square. So the laser moves from square to square, crossing each visited square along a diagonal.

Since there are finitely many squares and the motion is reversible, the path is a closed loop, and it never crosses a square twice: crossing a square in the opposite direction would force the loop to be its own reverse, which needs a perpendicular reflection, and that never happens. Each tile it meets is crossed in both of its halves (in through one, reflect, out through the other), so the loop consists of whole squares and whole tiles.

**Counting.** Let $a, b, c, d$ be the numbers of squares crossed going NW, NE, SW, SE. Each crossing moves the laser one unit vertically and one unit horizontally, and the loop closes up:
* north = south: $a + b = c + d$;
* west = east: $a + c = b + d$;
* a reflection in a horizontal or vertical mirror turns NW/SE travel into NE/SW travel and vice versa, so the two kinds alternate: $a + d = b + c$.

Adding the first two equations gives $a = d$; the first and third give $a = c$; the last two give $a = b$. So the loop crosses $4a$ squares, i.e. it uses $4a$ whole tiles.

**Finish.** Remove the tiles of this loop. What remains is again a set of squares tiled according to the rules, so we repeat. Each loop removes a multiple of 4 tiles, so the total number of triangles is a multiple of 4. ∎

prompt:
Fill in the spaces of the grid below with positive integers so that in each $2 \times 2$ square with top left number $a$, top right number $b$, bottom left number $c$, and bottom right number $d$, either $a + d = b + c$ or $ad = bc$.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 3 & 9 & \phantom{00} & \phantom{00} & \phantom{00}\\\hline & 11 & & 7 & 2\\\hline 10 & & & & 16\\\hline 15 & & & & \\\hline 20 & 36 & & & 32\\\hline\end{array}$$

You do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible; you merely need to find an answer that satisfies the constraints above.

solutions.title: Columns increase; use divisibility to pick the rule
solutions.body:
**Columns increase.** In a $2\times2$ square, if $a < c$ then $b < d$ under either rule ($d = b + (c - a)$ or $d = b\cdot\frac ca$). Since $9 < 11$ in column 2, every number in row 1 is less than the one below it, and similarly for the other pairs of rows ($2 < 16$ in column 5; $10 < 15 < 20$ in column 1). The implication also runs right-to-left, since both rules are symmetric, so **every column increases downward**.

**Choosing the rule.** For a square with three entries known, the fourth is $b + c - a$ (additive) or $\frac{bc}{a}$ (multiplicative), and the multiplicative option only exists when $a \mid bc$. For example, in rows 4–5, columns 1–2: $15, x / 20, 36$ gives $x = 31$ or $x = 27$. Working through the grid with these two options and the increasing columns, trial and error quickly settles every square:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 3 & 9 & 12 & 6 & 1\\\hline 5 & 11 & 14 & 7 & 2\\\hline 10 & 22 & 28 & 21 & 16\\\hline 15 & 27 & 33 & 26 & 21\\\hline 20 & 36 & 44 & 37 & 32\\\hline\end{array}$$

**Check** (each $2\times2$ square, rule used): e.g. $3, 9 / 5, 11$: $3 + 11 = 9 + 5$; $9, 12 / 11, 14$: additive; $12, 6 / 14, 7$: $12\cdot7 = 6\cdot14$; $6, 1 / 7, 2$: additive; $5, 11 / 10, 22$: $5\cdot22 = 11\cdot10$; $14, 7 / 28, 21$: additive; $7, 2 / 21, 16$: additive; $15, 27 / 20, 36$: $15\cdot36 = 27\cdot20$; $26, 21 / 37, 32$: additive. All 16 squares satisfy one of the rules, and a computer search confirms this is the only solution.

prompt:
Suppose $a$, $b$, and $c$ are distinct positive real numbers such that
$$\begin{aligned} abc &= 1000,\\ bc(1 - a) + a(b + c) &= 110.\end{aligned}$$
If $a < 1$, show that $10 < c < 100$.
answer: Adding gives $ab + bc + ca = 1110$, so $a, b, c$ are roots of $f(x) = x^3 - dx^2 + 1110x - 1000$; compare with $g(x) = (x-1)(x-10)(x-100) = x^3 - 111x^2 + 1110x - 1000$: $g - f = (d - 111)x^2$, and $g(a) < 0$ forces $g(b), g(c) < 0$, so $b, c \in (0,1)\cup(10,100)$, and $bc > 1000$ rules out $(0, 1)$.

solutions.title: Compare with $(x-1)(x-10)(x-100)$
solutions.body:
Expanding the second equation, $bc - abc + ab + ac = 110$; adding $abc = 1000$ gives
$$ab + bc + ca = 1110.$$
So $a, b, c$ are the roots of
$$f(x) = (x - a)(x - b)(x - c) = x^3 - dx^2 + 1110x - 1000,\qquad d = a + b + c.$$
Compare with
$$g(x) = (x - 1)(x - 10)(x - 100) = x^3 - 111x^2 + 1110x - 1000.$$
Then $g(x) - f(x) = (d - 111)x^2$.

Since $0 < a < 1$, all three factors of $g(a)$ are negative, so $g(a) < 0$. As $f(a) = 0$, $(d - 111)a^2 = g(a) < 0$, so $d < 111$. Hence for every $x \ne 0$, $g(x) - f(x) < 0$; in particular
$$g(b) = g(b) - f(b) < 0,\qquad g(c) = g(c) - f(c) < 0.$$
For positive $x$, $g(x) < 0$ exactly when $0 < x < 1$ or $10 < x < 100$. So $b, c \in (0, 1) \cup (10, 100)$.

Finally $bc = \frac{1000}{a} > 1000$. If $c < 1$ then $b > 1000$, impossible; so $c > 10$ and therefore $10 < c < 100$ (and likewise for $b$). ∎

prompt: Let $P$ be a convex $n$-gon in the plane with vertices labeled $V_1, \dots, V_n$ in counterclockwise order. A point $Q$ not outside $P$ is called a *balancing point* of $P$ if, when the triangles $QV_1V_2, QV_2V_3, \dots, QV_{n-1}V_n, QV_nV_1$ are alternately colored blue and green, the total areas of the blue and green regions are the same. Suppose $P$ has exactly one balancing point. Show that the balancing point must be a vertex of $P$.
answer: $f(Q) = \sum (-1)^{i-1}[QV_iV_{i+1}]$ is an affine function of $Q$ on $P$, so its zero set in $P$ is empty, all of $P$, or the intersection of a line with $P$; a line meeting a convex polygon in exactly one point meets it at a vertex.

solutions.title: The difference of areas is affine
solutions.body:
For $Q$ in $P$ let
$$f(Q) = [QV_1V_2] - [QV_2V_3] + [QV_3V_4] - \dots + (-1)^{n-1}[QV_nV_1],$$
(blue minus green). $Q$ is a balancing point iff $f(Q) = 0$.

**$f$ is affine.** For $Q$ in the convex polygon, $Q$ lies on the inner side of each edge $V_iV_{i+1}$, so $[QV_iV_{i+1}] = \frac12|V_iV_{i+1}|\cdot\operatorname{dist}(Q, \text{line } V_iV_{i+1})$, and this distance is an affine function of the coordinates of $Q$ on the inner side. Hence $f(Q) = \alpha x + \beta y + \gamma$ on $P$ for some constants.

**Zero set.** If $\alpha = \beta = 0$, then either no point or every point of $P$ is balancing; neither gives exactly one. Otherwise $\{f = 0\}$ is a line $\ell$, and the balancing points are exactly the points of $\ell \cap P$. This is a convex set, a single point by assumption. If $\ell$ passed through an interior point of $P$, it would contain a whole small segment of $P$ around that point. So $\ell$ meets $P$ only in boundary points: $\ell$ is a supporting line, and $\ell \cap P$ is either an edge or a vertex. An edge has more than one point, so $\ell \cap P$ is a single vertex.

Hence the unique balancing point is a vertex of $P$. ∎

*(The situation really occurs: the official solution notes that the hexagon with vertices $(0,0), (0,2), (1,10), (3,10), (4, \frac{14}3), (4, \frac83)$ has exactly one balancing point, the vertex $(0,0)$: its triangles have areas $0, 1, 10, 13, 4, 0$ and $0 - 1 + 10 - 13 + 4 - 0 = 0$.)*

prompt:
Several players try out for the USAMTS basketball team, and they all have integer heights and weights when measured in centimeters and pounds, respectively. In addition, they all weigh less in pounds than they are tall in centimeters. All of the players weigh at least 190 pounds and are at most 197 centimeters tall, and there is exactly one player with every possible height-weight combination.

The USAMTS wants to field a competitive team, so there are some strict requirements.

(i) If person $P$ is on the team, then anyone who is at least as tall and at most as heavy as $P$ must also be on the team.

(ii) If person $P$ is on the team, then no one whose weight is the same as $P$'s height can also be on the team.

Assuming the USAMTS team can have any number of members (including zero), how many different basketball teams can be constructed?

solutions.title: Thresholds in each weight class
solutions.body:
The players are the pairs $(w, h)$ with $190 \le w < h \le 197$ (weight $w$, height $h$), i.e. 28 players.

**Shape of a team.** For a weight $w$, if $(w, h)$ is on the team then by (i) so is every $(w, h')$ with $h' \ge h$. So the team's players of weight $w$ are all those with height $\ge t_w$, for a threshold $t_w$ (or none). If weight class $w$ is used and $w' < w$, then $(w', t_w)$ is a player (since $t_w > w > w'$) who is at least as tall and lighter, so class $w'$ is used too, with $t_{w'} \le t_w$. Hence the used weights are $190, 191, \dots, 189 + j$ for some $0 \le j \le 7$, with
$$t_{190} \le t_{191} \le \dots \le t_{189+j} \le 197,$$
and conversely any such thresholds satisfy (i).

**Condition (ii).** The heights on the team are exactly $t_{190}, \dots, 197$ (class 190 has the smallest threshold), and the weights on the team are $190, \dots, 189 + j$. Condition (ii) says these sets are disjoint, i.e. $t_{190} \ge 190 + j$. (This also guarantees $t_w > w$ for each used $w$.)

**Count.** For fixed $j$ we need non-decreasing sequences of length $j$ with values in $\{190 + j, \dots, 197\}$, a set of $8 - j$ values. There are $\binom{(8 - j) + j - 1}{j} = \binom{7}{j}$ of them. So the number of teams is
$$\sum_{j=0}^{7}\binom7j = 2^7 = 128.$$

**Answer: 128**

solutions.title: Lattice paths (official idea)
solutions.body:
Plot players as lattice points (weight, height) in the triangle $190 \le x < y \le 197$. Rule (i) says a team is closed under moving up and to the left. Rule (ii) says that if the shortest team member of weight 190 has height $190 + m$, no one of weight $\ge 190 + m$ is on the team.

Record the team by the lowest chosen point $p_k$ in each used column $x = 190 + k$. These points form an up-right path from $p_0$ that ends, after extending it to height 198, at $(189 + m, 198)$. Such a path has $m - 1$ steps right and $7 - (m - 1)$ steps up, so there are $\binom{7}{m-1}$ teams for each $m = 1, \dots, 7$. Adding the empty team:
$$1 + \sum_{m=1}^{7}\binom{7}{m-1} = 1 + (2^7 - 1) = 128.$$
A direct computer enumeration also gives 128.

**Answer: 128**

prompt:
Find all positive integers $n$ that have distinct positive divisors $d_1, d_2, \dots, d_k$, where $k > 1$, that are in arithmetic progression and
$$n = d_1 + d_2 + \dots + d_k.$$
Note that $d_1, d_2, \dots, d_k$ do not have to be all the divisors of $n$.
answer: Exactly the positive multiples of 6 ($n = 6m$ via $m + 2m + 3m$).

solutions.title: Reduce to coprime terms
solutions.body:
**Multiples of 6 work:** $n = 6m$ has divisors $m, 2m, 3m$ in arithmetic progression with sum $6m$.

**Nothing else works.** Suppose $d_1 < d_2 < \dots < d_k$ ($k \ge 2$) are divisors of $n$ in arithmetic progression with sum $n$. Let $g = \gcd(d_1, \dots, d_k)$; then $\frac{d_i}{g}$ are divisors of $\frac ng$ in arithmetic progression with sum $\frac ng$. So it suffices to show that when the $d_i$ have no common factor, $n = 6$ (then the original $n = 6g$).

* *Consecutive terms are coprime:* a common divisor $r$ of $d_i, d_{i+1}$ divides the common difference, hence every term, so $r = 1$.
* *$k = 2$ is impossible:* $n = d_1 + d_2$ with $d_1 < d_2$ gives $\frac n2 < d_2 < n$, but a proper divisor of $n$ is at most $\frac n2$.
* *$k \ge 3$:* $d_{k-1}$ and $d_k$ are coprime divisors of $n$, so $d_{k-1}d_k \mid n$ and $n \ge d_{k-1}d_k \ge k\,d_{k-1}$ (as $d_k \ge k$ for $k$ distinct positive integers). For $k \ge 3$, $d_{k-1}$ is at least the average $\frac nk$ of the progression, so $k\,d_{k-1} \ge n$. Hence all inequalities are equalities: $d_{k-1}$ equals the average, which for an arithmetic progression happens only when $k = 3$, and $d_k = k = 3$. So $(d_1, d_2, d_3) = (1, 2, 3)$ and $n = 6$.

**Answer: all positive multiples of 6.** ∎

prompt:
In the $6\times 8$ grid below (rows listed from top to bottom, blank squares shown as $\cdot$), the shortest path through unit squares between the pair of 2's has length 2.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&6&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\\hline \cdot&10&1&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\\hline \cdot&\cdot&\cdot&2&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&8\\\hline \cdot&5&\cdot&\cdot&2&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\\hline \cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&7&9&\cdot\\\hline \cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&3&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\\hline\end{array}$$

Fill in some of the unit squares in the grid so that

(i) exactly half of the squares in each row and column contain a number,

(ii) each of the numbers 1 through 12 appears exactly twice, and

(iii) for $n = 1, 2, \ldots, 12$, the shortest path between the pair of $n$'s has length exactly $n$.

You do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible; you merely need to find an answer that satisfies the constraints above.

solutions.title: Deduction
solutions.body:
Write $(r,c)$ for the square in row $r$ (from the top) and column $c$ (from the left). The length of the shortest path between two squares is $|r_1-r_2|+|c_1-c_2|$. By (i), every row ends up with exactly 4 numbers and every column with exactly 3.

**The 12's and the 10.** The only pairs of squares at distance $5+7=12$ are the two pairs of opposite corners. The only square at distance 10 from the given 10 at $(2,2)$ is $(6,8)$ (we need $|r-2|\le 4$ and $|c-2|\le 6$ to add up to 10). So $(6,8)=10$, and the 12's go in the other two corners $(1,8)$ and $(6,1)$.

**The 11's.** Two squares at distance 11 differ by $5$ rows and $6$ columns, or by $4$ rows and $7$ columns; either way one of them is a corner. The only free corner is $(1,1)$, so one 11 is there, and the other is at $(6,7)$ or $(5,8)$. Column 8 already holds $12, 8, 10$, so the 11 is at $(6,7)$. Row 6 now holds $12,3,11,10$ and is full.

**The 7, 8, 9.** The squares at distance 7 from the 7 at $(5,6)$ that are still allowed are $(3,1)$ and $(1,3)$. The second 8 (distance 8 from $(3,8)$) can only go in $(4,1)$, $(6,3)$ or $(5,2)$, and $(6,3)$ is excluded because row 6 is full. The second 9 (distance 9 from $(5,7)$) can only go in $(2,1)$ or $(1,2)$. So the 8 and the 9 both go in columns 1 and 2, which together already contain 11, 12, 10, 5; after placing them, columns 1 and 2 hold 3 numbers each. Hence the 7 cannot go in column 1, so $(1,3)=7$. Row 1 is now full ($11,7,6,12$), so the 9 is at $(2,1)$; column 1 is then full, so the 8 is at $(5,2)$.

**The rest.** The second 6 (distance 6 from $(1,5)$) is forced to $(5,3)$, which fills row 5 ($8,6,7,9$). Column 3 is now full ($7,1,6$), so the second 1, which must be next to $(2,3)$, is at $(2,4)$; this fills row 2 ($9,10,1,1$). The numbers still to place are a 5, a 3 and two 4's. Columns 1, 2, 3, 5 and 8 are full, so the two missing numbers of row 3 go in $(3,6)$ and $(3,7)$. Neither is at distance 3 from the 3 at $(6,5)$, and the two 4's cannot both be there, so these squares hold the 5 and one 4. The 5 must be at distance 5 from $(4,2)$, so $(3,6)=5$ and $(3,7)=4$. Column 7 is now full, so the last two numbers go in $(4,4)$ and $(4,6)$; the 4 needs distance 4 from $(3,7)$, so $(4,4)=4$ and $(4,6)=3$.

**Check.** Rows contain 4 numbers each and columns 3 each. Distances: 1's $(2,3),(2,4)$: 1; 2's $(3,4),(4,5)$: 2; 3's $(4,6),(6,5)$: 3; 4's $(3,7),(4,4)$: 4; 5's $(3,6),(4,2)$: 5; 6's $(1,5),(5,3)$: 6; 7's $(1,3),(5,6)$: 7; 8's $(3,8),(5,2)$: 8; 9's $(2,1),(5,7)$: 9; 10's $(2,2),(6,8)$: 10; 11's $(1,1),(6,7)$: 11; 12's $(1,8),(6,1)$: 12. Every step above was forced, so this is the only solution.

prompt:
A net for a polyhedron is cut along an edge to give two pieces. For example, we may cut a cube net along the red edge to form two pieces as shown.

Are there two distinct polyhedra for which this process may result in the same two pairs of pieces? If you think the answer is no, prove that no pair of polyhedra can result in the same two pairs of pieces. If you think the answer is yes, prove an example; a clear example will suffice as proof.
answer: Yes. For example, glue a square pyramid with all edges equal to the cube edge onto two **opposite** faces of a cube, or onto two **adjacent** faces. Both polyhedra have nets that, cut along one edge, give the same two pieces: each piece is a domino of two squares with the four triangles of one pyramid attached, as a fan, to a long side of one of the two squares.

solutions.title: Construction
solutions.body:
Take a unit cube and a square pyramid all of whose edges have length 1 (its four lateral faces are equilateral triangles). Gluing such a pyramid onto a face of the cube removes that square face and adds four triangles. Glue pyramids onto two faces of the cube:

- **Polyhedron $A$:** pyramids on two opposite faces (top and bottom);
- **Polyhedron $B$:** pyramids on two adjacent faces (top and front).

These are not congruent: in $A$ each of the four square faces shares an edge with exactly two other square faces, while in $B$ the back face shares edges with three square faces (left, bottom, right). Each has 4 square faces and 8 triangular faces.

**The piece.** Let $T$ be the planar shape formed by two unit squares sharing a side (a domino, drawn vertically), together with a fan of four equilateral triangles: one triangle sits on the outer vertical side of the **upper** square, and the other three triangles follow around the common apex of the fan, each sharing a side with the previous one. (The four triangles of a fan are exactly the lateral faces of one pyramid, unrolled around its apex.) Let $T'$ be the mirror image of $T$, which is the same as $T$ rotated by $180^\circ$ (fan on the outer side of the **lower** square). The cut-out pieces of both nets below are $T$ and $T'$.

What we need for a polyhedron is a split of its faces into two groups, each group consisting of two adjacent squares $P$, $Q$ plus the four triangles of one pyramid whose (removed) base face is adjacent to $P$ along an edge perpendicular to the edge $PQ$. Then the fan of that pyramid can be unfolded hinged on that edge of $P$, giving a copy of $T$ (or $T'$), and the two groups are joined along one more common edge to form a net.

**Polyhedron $A$** (pyramids on top and bottom; squares front $F$, right $R$, back $K$, left $L$). Group 1: squares $F, R$ with the top fan hinged on the top edge of $F$. Group 2: squares $K, L$ with the bottom fan hinged on the bottom edge of $L$. Laying the belt $F, R, K, L$ out in a row with the top fan above $F$ and the bottom fan below $L$ gives a net of $A$; cutting it along the edge $RK$ yields the two pieces. (The top edge of $F$ is perpendicular to the edge $FR$, and the bottom edge of $L$ to the edge $KL$.)

**Polyhedron $B$** (pyramids on top and front; squares left $L$, back $K$, bottom $D$, right $R$). The top face is adjacent to both $L$ and $K$, and the front face is adjacent to both $D$ and $R$. Group 1: squares $L, K$ with the top fan hinged on the top edge of $L$ (perpendicular to the edge $LK$). Group 2: squares $R, D$ with the front fan hinged on the front edge of $D$ (perpendicular to the edge $RD$). The two groups are joined along the common edge of $K$ and $D$ (the back bottom edge of the cube), which unfolds to a net of $B$; cutting along that edge yields the two pieces.

In both cases each piece is a domino with a fan of four triangles attached to a long side of one end square, and the fan can be unrolled in the same direction in both cases, so the two pieces from $A$ and the two pieces from $B$ are the same pair $T$, $T'$ (up to rotation and reflection). Hence two distinct polyhedra can produce the same two pieces.

prompt:
For all positive integers $n$, show that
$$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k\cdot k!\cdot\binom{n}{k}}{n^k} = 1.$$
answer: Proof: the sum of the last $r+1$ terms equals $\dfrac{n!}{r!\,n^{n-r-1}}$ (induction on $r$), so the full sum is $n$. Alternatively, the terms divided by $n$ are the probabilities that the first repeat in rolls of an $n$-sided die happens on roll $k+1$.

solutions.title: Induction on tail sums
solutions.body:
Fix $n$ and write
$$a_k = \frac{k\cdot k!\binom{n}{k}}{n^k} = \frac{k\cdot n!}{(n-k)!\,n^k}.$$
For $0\le r\le n-1$ let $S_r = a_{n-r} + a_{n-r+1} + \cdots + a_n$ be the sum of the last $r+1$ terms. We claim
$$S_r = \frac{n!}{r!\,n^{\,n-r-1}}.$$

For $r=0$: $S_0 = a_n = \dfrac{n\cdot n!}{n^n} = \dfrac{n!}{0!\,n^{n-1}}$.

If the claim holds for $r = m-1$ (where $1\le m\le n-1$), then
$$S_m = S_{m-1} + a_{n-m} = \frac{n!}{(m-1)!\,n^{n-m}} + \frac{(n-m)\,n!}{m!\,n^{n-m}} = \frac{n!\,\big(m + (n-m)\big)}{m!\,n^{n-m}} = \frac{n!}{m!\,n^{\,n-m-1}}.$$

Taking $r = n-1$ gives $\sum_{k=1}^n a_k = S_{n-1} = \dfrac{n!}{(n-1)!\,n^0} = n$, and dividing by $n$ gives the identity.

solutions.title: Probability
solutions.body:
Roll a fair $n$-sided die repeatedly until some number appears for the second time.

The first $k$ rolls are all distinct in $k!\binom nk$ of the $n^k$ equally likely sequences (choose which $k$ values appear, then their order). Given that, the $(k+1)$st roll repeats one of them with probability $\frac kn$. So the probability that the first repeat happens on roll $k+1$ is
$$\frac kn\cdot\frac{k!\binom nk}{n^k} = \frac{k\cdot k!\binom nk}{n^{k+1}}.$$
These events for $k=1,\ldots,n$ are disjoint, and one of them must occur, because by the pigeonhole principle $n+1$ rolls of an $n$-sided die always contain a repeat. Hence
$$\sum_{k=1}^n \frac{k\cdot k!\binom nk}{n^{k+1}} = 1,$$
which is the required identity after taking a factor $\frac1n$ out of the sum.

prompt: Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$, $P(a+b) - P(b)$ is a multiple of $P(a)$.
answer: $P(x) = c$ or $P(x) = cx$, where $c$ is any integer.

solutions.title: Comparing leading terms
solutions.body:
**These work.** If $P(x) = c$ then $P(a+b)-P(b) = 0$, a multiple of $c$. If $P(x)=cx$ then $P(a+b)-P(b) = ca = P(a)$.

**No others.** Suppose $P$ works and $\deg P = d \ge 1$. Fix an integer $b$ and let
$$H(x) = P(x+b) - P(b), \qquad r(x) = H(x) - P(x).$$
$H$ has the same degree $d$ and the same leading coefficient as $P$, so $\deg r < d$ (or $r = 0$). For every integer $a$, $P(a)$ divides $H(a)$ and $P(a)$, hence divides $r(a)$. Since $\deg r < \deg P$, we have $|r(a)| < |P(a)|$ for all sufficiently large integers $a$, and a multiple of $P(a)$ smaller in absolute value than $P(a)$ must be $0$. So $r(a) = 0$ for infinitely many $a$, and the polynomial $r$ is identically zero. Therefore
$$P(x+b) = P(x) + P(b) \quad\text{for all } x \text{ and all integers } b.$$

Taking $x = b = 0$ gives $P(0) = 2P(0)$, so $P(0)=0$. Taking $b=1$ gives $P(x+1) = P(x) + P(1)$, so by induction $P(k) = kP(1)$ for every positive integer $k$. The polynomials $P(x)$ and $P(1)\,x$ agree at infinitely many points, so $P(x) = cx$ with $c = P(1)$, an integer.

Hence the solutions are the constant polynomials $P(x)=c$ and the linear polynomials $P(x)=cx$, $c\in\mathbb Z$.

prompt:
Let $n > 1$ be an even positive integer. A $2n \times 2n$ grid of unit squares is given, and it is partitioned into $n^2$ contiguous $2 \times 2$ blocks of unit squares. A subset $S$ of the unit squares satisfies the following properties:

(i) For any pair of squares $A$, $B$ in $S$, there is a sequence of squares in $S$ that starts with $A$, ends with $B$, and has any two consecutive elements sharing a side; and

(ii) In each of the $2 \times 2$ blocks of squares, at least one of the four squares is in $S$.

An example for $n = 2$ is shown, with the squares of $S$ shaded and the four $2\times 2$ blocks of squares outlined in bold.

In terms of $n$, what is the minimum possible number of elements in $S$?

solutions.title: Lower bound and construction
solutions.body:
Write $n = 2k$; we show the minimum is $6k^2 - 2 = \frac32 n^2 - 2$.

Place the grid with corners at $(0,0)$ and $(4k,4k)$. The blocks are $[2a,2a+2]\times[2b,2b+2]$. Call the $(2k+1)^2$ lattice points with both coordinates even the **block corners**. Every unit square $[x,x+1]\times[y,y+1]$ has exactly one corner with both coordinates even; call it $\varphi$ of the square. It is a corner of the block containing the square, and the four squares of a block are sent by $\varphi$ to the four different corners of that block.

**Lemma.** In a $(2k+1)\times(2k+1)$ grid of cells, let $U$ be a set of $s$ cells, connected through shared sides, such that every $2\times 2$ subgrid contains a cell of $U$. Then $s \ge 2k^2 - 1$.

*Proof.* The $(2k)^2$ interior lattice points of this grid are each the center of a $2\times 2$ subgrid, so each is a corner of some cell of $U$. Order the cells of $U$ so that each cell after the first shares a side with an earlier one (possible because $U$ is connected). The first cell has 4 corners, and each later cell shares a side, hence two corners, with an earlier cell, so it contributes at most 2 new corners. Thus the cells of $U$ have at most $4 + 2(s-1) = 2s+2$ corners in total, and $2s+2 \ge 4k^2$. $\blacksquare$

**Lower bound.** Let $S$ satisfy (i) and (ii), and let $V = \varphi(S)$, a set of block corners. Think of the block corners as the cells of a $(2k+1)\times(2k+1)$ grid (two block corners are adjacent if they differ by 2 in one coordinate). The four corners of a block form a $2\times 2$ subgrid, and by (ii) the block contains a square of $S$, whose $\varphi$ is one of these corners; so every $2\times2$ subgrid meets $V$.

If two squares of $S$ share a side and lie in **different** blocks, they have the same $\varphi$ (the shared side lies on a block boundary line, and both squares touch the same even–even endpoint of it). If they share a side and lie in the **same** block, their $\varphi$'s are two adjacent corners of that block; join these two corners by an edge, forming a graph $G$ on $V$. Walking along a side-connected chain of squares of $S$ (property (i)), $\varphi$ either stays put or moves along an edge of $G$, so $G$ is connected. In particular $V$ is connected as a set of cells, and the lemma gives $|V| \ge 2k^2 - 1$.

Choose a spanning tree of $G$; it has $|V| - 1 \ge 2k^2 - 2$ edges. Each tree edge comes from a pair of squares of $S$ in one block; assign the edge to that block (choosing one block if there are several). Suppose a block gets $t$ tree edges. These edges join corners of this block and contain no cycle, so they touch at least $t+1$ distinct corners, and each of those corners is $\varphi$ of a different square of $S$ in this block. So the block contains at least $t+1$ squares of $S$, and at least 1 if $t=0$ by (ii). Summing over the $4k^2$ blocks,
$$|S| \ge 4k^2 + (2k^2 - 2) = 6k^2 - 2.$$

**Construction.** Number the rows and columns $1$ to $4k$ and write $(i,j)$ for row $i$, column $j$. Shade:

- the $4k-2$ squares $(i,2)$ for $2 \le i \le 4k-1$;
- for each $m = 1, \ldots, k$, the $4k-3$ squares $(4m-1, j)$ for $3 \le j \le 4k-1$;
- for each $m = 1, \ldots, k$, the $2k-1$ squares $(4m-2, j)$ for $j = 3, 5, 7, \ldots, 4k-1$.

The total is $(4k-2) + k(4k-3) + k(2k-1) = 6k^2 - 2$. It is connected: the rows $4m-1$ hang off column 2, and each square $(4m-2, j)$ sits directly above $(4m-1, j)$. Every block is hit: the blocks in rows $4m-3, 4m-2$ meet row $4m-2$, which contains $(4m-2,2)$ and a square in each pair of columns $\{3,4\},\{5,6\},\ldots,\{4k-1,4k\}$; the blocks in rows $4m-1, 4m$ meet row $4m-1$, which contains columns $2, 3, \ldots, 4k-1$. (For $k=1$ this is the central $2\times 2$ square of the $4\times 4$ grid.)

Hence the minimum is $6k^2 - 2 = \frac32 n^2 - 2$.

*Note.* The official solution's text describes the last family of squares with a misprinted formula; the description above matches the official diagram and was checked by computer for $k = 1, \ldots, 5$.

prompt:
Fill in each space of the grid with either a 0 or a 1 so that all 16 strings of four consecutive numbers across and down are distinct.

You do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible; you merely need to find an answer that satisfies the constraints above.

solutions.title: Deduction
solutions.body:
The grid has 8 rows of length 4 and 8 columns of length 4, so the 16 strings must be exactly the 16 binary strings of length 4. Number the columns $1$ to $9$ from the left and the rows $1$ to $9$ from the top (row 1 is the single square at the top left, row 9 is the bottom row, columns $6$–$9$).

**Parity.** Among all 16 strings of length 4 there are exactly 32 zeros. Every square lies in one across string and one down string, except the top-left square (only in column 1) and the bottom-right square (only in row 9). The top-left square is a given 0, so if the bottom-right square were 1, the total number of zeros counted over all strings would be $2\cdot(\text{zeros}) - 1$, which is odd. Hence the bottom-right square is $0$.

**1111 and 0000.** Every across and down string other than column 7 now contains a 0 (given or just found), so column 7 must be $1111$. The string $0000$ must then be column 5 or column 6, the only other strings with no given 1. If column 5 were $0000$, then row 3 ($0\,?\,1\,?$), row 5 ($0\,?\,1\,?$) and rows 6, 7, 8 (first square 0 from column 5, third square 1 from column 7) would give five strings of the form $0x1x$, but only four such strings exist. So column 6 is $0000$.

**The pattern $0x1x$.** Now rows 3, 5, 8 and 9 are of the form $0x1x$ (row 9 is $0\,?\,1\,0$), so no other string may have this form. This forces, in turn:

- the third square of column 3 (row 4) is 0, since column 3 is $0\,1\,?\,?$;
- the first squares of rows 6 and 7 (column 5) are 1, since these rows are $?\,0\,1\,?$ and $?\,0\,1\,0$;
- the top square of column 5 (row 5) is 1, since column 5 is $?\,1\,1\,0$. So column 5 is $1110$ and row 7 is $1010$.

**The rest.**

- Row 6 is $1\,0\,1\,?$, and $1010$ is used, so row 6 is $1011$.
- Column 8 is $1\,0\,?\,1$, and $1011$ is used, so column 8 is $1001$ and row 8 is $0010$.
- Column 2 is $1\,?\,?\,0$; since $1010$ and $1110$ are used, its third square (row 4) is 0. So row 4 is $1000$, and then column 2 is $1100$.
- Row 3 is $0\,1\,1\,?$ and row 9 is $0110$, so row 3 is $0111$.
- Row 5 is $0\,?\,1\,1$ and $0111$ is used, so row 5 is $0011$ and column 3 is $0100$.
- Row 2 is $?\,1\,0\,?$. If its last square were 0, row 2 would be $x100$, but $0100$ and $1100$ are both used. So it is 1, and column 4 is $1101$.
- At this point exactly seven strings beginning with 0 are present, so the first square of row 2 is 0. Row 2 is $0101$ and column 1 is $0001$.

This is the grid in the answer, and since every step was forced it is the only solution (an exhaustive computer search confirms this).

**Check.** Across: $0101, 0111, 1000, 0011, 1011, 1010, 0010, 0110$. Down: column 1 $0001$, column 2 $1100$, column 3 $0100$, column 4 $1101$, column 5 $1110$, column 6 $0000$, column 7 $1111$, column 8 $1001$. These are all 16 strings of length 4, each once.

prompt:
Fames is playing a computer game with falling two-dimensional blocks. The playing field is 7 units wide and infinitely tall with a bottom border. Initially the entire field is empty. Each turn, the computer gives Fames a $1 \times 3$ solid rectangular piece of three unit squares. Fames must decide whether to orient the piece horizontally or vertically and which column(s) the piece should occupy (3 consecutive columns for horizontal pieces, 1 column for vertical pieces). Once he confirms his choice, the piece is dropped straight down into the playing field in the selected columns, stopping all three of the piece's squares as soon as the piece hits either the bottom of the playing field or any square from another piece. All of the pieces must be contained completely inside the playing field after dropping and cannot partially occupy columns.

If at any time a row of 7 spaces is all filled with squares, Fames scores a point.

Unfortunately, Fames is playing in invisible mode, which prevents him from seeing the state of the playing field or how many points he has, and he has already arbitrarily dropped some number of pieces without remembering what he did with them or how many there were.

For partial credit, find a strategy that will allow Fames to eventually earn at least one more point. For full credit, find a strategy for which Fames can correctly announce "I have earned at least one more point" and know that he is correct.
answer: Drop horizontal pieces in columns 3–5, 1–3, 5–7, then again 3–5, 1–3, 5–7, then one vertical piece in column 4. The last piece always completes a row that was not full before, so Fames can announce the point.

solutions.title: Seven pieces
solutions.body:
Number the columns $1$ to $7$ and let the **height** of a column be the number of the lowest empty row above all its squares (rows numbered $0, 1, 2, \ldots$ from the bottom). A horizontal piece in columns $c, c+1, c+2$ lands in row $\max(h_c, h_{c+1}, h_{c+2})$; a vertical piece in column $c$ occupies rows $h_c, h_c+1, h_c+2$. (Filled rows are not removed; the problem only awards a point.)

**First round.** Drop horizontal pieces $X$ in columns 3–5, then $Y$ in columns 1–3, then $Z$ in columns 5–7. Since $Y$ and $Z$ each share a column with $X$, both land above $X$. Let $y$ and $z$ be their rows. Now columns 1–3 have height $y+1$, columns 5–7 have height $z+1$, and column 4 has height at most $\min(y,z)$, since $X$ is its top square and lies below both. By the left–right symmetry of the strategy we may assume $z \ge y$.

**Second round.** Drop horizontal pieces in columns 3–5, 1–3, 5–7 again.

- The piece in columns 3–5 lands in row $\max(y+1, h_4, z+1) = z+1$.
- The piece in columns 1–3 lands in row $\max(y+1, y+1, z+2) = z+2$.
- The piece in columns 5–7 lands in row $\max(z+2, z+1, z+1) = z+2$.

Now row $z+2$ is filled in columns 1–3 and 5–7, and column 4 has height exactly $z+2$, so square $(z+2, 4)$ is empty and row $z+2$ is not yet complete.

**Last piece.** Drop a vertical piece in column 4. It occupies rows $z+2, z+3, z+4$ of column 4, so row $z+2$ becomes completely filled at this moment. This is a new point, whatever the earlier pieces were (the case $y > z$ is the mirror image).

So after these seven pieces Fames can correctly announce that he has earned at least one more point. (Simply dropping vertical pieces in every column over and over would eventually score, but Fames could never be sure when that had happened.) A computer simulation from thousands of random starting positions confirms the strategy.

prompt: For $n > 1$, let $a_n$ be the number of zeroes that $n!$ ends with when written in base $n$. Find the maximum value of $\dfrac{a_n}{n}$.

solutions.title: Legendre's formula
solutions.body:
**The value $\frac12$ occurs.** In base 2, $2! = 10_2$ ends in one zero, so $a_2 = 1$ and $a_2/2 = \frac12$.

**Upper bound.** The number of trailing zeros of $n!$ in base $n$ is the largest $a$ with $n^a \mid n!$. Let $p$ be a prime dividing $n$, and write $n = p^k m$ with $p \nmid m$. If $n^a \mid n!$ then $p^{ka} \mid n!$, so $ka \le \nu_p(n!)$. By Legendre's formula,
$$\nu_p(n!) = \sum_{j\ge1}\left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^j}\right\rfloor < \sum_{j\ge 1}\frac{n}{p^j} = \frac{n}{p-1}.$$
Therefore
$$\frac{a_n}{n} < \frac{1}{k(p-1)}.$$
If $n$ has an odd prime factor $p$, this gives $\frac{a_n}{n} < \frac1{p-1} \le \frac12$. Otherwise $n = 2^k$; if $k \ge 2$, this gives $\frac{a_n}{n} < \frac1k \le \frac12$. The only remaining case is $n = 2$.

Hence the maximum value of $\frac{a_n}{n}$ is $\frac12$, attained only at $n=2$. (A direct computation for $2 \le n < 400$ agrees.)

prompt: Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with $AB < AC$. Let the angle bisector of $\angle BAC$ meet $BC$ at $D$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. Let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $B$ to $AD$. Extend $BP$ to meet $AM$ at $Q$. Show that $DQ$ is parallel to $AB$.
answer: Proof: with $L = BP\cap AC$ one gets $AL = AB$, and then $\vec{AQ} = \frac{c}{b+c}(\vec{AB}+\vec{AC})$ and $\vec{AD} = \frac{b\,\vec{AB} + c\,\vec{AC}}{b+c}$, so $\vec{QD} = \frac{b-c}{b+c}\vec{AB}$.

solutions.title: Reflection and vectors
solutions.body:
Let $b = AC$ and $c = AB$, so $c < b$. Let line $BP$ meet line $AC$ at $L$.

**$AL = AB$.** In triangles $APB$ and $APL$, the angles at $P$ are right angles, the angles at $A$ are equal because $AP$ bisects $\angle BAC$, and the side $AP$ is shared. So the triangles are congruent, $AL = AB = c$, and $L$ lies on segment $AC$ (as $c < b$). Hence, with vectors from $A$,
$$\vec{AL} = \frac{c}{b}\,\vec{AC}.$$

**Locating $Q$.** Points of line $BL$ are $\vec{AB} + s(\vec{AL} - \vec{AB}) = (1-s)\vec{AB} + \frac{sc}{b}\vec{AC}$, and points of line $AM$ are $\frac u2(\vec{AB} + \vec{AC})$. Since $\vec{AB}$ and $\vec{AC}$ are independent, $Q$ corresponds to $1 - s = \frac u2 = \frac{sc}{b}$, so $s = \frac{b}{b+c}$ and
$$\vec{AQ} = \frac{c}{b+c}\left(\vec{AB} + \vec{AC}\right).$$

**Locating $D$.** By the angle bisector theorem $BD : DC = c : b$, so
$$\vec{AD} = \frac{b\,\vec{AB} + c\,\vec{AC}}{b+c}.$$

**Conclusion.**
$$\vec{QD} = \vec{AD} - \vec{AQ} = \frac{b-c}{b+c}\,\vec{AB},$$
a nonzero multiple of $\vec{AB}$. Therefore $DQ \parallel AB$.

(Equivalently: $PM$ is a midline of triangle $BLC$, so $PM \parallel AC$ and $PM = \frac{b-c}{2}$; then $\frac{MQ}{QA} = \frac{PM}{AL} = \frac{b-c}{2c}$, so $\frac{MQ}{MA} = \frac{b-c}{b+c}$, which equals $\frac{MD}{MB} = \frac{a/2 - ac/(b+c)}{a/2}$ with $a = BC$. The homothety at $M$ with this ratio sends $B \mapsto D$ and $A \mapsto Q$, so $DQ \parallel AB$.)

prompt: Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{100}$ be a sequence of integers. Initially, $a_1 = 1$, $a_2 = -1$ and the remaining numbers are 0. After every second, we perform the following process on the sequence: for $i = 1, 2, \ldots, 99$, replace $a_i$ with $a_i + a_{i+1}$, and replace $a_{100}$ with $a_{100} + a_1$. (All of this is done simultaneously, so each new term is the sum of two terms of the sequence from before any replacements.) Show that for any integer $M$, there is some index $i$ and some time $t$ for which $|a_i| > M$ at time t.
answer: Proof: with $\omega = e^{2\pi i/100}$, the quantity $F_t = \sum_i a_i\omega^i$ at time $t$ equals $(1+\omega^{-1})^t(\omega - \omega^2)$, whose absolute value tends to infinity because $|1+\omega^{-1}| = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{100} > 1$; but $|F_t| \le 100\max_i |a_i|$.

solutions.title: Roots of unity filter
solutions.body:
Take indices modulo 100, so that $a_{101} = a_1$ and the process is: every $a_i$ is replaced by $a_i + a_{i+1}$ for all $i$ simultaneously. Let $\omega = e^{2\pi i/100}$, and at each time $t$ define the complex number
$$F_t = \sum_{i=1}^{100} a_i\,\omega^{i}.$$
Because $\omega^{100} = 1$, the exponent can also be read modulo 100. After one step,
$$F_{t+1} = \sum_{i=1}^{100} (a_i + a_{i+1})\,\omega^{i} = F_t + \omega^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^{100} a_{i+1}\,\omega^{i+1} = (1 + \omega^{-1})\,F_t.$$
Initially $F_0 = \omega - \omega^2 = \omega(1-\omega) \ne 0$. Hence
$$F_t = (1+\omega^{-1})^t\,\omega(1-\omega), \qquad |F_t| = |1+\omega^{-1}|^t\,|1-\omega|.$$
Now $|1 + \omega^{-1}| = |1 + e^{-2\pi i/100}| = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{100} > 1$, so $|F_t| \to \infty$ as $t \to \infty$.

On the other hand, by the triangle inequality, $|F_t| \le \sum_i |a_i| \le 100\max_i |a_i|$ at time $t$. Given $M$, choose $t$ with $|F_t| > 100M$; then some $|a_i| > M$ at time $t$.

*Remark.* The same argument works with 100 replaced by any $N \ge 4$, since then $|1+\omega^{-1}| = 2\cos\frac{\pi}{N} > 1$. For $N = 2$ or $3$ the statement fails: for $N=2$ the sequence becomes $0, 0$ after one step, and for $N=3$ it returns to $1, -1, 0$ every 6 steps.

prompt:
Fill in each cell of the $9\times 9$ grid with one of the numbers 1, 2, or 3. After all numbers are filled in, if a row, column, or any diagonal has a number of cells equal to a multiple of 3, then it must have the same amount of 1's, 2's, and 3's. (There are 10 such diagonals, and they are all marked in the grid by a gray dashed line.) Some numbers have been given to you:

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \phantom{0} & 2 & 1 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline 3 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 2 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 2 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 3 & 2 & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & 2 & 1 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 1 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 3\\\hline 3 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 3 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 3\\\hline 2 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 2 & 3 & \phantom{0}\\\hline 3 & 2 & 3 & 2 & \phantom{0} & 2 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 3\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 3 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 1\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 1 & 3 & \phantom{0}\\\hline\end{array}$$

The 10 marked diagonals are the diagonals (in both directions) of length 3, 6 and 9.

You do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible; you merely need to find an answer that satisfies the constraints above.

solutions.title: Start with the most constrained lines
solutions.body:
Each row and column has 9 cells, so it must contain exactly three 1's, three 2's and three 3's; each marked diagonal of length 3, 6 or 9 must contain one, two or three of each number.

* **Row 7** already shows $3,2,3,2,\_,2,\_,\_,3$: three 3's and three 2's. So its three empty cells (columns 5, 7, 8) are all 1.
* **Column 1** already has 3 (row 2), 3 (row 5), 2 (row 6), 3 (row 7): the 3's are used up, so its other five cells hold three 1's and two 2's.
* Each length-3 diagonal in a corner must be exactly $\{1,2,3\}$, so once two of its cells are known the third is forced.

Continuing to count what each row, column and diagonal still needs gives the completed grid
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 1 & 2 & 1 & 3 & 2 & 3 & 3 & 1 & 2\\\hline 3 & 3 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 2 & 1\\\hline 2 & 3 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 3 & 2 & 1\\\hline 1 & 2 & 1 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 3\\\hline 3 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 3\\\hline 2 & 1 & 3 & 3 & 1 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 2\\\hline 3 & 2 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 1 & 3\\\hline 2 & 1 & 2 & 1 & 3 & 3 & 3 & 2 & 1\\\hline 1 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 3 & 2 & 1 & 3 & 2\\\hline\end{array}$$

**Check.** Every row and every column contains three 1's, three 2's and three 3's, every given number is in place, and each of the 10 marked diagonals (lengths 3, 6, 9, 6, 3 in each direction) contains equally many 1's, 2's and 3's. A computer search confirms that this is the only solution.

**Answer: the grid above.**

prompt:
A *tower of height $h$* is a stack of contiguous rows of squares of height $h$ such that

(i) the bottom row of the tower has $h$ squares,

(ii) each row above the bottom row has one fewer square than the row below it, and within each row the squares are contiguous,

(iii) the squares in any given row all lie directly above a square in the row below.

A tower is called *balanced* if when the squares of the tower are colored black and white in a checkerboard fashion, the number of black squares is equal to the number of white squares. For example, the figure shows a tower of height 5 that is not balanced, since there are 7 white squares and 8 black squares.

How many balanced towers are there of height 2016?

solutions.title: Count row by row
solutions.body:
A row of $k$ squares sits on the row of $k+1$ squares below it, so it is either flush with the left end or flush with the right end of that row: **2 choices** for each of the $h-1$ rows above the bottom.

* A row with an **even** number of squares always has equally many black and white squares.
* A row with an **odd** number of squares has one extra square of the colour of its end squares. Shifting the row by one square swaps the colours, so of the 2 choices for an odd row, exactly one gives an extra black and the other an extra white.

So the tower is balanced exactly when the number of odd rows with an extra black square equals the number with an extra white square.

For $h = 2016$ the row lengths are $1, 2, \dots, 2016$: there are 1008 odd rows and 1008 even rows. The bottom row (2016 squares, even) is fixed; the other 1007 even rows can each be chosen in 2 ways freely, giving $2^{1007}$. Among the 1008 odd rows we must pick 504 to have an extra black square (the rest get an extra white); this choice determines how each odd row is placed, in $\binom{1008}{504}$ ways.

Total: $2^{1007}\binom{1008}{504}$.

**Answer: $2^{1007}\dbinom{1008}{504}$**

prompt: Find all positive integers $n$ for which $(x^n + y^n + z^n)/2$ is a perfect square whenever $x$, $y$, and $z$ are integers such that $x + y + z = 0$.

solutions.title: Test one triple, then prove the survivors work
solutions.body:
**Necessary condition.** Take $x = 2$, $y = z = -1$. Then
$$\frac{x^n+y^n+z^n}{2} = \frac{2^n + 2(-1)^n}{2} = 2^{n-1} + (-1)^n$$
must be a perfect square $m^2$.

* **$n$ even:** $2^{n-1} + 1 = m^2$, so $2^{n-1} = (m-1)(m+1)$. Both factors are powers of 2 differing by 2, so they are 2 and 4: $m = 3$, $2^{n-1} = 8$, $n = 4$.
* **$n$ odd:** $2^{n-1} - 1 = m^2$. $n = 1$ gives $0 = 0^2$. If $n \ge 3$, $n-1$ is even and $(2^{(n-1)/2}-1)(2^{(n-1)/2}+1) = m^2$. The two factors are odd and differ by 2, so they are coprime, hence both are perfect squares. But two positive squares never differ by 2 ($1$ and $3$ are the only candidates below 4 and squares differ by at least 3 after that). Contradiction. (Alternatively: for $n \ge 3$, $2^{n-1}-1 \equiv 3 \pmod 4$, which is never a square.)

So only $n = 1$ and $n = 4$ can work.

**Sufficiency.** For $n = 1$: $(x+y+z)/2 = 0 = 0^2$. For $n = 4$, substitute $z = -(x+y)$:
$$\frac{x^4 + y^4 + (x+y)^4}{2} = x^4 + 2x^3y + 3x^2y^2 + 2xy^3 + y^4 = (x^2 + xy + y^2)^2,$$
a perfect square.

**Answer: $n = 1$ and $n = 4$**

prompt: Find all functions $f(x)$ from nonnegative reals to nonnegative reals such that $f(f(x)) = x^4$ and $f(x) \le Cx^2$ for some constant $C$.
answer: Only $f(x) = x^2$. (If $f(t) = a t^2$ with $a \ne 1$, iterating gives points $t_n$ with $f(t_n) = a^{(-2)^n} t_n^2$, contradicting $f(x) \le Cx^2$.)

solutions.title: Follow the orbit of a bad point
solutions.body:
Clearly $f(x) = x^2$ works: $f(f(x)) = (x^2)^2 = x^4$ and $f(x) \le 1\cdot x^2$. We show it is the only solution.

**$f(0) = 0$:** from $0 \le f(0) \le C\cdot 0 = 0$.

**$f(t) > 0$ for $t > 0$:** if $f(t) = 0$ then $t^4 = f(f(t)) = f(0) = 0$, so $t = 0$.

**$f(t) = t^2$ for $t > 0$:** suppose $f(t) = a t^2$ with $a > 0$, $a \neq 1$. Define $t_0 = t$ and $t_{k+1} = f(t_k)$; all $t_k > 0$. We claim
$$f(t_k) = a^{(-2)^k}\, t_k^2 .$$
For $k = 0$ this is the assumption. If $f(t_k) = a_k t_k^2$ with $a_k = a^{(-2)^k}$, then $t_{k+1} = a_k t_k^2$, so $t_k^4 = t_{k+1}^2/a_k^2$ and
$$f(t_{k+1}) = f(f(t_k)) = t_k^4 = a_k^{-2}\, t_{k+1}^2 = a^{(-2)^{k+1}} t_{k+1}^2.$$

Now if $a > 1$, the exponents $(-2)^k$ for even $k$ tend to $+\infty$, and if $0 < a < 1$, the exponents for odd $k$ tend to $-\infty$; either way $a^{(-2)^k}$ is unbounded. But $f(t_k)/t_k^2 \le C$ for all $k$. Contradiction.

Hence $f(x) = x^2$ for every $x \ge 0$. ∎

**Answer: $f(x) = x^2$**

prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with perimeter $\frac52$ and $AC = BD = 1$. Determine the maximum possible area of $ABCD$.

solutions.title: Varignon rhombus
solutions.body:
Let $P, Q, R, S$ be the midpoints of $AB, BC, CD, DA$. By Varignon's theorem $PQRS$ is a parallelogram with sides $PQ = RS = \frac{AC}{2}$ and $QR = SP = \frac{BD}{2}$, so here all four sides are $\frac12$: $PQRS$ is a **rhombus**, its diagonals $PR$ and $QS$ are perpendicular and bisect each other at a point $O$. Also $[ABCD] = 2[PQRS]$ (the four corner triangles cut off, like $APS$, have a quarter of the area of the triangle $ABD$, etc.).

**Bounding the diagonals.** In vectors, $\vec{PR} = \frac{C + D}{2} - \frac{A + B}{2} = \frac{\vec{AD} + \vec{BC}}{2}$, so $PR \le \frac{AD + BC}{2}$. Similarly $QS \le \frac{AB + CD}{2}$. Adding,
$$PR + QS \le \frac{AB+BC+CD+DA}{2} = \frac54.$$

Let $x = PO = \frac{PR}{2}$ and $y = QO = \frac{QS}{2}$. Then $x + y \le \frac58$, and from the right triangle $POQ$, $x^2 + y^2 = PQ^2 = \frac14$. The rhombus has area $\frac12 PR\cdot QS = 2xy$, and
$$2xy = (x+y)^2 - (x^2+y^2) \le \frac{25}{64} - \frac{16}{64} = \frac{9}{64}.$$
So $[ABCD] = 2[PQRS] \le \frac{9}{32}$.

**Equality.** Take $ABCD$ a rectangle with sides $\frac{5+\sqrt7}{8}$ and $\frac{5-\sqrt7}{8}$: the perimeter is $2\cdot\frac{10}{8} = \frac52$, the diagonal is $\sqrt{\frac{(5+\sqrt7)^2 + (5-\sqrt7)^2}{64}} = \sqrt{\frac{64}{64}} = 1$, and the area is $\frac{25-7}{64} = \frac{9}{32}$.

**Answer: $\frac{9}{32}$**

solutions.title: Aim for 2 shaded cells per line
solutions.body:
Every row and every column must contain the same shaded area $s$, so the total shaded area is $11s$, and it may be at most $\frac{121}{2}$; hence $1 \le s \le 5$. Small regions (single cells, dominoes) are the most flexible, so aim for $s = 2$ using small regions.
