solutions.title: Start at a dead end
solutions.body:
A counter whose row and column contain other counters in only **one** direction can be entered only from that direction, and then it could only be left by reversing. So such a counter must be the first or the last one. There are exactly two such counters: the bottom counter of the long right-hand column (only counters above it) and the lone counter in the second row (its row is otherwise empty and its column has a counter only below it). So the path starts at one and ends at the other.

Starting at the bottom: go up the right-hand column ($1 \to 6$), then left to the next counter in that row ($7$), down ($8$), right along the bottom long row ($9$), and continue, always turning so that no counter is left with all of its row- and column-mates removed (such a counter could never be reached). Following this rule (backing up whenever a choice leads to a stranded counter) gives the order
$$\begin{array}{ccccccccccc}28 & 27 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot\\ \cdot & \cdot & 33 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot\\ \cdot & 26 & \cdot & \cdot & 25 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot\\ 29 & \cdot & \cdot & 16 & \cdot & 15 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot\\ 30 & 31 & 32 & 17 & \cdot & 14 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot\\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 18 & \cdot & 13 & 12 & 11 & 19 & \cdot & \cdot\\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 24 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 23 & \cdot\\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 10 & 20 & \cdot & \cdot\\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 7 & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 6\\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 8 & 9 & 21 & 22 & 5\\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 4\\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 3\\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 2\\ \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & \cdot & 1\end{array}$$
**Check.** Each step moves to the nearest *remaining* counter in a straight line, no step reverses the previous direction, and all $33$ counters are collected. For example $8 \to 9$ moves right along the bottom long row, $9 \to 10$ moves up two rows (the counters in between were already gone or absent), and $32 \to 33$ moves up to the isolated counter in the second row. (A computer search over all starting counters and moves confirms this is the only solution.)

**Answer:** the numbering above.

prompt: Find, with proof, the minimum positive integer $n$ with the following property: for any coloring of the integers $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ using the colors red and blue (that is, assigning the color "red" or "blue" to each integer in the set), there exist distinct integers $a, b, c$ between $1$ and $n$, inclusive, all of the same color, such that $2a + b = c$.

solutions.title: A coloring of 1–14, then two cases for 15
solutions.body:
Call $(a, b, c)$ *good* if $a, b, c$ are distinct, $2a + b = c$, and all three have the same color.

**$n = 14$ is not enough.** Color $1, 2, 3$ red, $4, \dots, 12$ blue, and $13, 14$ red.

* If $a, b \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, then $4 \le 2a + b \le 9$, so $c$ is blue.
* If $a, b \in \{4, \dots, 12\}$, then $2a + b \ge 13$ (as $a \ne b$, the smallest is $2\cdot 4 + 5$), so $c$ is red or larger than $14$.
* If $a$ or $b$ is $13$ or $14$, then $2a + b \ge 15$.
* Mixed pairs $\{a, b\}$ (one from each red block) are both red only if one is in $\{1,2,3\}$ and the other in $\{13, 14\}$, giving $c \ge 15$.

So there is no good triple, and $n \ge 15$.

**Every coloring of $1, \dots, 15$ has a good triple.** Suppose not.

*Case 1: $1$ and $2$ have the same color*, say red. Then in turn:
$4$ blue (from $(1, 2, 4)$), $5$ blue ($(2, 1, 5)$), $13$ red ($(4, 5, 13)$), $15$ blue ($(1, 13, 15)$), $7$ red ($(4, 7, 15)$), $3$ blue ($(2, 3, 7)$), $9$ blue ($(1, 7, 9)$). But now $(3, 9, 15)$ is a blue good triple. Contradiction.

*Case 2: $1$ and $2$ have different colors*, say $1$ red and $2$ blue. If some $x$ with $5 \le x \le 13$ is red, then $x + 2$ is blue (from $(1, x, x+2)$), so $x - 2$ is red (from $(2, x - 2, x + 2)$), and then $(1, x - 2, x)$ is a red good triple. So $5, 6, \dots, 13$ are all blue — but then $(2, 5, 9)$ is a blue good triple. Contradiction.

(A computer check of all $2^{14}$ and $2^{15}$ colorings agrees.)

**Answer: $n = 15$**

prompt: Let $S$ be a subset of $\{1, 2, \dots, 500\}$ such that no two distinct elements of $S$ have a product that is a perfect square. Find, with proof, the maximum possible number of elements in $S$.

solutions.title: One element per squarefree part
solutions.body:
Every positive integer can be written uniquely as $n = f(n)\cdot s^2$ with $f(n)$ squarefree (the *squarefree part*). Then $mn$ is a perfect square if and only if $f(m) = f(n)$: indeed $mn = f(m)f(n)(st)^2$ is a square iff $f(m)f(n)$ is, and a product of two squarefree numbers is a square iff they are equal.

So the elements of $S$ have distinct squarefree parts, each at most $500$. Hence $|S|$ is at most the number $|T|$ of squarefree integers in $\{1, \dots, 500\}$, and $S = T$ itself works (two distinct squarefree numbers have different squarefree parts).

**Counting $T$ by inclusion–exclusion.** A number is not squarefree iff it is divisible by $p^2$ for some prime $p$; the relevant squares are $4, 9, 25, 49, 121, 169, 289, 361$ ($23^2 = 529 > 500$). Products of two of them that are $\le 500$: $36, 100, 196, 225, 484$; no product of three is $\le 500$ ($4\cdot9\cdot25 = 900$). So the number of non-squarefree integers is
$$(125 + 55 + 20 + 10 + 4 + 2 + 1 + 1) - (13 + 5 + 2 + 2 + 1) = 218 - 23 = 194,$$
where $\lfloor 500/36\rfloor = 13$, $\lfloor 500/100 \rfloor = 5$, $\lfloor 500/196\rfloor = 2$, $\lfloor 500/225\rfloor = 2$, $\lfloor 500/484\rfloor = 1$. Therefore $|T| = 500 - 194 = 306$.

**Answer: 306**

prompt:
Let $m, n, k$ be positive integers such that $k \le mn$. Let $S$ be the set consisting of the $(m + 1)$-by-$(n + 1)$ rectangular array of points on the Cartesian plane with coordinates $(i, j)$ where $i, j$ are integers satisfying $0 \le i \le m$ and $0 \le j \le n$. The diagram below shows the example where $m = 3$ and $n = 5$, with the points of $S$ indicated by black dots.

Prove that there exist points $A, B, C$ in $S$ such that the area of $\triangle ABC$ is $\frac k2$.
answer: Take $A = (0, 0)$, $B = (m, 1)$, $C = (my - k, y)$ with $y = \lceil k/m \rceil$: then $C \in S$ and $[ABC] = \frac{|m\cdot y - 1\cdot(my - k)|}{2} = \frac k2$.

solutions.title: A thin triangle through the origin
solutions.body:
Let $y = \left\lceil \frac km \right\rceil$ and $x = my - k$. Since $1 \le k \le mn$, we have $1 \le y \le n$, and by the definition of the ceiling, $\frac km \le y < \frac km + 1$, i.e. $0 \le my - k < m$. So $0 \le x < m$.

Take $A = (0, 0)$, $B = (m, 1)$, $C = (x, y)$; all three are in $S$ (as $n \ge 1$). By the cross-product (shoelace) formula,
$$[ABC] = \frac12\left|m\cdot y - 1\cdot x\right| = \frac12\,|my - (my - k)| = \frac k2.$$
(In particular the triangle is non-degenerate.) ∎

solutions.title: Slide a vertex parallel to a side (official approach)
solutions.body:
Let $A = (0, 1)$ and $B = (m, 0)$, and $D = (k, 1)$. Triangle $ABD$ has base $AD = k$ on the line $y = 1$ and height $1$, so $[ABD] = \frac k2$; but $D$ may lie outside $S$.

Line $AB$ has slope $-\frac1m$, so the points $C_t = (k - mt, 1 + t)$ lie on the line through $D$ parallel to $AB$, and $[ABC_t] = [ABD] = \frac k2$ for every $t$. Choose $t = \left\lfloor \frac{k - 1}{m} \right\rfloor$. From $1 \le k \le mn$, $0 \le t \le n - 1$, so $1 \le 1 + t \le n$. And $\frac{k-1}{m} - 1 < t \le \frac{k-1}{m}$ gives $1 \le k - mt \le m$. So $C_t \in S$ and $\triangle ABC_t$ has area $\frac k2$. ∎

prompt:
Define a sequence of positive rational numbers $x_0, x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots$ by $x_0 = 2$, $x_1 = 3$, and for all $n \ge 2$,
$$x_n = \frac{x_{n-1}^2 + 5}{x_{n-2}}.$$
(a) Prove that $x_n$ is an integer for all $n \ge 0$.

(b) Prove that if $x_n$ is prime, then either $n = 0$ or $n = 2^k$ for some integer $k \ge 0$.
answer: (a) $x_nx_{n-2} - x_{n-1}^2 = 5$ for all $n$ forces $\frac{x_n + x_{n-2}}{x_{n-1}}$ to be constant $= 3$, so $x_n = 3x_{n-1} - x_{n-2}$. (b) Extend to negative indices ($x_{-n} = x_n$); if a prime $p$ divides $x_{-a}$ and $x_a$ then it divides $x_{ja}$ for all odd $j$. For $n = 2^k m$ with $m > 1$ odd, a prime factor of $x_{2^k}$ is a proper factor of $x_n$.

solutions.title: A linear recurrence and periodic zeros mod $p$
solutions.body:
**(a)** For $n \ge 2$ the definition says $x_nx_{n-2} - x_{n-1}^2 = 5$. Comparing this for $n$ and $n + 1$:
$$x_nx_{n-2} - x_{n-1}^2 = x_{n+1}x_{n-1} - x_n^2 \ \Longrightarrow\ x_n(x_n + x_{n-2}) = x_{n-1}(x_{n+1} + x_{n-1}).$$
Dividing by $x_nx_{n-1} > 0$: $\frac{x_n + x_{n-2}}{x_{n-1}} = \frac{x_{n+1} + x_{n-1}}{x_n}$, so this ratio is the same for all $n \ge 2$. With $x_2 = \frac{9 + 5}{2} = 7$ it equals $\frac{7 + 2}{3} = 3$. Hence
$$x_n = 3x_{n-1} - x_{n-2}\qquad(n \ge 2),$$
and by induction every $x_n$ is an integer. Also $x_n - x_{n-1} = 2x_{n-1} - x_{n-2} > 0$ inductively, so the sequence is strictly increasing: $2, 3, 7, 18, 47, 123, \dots$

**(b)** Use the recurrence to define $x_n$ for negative $n$ as well ($x_{n-2} = 3x_{n-1} - x_n$). Then $x_{-1} = 3\cdot2 - 3 = 3 = x_1$; since $n \mapsto x_{-n}$ satisfies the same recurrence with the same two starting values, $x_{-n} = x_n$ for all $n$.

**Lemma.** Let $p$ be a prime with $p \mid x_a$ and $p \mid x_b$, $a < b$, $r = b - a$. Then $p \mid x_{a + jr}$ for all $j \ge 0$.

*Proof.* Work mod $p$. Any sequence satisfying $y_{k} = 3y_{k-1} - y_{k-2}$ with $y_0 \equiv 0$ is determined by $y_1$, linearly: $y_k \equiv c_k y_1$, where $(c_k)$ is the solution with $c_0 = 0$, $c_1 = 1$. Apply this to $y_k = x_{a+k}$ and $z_k = x_{b+k}$. If $x_{a+1} \equiv 0$, two consecutive terms vanish and all terms are $\equiv 0$. Otherwise $0 \equiv x_b = y_r \equiv c_r x_{a+1}$ gives $c_r \equiv 0$, so $x_{b+r} = z_r \equiv c_r x_{b+1} \equiv 0$. Repeating (with the pair $b, b + r$) gives the claim. $\square$

**Finish.** Let $n \ge 1$ not be a power of $2$; write $n = 2^k m$ with $m > 1$ odd. Let $p$ be a prime factor of $x_{2^k} \ge 3$. Then $p \mid x_{2^k} = x_{-2^k}$, and the lemma with $a = -2^k$, $r = 2^{k+1}$ gives $p \mid x_{-2^k + j2^{k+1}} = x_{(2j - 1)2^k}$; with $j = \frac{m+1}{2}$ this is $x_n$. Since the sequence is increasing, $x_n > x_{2^k} \ge p$, so $x_n$ has a prime factor smaller than itself and is composite. Hence $x_n$ prime implies $n = 0$ or $n = 2^k$. ∎

(The converse fails: $x_0, x_1, x_2, x_4, x_8 = 2, 3, 7, 47, 2207$ are prime but $x_{16} = 4870847 = 1087\cdot 4481$.)

solutions.title: Closed form with the golden ratio
solutions.body:
Let $v = \varphi^2 = \frac{3 + \sqrt5}{2}$, so $v + v^{-1} = 3$ and $v - v^{-1} = \sqrt5$. Put $y_n = v^n + v^{-n}$. Then $y_0 = 2$, $y_1 = 3$, and
$$y_ny_{n-2} - y_{n-1}^2 = v^2 + v^{-2} - 2 = (v - v^{-1})^2 = 5,$$
so $y_n = \frac{y_{n-1}^2 + 5}{y_{n-2}}$: $x_n = y_n$ for all $n$ (these are the Lucas numbers $L_{2n}$). Also $y_n = 3y_{n-1} - y_{n-2}$, which gives (a).

For (b), let $n = 2^k m$ with $m > 1$ odd and $u = v^{2^k}$, so $x_{2^k} = u + u^{-1}$ and $x_n = u^m + u^{-m}$. For odd $m$,
$$u^m + u^{-m} = (u + u^{-1})\left(u^{m-1} - u^{m-3} + u^{m-5} - \dots + u^{-(m-1)}\right),$$
and the second factor is a signed sum of terms $u^j + u^{-j}$ (plus possibly $\pm1$), each an integer polynomial in $u + u^{-1}$ (e.g. $u^2 + u^{-2} = (u + u^{-1})^2 - 2$). So $x_{2^k} \mid x_n$ with $1 < x_{2^k} < x_n$, and $x_n$ is composite. ∎

prompt:
A $5 \times 5$ **Latin Square** is a $5 \times 5$ grid of squares in which each square contains one of the numbers $1$ through $5$ such that every number appears exactly once in each row and column. A partially completed grid (with numbers in some of the squares) is **puzzle-ready** if there is a *unique* way to fill in the remaining squares to complete a Latin Square.

Below is a partially completed grid with seven squares filled in and an additional three squares shaded. Determine what numbers must be filled into the shaded squares to make the grid (now with ten squares filled in) puzzle-ready, and then complete the Latin Square.

There is a unique solution, but you do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible. You merely need to find an answer that satisfies the constraints above. (Note: In any other USAMTS problem, you need to provide a full proof. Only in this problem is an answer without justification acceptable.)
answer:
Shaded squares: row $3$, column $3$ gets $4$; row $4$, column $1$ gets $3$; row $4$, column $5$ gets $4$. Completed square:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 1 & 4 & 5 & 2 & 3\\\hline 5 & 1 & 3 & 4 & 2\\\hline 2 & 3 & 4 & 1 & 5\\\hline 3 & 2 & 1 & 5 & 4\\\hline 4 & 5 & 2 & 3 & 1\\\hline\end{array}$$

solutions.title: Choose the shaded values, then fill by singles
solutions.body:
Number rows $1$–$5$ from the top and columns $1$–$5$ from the left. The givens are $(1,1) = 1$, $(2,2) = 1$, $(2,3) = 3$, $(3,1) = 2$, $(3,2) = 3$, $(3,5) = 5$, $(4,4) = 5$, and the shaded squares are $(3,3)$, $(4,1)$, $(4,5)$.

**Shaded values.** Put $(3,3) = 4$, $(4,1) = 3$, $(4,5) = 4$. (These are allowed: row $3$ already has $2, 3, 5$; row $4$ has only $5$; column $1$ has $1, 2$; column $5$ has $5$.) Checking all possible choices for the three shaded squares by computer shows that this is the only choice that leaves exactly one completion.

**Completing the square.** With the ten numbers in place, each step below is forced because the square has only one value not already in its row or column:
- $(2,5) = 2$, $(3,4) = 1$ (row $3$ is now $2, 3, 4, \_, 5$), $(4,2) = 2$, $(4,3) = 1$;
- $(1,5) = 3$, $(2,4) = 4$, $(5,5) = 1$, $(1,4) = 2$;
- $(2,1) = 5$, $(5,1) = 4$, $(5,2) = 5$, $(5,3) = 2$, $(5,4) = 3$, $(1,2) = 4$, $(1,3) = 5$.

This gives
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 1 & 4 & 5 & 2 & 3\\\hline 5 & 1 & 3 & 4 & 2\\\hline 2 & 3 & 4 & 1 & 5\\\hline 3 & 2 & 1 & 5 & 4\\\hline 4 & 5 & 2 & 3 & 1\\\hline\end{array}$$
Every row and column contains $1$–$5$ once, and the forced chain shows the completion is unique, so the grid with these ten numbers is puzzle-ready.

**Answer:** shaded squares $4$, $3$, $4$ (in reading order), and the square above.

prompt:
Let $n$ be a fixed positive integer. Which is greater?

1. The number of $n$-tuples of integers whose largest value is $7$ and whose smallest value is $0$; or
2. The number of ordered triples $(A, B, C)$ that satisfy the following property: $A, B, C$ are subsets of $\{1, 2, 3, \dots, n\}$, and neither $C \subseteq A \cup B$, nor $B \subseteq A \cup C$.

Your answer can be: (1), (2), the two counts are equal, or it depends on $n$.

solutions.title: A bijection through the Venn diagram
solutions.body:
The sets $A, B, C$ split $\{1, \dots, n\}$ into $8$ Venn regions, and a triple $(A, B, C)$ is the same thing as a choice of region for each element. Label the regions $0$ to $7$ so that region $0$ is "in $B$ only" and region $7$ is "in $C$ only"; the other six regions get labels $1$ to $6$ in any fixed way.

Now send a triple $(A, B, C)$ to the $n$-tuple whose $k$-th entry is the label of the region containing $k$. This is a bijection between triples of subsets and $n$-tuples with entries in $\{0, \dots, 7\}$.

- $B \not\subseteq A \cup C$ means some element lies in $B$ only, i.e. the tuple contains a $0$.
- $C \not\subseteq A \cup B$ means some element lies in $C$ only, i.e. the tuple contains a $7$.

An integer tuple has largest value $7$ and smallest value $0$ exactly when all its entries lie in $\{0, \dots, 7\}$ and it contains both a $0$ and a $7$. So the bijection matches the triples in (2) exactly with the tuples in (1).

**Answer: the two counts are equal.**

solutions.title: Count both directly
solutions.body:
**(1)** The entries lie in $\{0, \dots, 7\}$ and both $0$ and $7$ must occur. By inclusion–exclusion there are $8^n - 7^n - 7^n + 6^n$ such tuples.

**(2)** Each element independently chooses one of the $8$ Venn regions. We need the region "$B$ only" and the region "$C$ only" to be nonempty. Again by inclusion–exclusion the count is $8^n - 2\cdot 7^n + 6^n$.

Both equal $8^n - 2\cdot 7^n + 6^n$ (for example $0, 2, 42, 590$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$), so the counts are equal for every $n$.

prompt:
Let $x$ and $y$ be distinct real numbers such that
$$\sqrt{x^2 + 1} + \sqrt{y^2 + 1} = 2021x + 2021y.$$
Find, with proof, the value of
$$\left(x + \sqrt{x^2 + 1}\right)\left(y + \sqrt{y^2 + 1}\right).$$

solutions.title: Use $(\sqrt{t^2+1} - t)(\sqrt{t^2+1} + t) = 1$
solutions.body:
Write $u = x + \sqrt{x^2 + 1}$ and $v = y + \sqrt{y^2 + 1}$. Both are positive, since $\sqrt{t^2 + 1} > |t|$. Because $(\sqrt{t^2 + 1} - t)(\sqrt{t^2 + 1} + t) = 1$, we have $\sqrt{x^2 + 1} - x = \frac1u$ and $\sqrt{y^2 + 1} - y = \frac1v$.

Subtract $x + y$ from both sides of the given equation:
$$\frac1u + \frac1v = 2020(x + y), \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \frac{u + v}{uv} = 2020(x + y).$$
Also $u + v = (x + y) + \left(\sqrt{x^2 + 1} + \sqrt{y^2 + 1}\right) = (x + y) + 2021(x + y) = 2022(x + y)$. Hence
$$\frac{2022(x + y)}{uv} = 2020(x + y).$$
The left side of the original equation is at least $2$, so $2021(x + y) \ge 2$ and $x + y \ne 0$. Dividing by $x + y$,
$$uv = \frac{2022}{2020} = \frac{1011}{1010}.$$
(Such $x \ne y$ exist; for example $y = 0.001$ gives $x \approx -0.0000104$, and the product is $1.000990\ldots = \frac{1011}{1010}$.)

**Answer:** $\dfrac{1011}{1010}$.

prompt:
Let $ABC$ be a scalene triangle, and let $X, Y, Z$ be points on sides $BC, CA, AB$, respectively. Let $I$ and $O$ denote the incenter and circumcenter, respectively, of triangle $ABC$. Suppose that
$$\frac{BX - CX}{BA - CA} = \frac{CY - AY}{CB - AB} = \frac{AZ - BZ}{AC - BC}.$$
Prove that there exists a point $P$ on line $IO$ such that $PX \perp BC$, $PY \perp CA$, and $PZ \perp AB$.
answer: Let $\alpha$ be the common ratio and $P = O + \alpha(I - O)$. Projecting onto $BC$ sends $O$ to the midpoint $M$ of $BC$ and $I$ to the incircle touch point $D$, so $P$ projects to $M + \alpha(D - M)$. Since $MX = \frac{BX - CX}{2}$ and $MD = \frac{BA - CA}{2}$ (directed along $BC$), this point is $X$. The same holds on the other two sides.

solutions.title: Project line $IO$ onto each side
solutions.body:
Let $a = BC$, $b = CA$, $c = AB$, $s = \frac{a + b + c}{2}$, and let $\alpha$ be the common value of the three ratios. All denominators are nonzero because the triangle is scalene.

Define $P = O + \alpha(I - O)$, a point of line $IO$. (If $\alpha = 0$ then $P = O$; if $\alpha = 1$ then $P = I$.) We show that the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $BC$ is $X$, and likewise for the other sides.

**Side $BC$.** Orthogonal projection $\pi$ onto line $BC$ is an affine map, so $\pi(P) = \pi(O) + \alpha(\pi(I) - \pi(O))$. The circumcenter projects to the midpoint $M$ of $BC$, and the incenter projects to the touch point $D$ of the incircle with $BC$. Put a coordinate on line $BC$ with $B = 0$ and $C = a$. Then
- $X$ has coordinate $BX$, so $X - M = BX - \frac a2 = \frac{BX - CX}{2}$ (using $BX + CX = a$);
- $D$ has coordinate $BD = s - b = \frac{a + c - b}{2}$, so $D - M = \frac{c - b}{2} = \frac{BA - CA}{2}$.

Therefore
$$\pi(P) = M + \alpha(D - M) = M + \frac{BX - CX}{BA - CA}\cdot\frac{BA - CA}{2} = M + \frac{BX - CX}{2} = X.$$
So $X$ is the foot of the perpendicular from $P$ to $BC$, i.e. $PX \perp BC$.

**Sides $CA$ and $AB$.** The same computation applies after relabelling $A \to B \to C \to A$. On line $CA$ (coordinate $0$ at $C$), the midpoint is at $\frac b2$ and the touch point is at $s - c$, so the touch point minus the midpoint is $\frac{a - c}{2} = \frac{CB - AB}{2}$, while $Y$ minus the midpoint is $\frac{CY - AY}{2}$. Since $\frac{CY - AY}{CB - AB} = \alpha$ as well, the projection of the **same** point $P$ onto $CA$ is $Y$. Similarly, $\frac{AZ - BZ}{AC - BC} = \alpha$ gives that the projection of $P$ onto $AB$ is $Z$.

Hence $PX \perp BC$, $PY \perp CA$, $PZ \perp AB$, with $P$ on line $IO$. (Because the triangle is scalene, $I \ne O$, so line $IO$ is well defined.) ∎

prompt:
For a finite nonempty set $A$ of positive integers, $A = \{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n\}$, we say the **calamitous complement** of $A$ is the set of all positive integers $k$ for which there do not exist nonnegative integers $w_1, w_2, \dots, w_n$ with
$$k = a_1w_1 + a_2w_2 + \dots + a_nw_n.$$
The calamitous complement of $A$ is denoted $cc(A)$. For example, $cc(\{5, 6, 9\}) = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 7, 8, 13\}$.

Find all pairs of positive integers $a, b$ with $1 < a < b$ for which there exists a set $G$ satisfying all of the following properties:

1. $G$ is a set of at most three positive integers,
2. $cc(\{a, b\})$ and $cc(G)$ are both finite sets, and
3. $cc(G) = cc(\{a, b\}) \cup \{m\}$ for some $m$ not in $cc(\{a, b\})$.
answer: Exactly the pairs with $a \in \{2, 3\}$ and $\gcd(a, b) = 1$: $(a, b) = (2, 2k + 1)$, $(3, 3k + 1)$, $(3, 3k + 2)$ for positive integers $k$ (take $G = \{a, a + b, 2b\}$, $m = b$).

solutions.title: Construction for $a \le 3$; generator-forcing argument for $a \ge 4$
solutions.body:
Write $\langle X\rangle$ for the set of nonnegative integer combinations of elements of $X$ (including $0$), and $S = \langle a, b\rangle$. Then $cc(X)$ is the set of positive integers not in $\langle X\rangle$, and property 3 says exactly
$$\langle G\rangle = S \setminus \{m\} \quad\text{for some positive } m \in S.$$
By the Frobenius coin problem, $cc(\{a, b\})$ is finite iff $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, so we need $\gcd(a, b) = 1$. Then $cc(G)$ is automatically finite once property 3 holds.

**These pairs work.** Let $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, $a \in \{2, 3\}$, and $G = \{a, a + b, 2b\}$. We claim $\langle G\rangle = S \setminus \{b\}$.
- Every element of $G$ is in $S$, so $\langle G\rangle \subseteq S$.
- $b \notin \langle G\rangle$: since $a + b$ and $2b$ exceed $b$, $b$ would have to be a multiple of $a$, impossible.
- Every other $xa + yb \in S$ is in $\langle G\rangle$. If $y = 0$ it is $x\cdot a$. If $y = 1$, $x \ge 1$, it is $(x - 1)a + (a + b)$. If $y \ge 2$: we have $3b \in \langle G\rangle$, because $3b = (a + b) + (b - 1)a$ when $a = 2$, and $3b = b\cdot a$ when $a = 3$. Every $yb$ with $y \ge 2$ is a sum of $2b$'s and $3b$'s, so $xa + yb \in \langle G\rangle$.

**No pair with $a \ge 4$ works.** Suppose $\gcd(a, b) = 1$, $4 \le a < b$, and $G$ exists. If $m \notin \{a, b\}$, then $a, b \in \langle G\rangle$, so $S \subseteq \langle G\rangle$, a contradiction. So $m$ is one of $a, b$. Call it $q$ and call the other one $p$. Then $p, q \ge 4$, $\gcd(p, q) = 1$, and $\langle G\rangle = S \setminus \{q\}$. (The order of $p$ and $q$ does not matter below.)

Recall that an element of $\langle G\rangle$ which is **not** a sum of two smaller positive elements of $\langle G\rangle$ must belong to $G$.

1. **$p \in G$.** The elements of $S$ below $p$ are multiples of $q$. A sum of multiples of $q$ equal to $p$ would force $q \mid p$, so $p$ is not such a sum.
2. **$p + q \in G$.** The elements of $S$ below $p + q$ are pure multiples of $p$ or of $q$, and $q \notin \langle G\rangle$. Suppose $p + q = ip + jq$ is a sum of smaller elements of $\langle G\rangle$, collected by type. We cannot have $i = j = 1$: the summands would then be $p$ and $q$, but $q \notin \langle G\rangle$. So $(i - 1)p = (1 - j)q$ with $i \ne 1$. Then $q \mid i - 1$. If $i = 0$, then $q \mid -1$, which is impossible. Otherwise $i \ge q + 1$, and $ip > p + q$. Either way this is a contradiction.
3. **The third element.** Every element of $S \setminus \{q\}$ below $2q$ is $xp + yq$ with $y \le 1$, and these all lie in $\langle p, p + q\rangle$ (as in the construction above). But $2q \notin \langle p, p + q\rangle$: writing $2q = (x + y)p + yq$, the case $y = 2$ is impossible, $y = 1$ gives $p \mid q$, and $y = 0$ gives $p \mid 2$. Since $2q \in S \setminus \{q\} = \langle G\rangle$, $G$ must have a third element $g$, and $g \le 2q$. If $g < 2q$, then $g \in \langle p, p + q\rangle$, and $\langle G\rangle = \langle p, p + q\rangle$ would miss $2q$. So $g = 2q$ and $G = \{p, p + q, 2q\}$.
4. **Contradiction at $3q$.** $3q \in S \setminus \{q\}$, so $3q = xp + y(p + q) + z(2q) = (x + y)p + (y + 2z)q$. If $x + y = 0$, then $3q = 2zq$, which is impossible. Otherwise $q \mid x + y$ (since $\gcd(p, q) = 1$), so $(x + y)p \ge pq \ge 4q > 3q$, also impossible.

Hence $a \le 3$. With $\gcd(a, b) = 1$ this gives $a = 2$ with $b$ odd, or $a = 3$ with $3 \nmid b$. A computer search over small $a < b$ with $|G| \le 3$ agrees.

**Answer:** $(a, b) = (2, 2k + 1)$, $(3, 3k + 1)$, $(3, 3k + 2)$ for positive integers $k$.

solutions.title: A tree with all degrees odd
solutions.body:

prompt:
Sydney the squirrel is at $(0, 0)$ and is trying to get to $(2021, 2022)$. She can move only by reflecting her position over any line that can be formed by connecting two lattice points, provided that the reflection puts her on another lattice point. Is it possible for Sydney to reach $(2021, 2022)$?

Lattice points are points in the Cartesian plane where both coordinates are integers.
answer: **No.** A reflection between lattice points of different parity of $x + y$ would need a mirror line with no lattice points, so the parity of $x + y$ never changes; $0 + 0$ is even, $2021 + 2022$ is odd.

solutions.title: Parity of $x + y$ is invariant
solutions.body:
Call a lattice point **even** or **odd** according to the parity of the sum of its coordinates.

Suppose one move takes Sydney from a lattice point $P = (p, q)$ to a lattice point $P' = (p + u, q + v)$, where $(u, v) \ne (0, 0)$. Then the mirror line is the perpendicular bisector of $PP'$, i.e. the set of points $(x, y)$ with
$$u\left(x - p - \tfrac u2\right) + v\left(y - q - \tfrac v2\right) = 0 \iff 2\big(u(x - p) + v(y - q)\big) = u^2 + v^2.$$
Now suppose $P$ and $P'$ have different parity, i.e. $u + v$ is odd. Then exactly one of $u, v$ is odd, so $u^2 + v^2$ is odd. For a lattice point $(x, y)$ the left-hand side is even, so **no** lattice point lies on this line. But Sydney may only reflect over lines through (two) lattice points. So every move keeps her on points of the same parity.

She starts at $(0, 0)$, which is even, while $2021 + 2022 = 4043$ is odd. So she can never reach $(2021, 2022)$.

**Answer: No.** ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $S$ be the set of $n^2$ cells in an $n \times n$ grid. Call a subset $T$ of $S$ a **double staircase** if

1. $T$ can be partitioned into $n$ horizontal nonoverlapping rectangles of dimensions $1 \times 1, 1 \times 2, \dots, 1 \times n$, and
2. $T$ can also be partitioned into $n$ vertical nonoverlapping rectangles of dimensions $1 \times 1, 2 \times 1, \dots, n \times 1$.

In terms of $n$, how many double staircases are there? (Rotations and reflections are considered distinct.)

An example of a double staircase when $n = 3$ is shown below.

solutions.title: Row and column lengths form "mountain" permutations
solutions.body:
**One tile per row and per column.** The $1 \times n$ tile fills a whole row, so every column meets $T$. There are $n$ vertical tiles and $n$ columns, and each vertical tile lies in a single column, so each column contains **exactly one** vertical tile. Hence each column of $T$ is one contiguous block. Likewise the $n \times 1$ tile shows that each row contains exactly one horizontal tile, so each row of $T$ is one contiguous block.

Let $h_1, \dots, h_n$ be the lengths of the row blocks (top to bottom) and $v_1, \dots, v_n$ those of the column blocks (left to right). Both are permutations of $1, \dots, n$.

**Call a permutation a *mountain* if no entry is smaller than both of its neighbours.** Equivalently, it increases up to $n$ and then decreases. The sequence $(h_i)$ must be a mountain. Indeed, suppose $h_j < h_i$ and $h_j < h_k$ with $i < j < k$, and say the $n$ lies at or before position $j$ (the other case is symmetric). Then the block in row $k$ is longer than the block in row $j$. So some column contains a cell of row $k$ but not of row $j$, and every column contains a cell of the full row (the row of $n$). Since that full row is above row $j$ and row $k$ is below it, this column has a cell, then a gap at row $j$, then a cell, contradicting that each column is one block. Similarly $(v_i)$ is a mountain.

**Counting mountains.** In a mountain of $1, \dots, k$ the entry $1$ must be at an end (otherwise it is smaller than both neighbours). Removing it and decreasing the other entries by $1$ gives a mountain of $1, \dots, k - 1$, and this is reversible. So there are $2^{k-1}$ mountains of length $k$.

**$T$ is determined by $(h, v)$.** We prove a stronger statement: any set of cells in an $n \times n$ grid whose row counts are a permutation $h$ of $1, \dots, n$ and whose column counts are a permutation $v$ of $1, \dots, n$ consists exactly of the cells $(i, j)$ with $h_i + v_j \ge n + 1$. Use induction on $n$; the cases $n = 0, 1$ are clear.
- The row with count $n$ and the column with count $n$ are full.
- Delete them. Every other row and column loses exactly one cell, so the counts become permutations of $0, \dots, n - 2$.
- The row and column with count $0$ are now empty. Before the deletion they had count $1$, and their only cell was in the full column (respectively, full row).
- Delete them as well. This leaves an $(n - 2) \times (n - 2)$ grid whose row and column counts are permutations of $1, \dots, n - 2$, namely $h_i - 1$ and $v_j - 1$.

By induction the remaining cells are those with $(h_i - 1) + (v_j - 1) \ge (n - 2) + 1$, i.e. $h_i + v_j \ge n + 1$. The deleted rows and columns also satisfy this rule: a full row has $h_i = n$, and a count-$1$ row meets only the column with $v_j = n$.

**Every pair of mountains occurs.** Given mountains $h$ and $v$, let $T$ be the set of cells with $h_i + v_j \ge n + 1$. Row $i$ consists of the $h_i$ columns with the largest values $v_j \ge n + 1 - h_i$. In a mountain the $k$ largest entries always occupy consecutive positions, so this row is a single block of length $h_i$. Likewise each column $j$ is a single block of length $v_j$. So the rows give a partition into tiles $1 \times 1, \dots, 1 \times n$ and the columns give one into $1 \times 1, \dots, n \times 1$, and $T$ is a double staircase.

Hence the number of double staircases is $\left(2^{n-1}\right)^2 = 4^{n-1}$. A brute-force count gives $1, 4, 16, 64$ for $n = 1, 2, 3, 4$.

**Answer:** $4^{n-1}$.

prompt:
Let $ABC$ be a triangle whose vertices are inside a circle $\Omega$. Prove that we can choose two of the vertices of $ABC$ such that there are infinitely many circles $\omega$ that satisfy the following properties:

1. $\omega$ is inside of $\Omega$,
2. $\omega$ passes through the two chosen vertices, and
3. the third vertex is in the interior of $\omega$.
answer: Let $C$ be the vertex farthest from the centre $O$ and shrink the circle centred at $O$ through $C$ by homotheties at $C$ until it first meets $A$ or $B$ (say $B$). That circle lies inside $\Omega$, passes through $B$ and $C$, and contains $A$ in its interior, so small perturbations among circles through $B$ and $C$ give infinitely many. If $A$ and $B$ are met at the same time, the circumcircle lies inside $\Omega$ and we perturb it among circles through $A$ and $B$.

solutions.title: Shrink a circle about the farthest vertex
solutions.body:
Let $O$ and $R$ be the centre and radius of $\Omega$. Label the vertices so that $OA, OB \le OC$. Then $OC < R$.

**A perturbation fact.** Suppose a circle $\omega_0$ passes through two vertices, has the third vertex strictly inside, and lies in the open disk of $\Omega$. Then infinitely many circles have the same three properties. Indeed, move the centre of $\omega_0$ slightly along the perpendicular bisector of the two chosen vertices, keeping the circle through them. The radius changes continuously. Since $\omega_0$ has positive distance both from $\Omega$ and from the third vertex, all sufficiently small moves still give circles inside $\Omega$ containing the third vertex in their interior.

**Shrinking.** Let $\gamma$ be the circle with centre $O$ through $C$. Its disk lies inside the open disk of $\Omega$, because its radius is $OC < R$, and $A$, $B$ lie in its closed disk. For $0 < r \le 1$ let $D_r$ be the image of this closed disk under the homothety with centre $C$ and ratio $r$. The $D_r$ are nested: $D_r \subset D_{r'}$ for $r < r'$, and their boundary circles meet only at $C$. They all lie inside $\gamma$'s disk, and they shrink to the point $C$ as $r \to 0$. Let $r_A$ be the smallest $r$ with $A \in D_r$ (so $A$ lies on the boundary circle of $D_{r_A}$), and define $r_B$ similarly. Both are positive since $A, B \ne C$.

**Case $r_A \ne r_B$**, say $r_A < r_B$. The boundary circle $\gamma'$ of $D_{r_B}$ passes through $B$ and $C$. It also contains $A$ in its interior: $A \in D_{r_A}$, and $D_{r_A}$ touches the boundary of $D_{r_B}$ only at $C \ne A$. And $\gamma'$ lies inside $\Omega$. By the perturbation fact we get infinitely many circles through $B$ and $C$ with $A$ inside.

**Case $r_A = r_B$.** Then $A$, $B$, $C$ all lie on the boundary circle of $D_{r_A}$, which is therefore the circumcircle $\Gamma$ of $ABC$, and $\Gamma$ lies strictly inside $\Omega$. Now use circles through $A$ and $B$. Choose coordinates with $A = (-1, 0)$ and $B = (1, 0)$, with $C$ above the $x$-axis ($y_C > 0$). The circle through $A$, $B$ with centre $(0, t)$ contains a point $(x, y)$ in its interior iff
$$x^2 + (y - t)^2 < 1 + t^2 \iff x^2 + y^2 - 1 - 2ty < 0.$$
For $C$ the left side is $0$ at $t = t_0$ (the circumcircle) and strictly decreasing in $t$, because $y_C > 0$. So for every $t > t_0$, $C$ is strictly inside. Since $\Gamma$ lies strictly inside $\Omega$, all $t$ slightly larger than $t_0$ give circles inside $\Omega$. That is infinitely many circles through $A$ and $B$ containing $C$.

In every case a suitable pair of vertices exists. ∎

answer: If $d$ is an integer, $e = a + b\lfloor c\rfloor$ and $f = bd$ work, by $\lfloor \lfloor y\rfloor / d\rfloor = \lfloor y/d\rfloor$. Conversely, comparing growth rates forces $f = bd$, and the set where both sides equal $k$ has length $f = bd$ on the right and $b$ times an integer on the left, so $d$ is an integer.

solutions.title: Compare slopes, then lengths of level sets
solutions.body:
Let $L(x)$ and $R(x)$ denote the left and right sides.

**If $d$ is a positive integer.** We use the standard fact that $\left\lfloor \frac{\lfloor y\rfloor}{q} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{y}{q} \right\rfloor$ for every real $y$ and positive integer $q$. To see it, write $\lfloor y\rfloor = kq + s$ with $0 \le s \le q - 1$; then $kq \le y < kq + s + 1 \le (k + 1)q$.

Let $N = \left\lfloor \frac{x + a}{b} \right\rfloor$, an integer. Then:
- $\left\lfloor \frac{N + c}{d} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{\lfloor N + c\rfloor}{d} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{N + \lfloor c\rfloor}{d} \right\rfloor$.
- Since $\lfloor c\rfloor$ is an integer, $N + \lfloor c\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{x + a + b\lfloor c\rfloor}{b} \right\rfloor$.
- Applying the fact again with $q = d$,
$$L(x) = \left\lfloor \frac{\left\lfloor \frac{x + a + b\lfloor c\rfloor}{b} \right\rfloor}{d} \right\rfloor = \left\lfloor \frac{x + a + b\lfloor c\rfloor}{bd} \right\rfloor.$$

So $e = a + b\lfloor c\rfloor > 0$ and $f = bd > 0$ work.

**If $e, f$ exist.** First, $f = bd$. Take $x = Nb - a$ with $N$ an integer. Then $L = \left\lfloor \frac{N + c}{d} \right\rfloor$ and $R = \left\lfloor \frac{Nb - a + e}{f} \right\rfloor$. Equal floors have arguments differing by less than $1$, so
$$\left| N\left(\frac1d - \frac bf\right) + \frac cd - \frac{e - a}{f} \right| < 1 \quad\text{for all integers } N.$$
This forces $\frac1d = \frac bf$, i.e. $f = bd$.

Now fix an integer $k$ and compare the sets where each side equals $k$. The set $\{x : R(x) = k\}$ is the interval $[kf - e, (k + 1)f - e)$, of length $f = bd$. On the other hand, $L(x) = k$ iff the integer $N = \left\lfloor \frac{x + a}{b} \right\rfloor$ satisfies $kd - c \le N < kd - c + d$. Each value of $N$ corresponds to an interval of $x$ of length $b$, and consecutive values give adjacent intervals. So $\{x : L(x) = k\}$ is an interval of length $b \cdot j_k$, where $j_k$ is the number of integers in $[kd - c, kd - c + d)$.

The two sets are equal, so $b\, j_k = bd$, i.e. $d = j_k$ is an integer. ∎

prompt:
Shown is a segment of length 19, marked with 20 points dividing the segment into 19 segments of length 1. Draw 20 semicircular arcs, each of whose endpoints are two of the 20 marked points, satisfying all of the following conditions:

1. When the drawing is complete, there will be:
   * 8 arcs with diameter 1,
   * 6 arcs with diameter 3,
   * 4 arcs with diameter 5,
   * 2 arcs with diameter 7.
2. Each marked point is the endpoint of exactly two arcs: one above the segment and one below the segment.
3. No two distinct arcs can intersect except at their endpoints.
4. No two distinct arcs can connect the same pair of points. (That is, there can be no full circles.)

Three arcs have already been drawn for you, as shown in the picture.

There is a unique solution, but you do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible. You merely need to find an answer that satisfies the conditions of the problem.

solutions.title: Build the arcs from the constraints
solutions.body:
Number the points $1, 2, \dots, 20$ from left to right. The given arcs are $6$–$11$ (above, diameter 5) and $8$–$9$, $13$–$14$ (below, diameter 1).

**Useful facts.**
* Every diameter is odd, so every arc joins an odd-numbered point to an even-numbered point.
* The 10 arcs above form a non-crossing matching of all 20 points, and so do the 10 arcs below. In a non-crossing matching, the points strictly inside an arc must be matched among themselves.
* Point 1 must be joined (above and below) to two *different* points among $2, 4, 6, 8$; likewise point 20 to two different points among $19, 17, 15, 13$.

**Above.** Inside the arc $6$–$11$ are points $7, 8, 9, 10$, which must be matched among themselves without crossing; diameter 3 for $7$–$10$ would force $8$–$9$ above as well, a full circle with the given arc $8$–$9$ below. So above we have $7$–$8$ and $9$–$10$. Points $1$–$5$ lie to the left of the big arc; an odd number of them must be joined over the arc $6$–$11$ to points $\ge 12$, which needs diameter $\ge 7$, so exactly $5$–$12$ (diameter 7) is drawn above. Points $1$–$4$ are then matched among themselves above ($1$–$2$, $3$–$4$ or $1$–$4$, $2$–$3$), and points $13$–$20$ among themselves.

**Finishing.** Only a handful of combinations remain for the left block ($1$–$6$ below) and the right block ($11$–$20$). Checking them against the required numbers of arcs of each diameter (only one more diameter-7 arc is allowed, and it must be on the right) and against the no-full-circle rule leaves exactly one possibility.

**Final drawing.**
* Above: $1$–$4$, $2$–$3$, $5$–$12$, $6$–$11$, $7$–$8$, $9$–$10$, $13$–$20$, $14$–$19$, $15$–$18$, $16$–$17$.
* Below: $1$–$6$, $2$–$5$, $3$–$4$, $7$–$10$, $8$–$9$, $11$–$16$, $12$–$15$, $13$–$14$, $17$–$20$, $18$–$19$.

**Check.** Diameters: 1 occurs for $2$–$3$, $7$–$8$, $9$–$10$, $16$–$17$, $3$–$4$, $8$–$9$, $13$–$14$, $18$–$19$ (8 arcs); 3 for $1$–$4$, $15$–$18$, $2$–$5$, $7$–$10$, $12$–$15$, $17$–$20$ (6 arcs); 5 for $6$–$11$, $14$–$19$, $1$–$6$, $11$–$16$ (4 arcs); 7 for $5$–$12$, $13$–$20$ (2 arcs). Each side is a nested (non-crossing) perfect matching, every point has one arc above and one below, and no pair appears on both sides. A computer search over all non-crossing matchings confirms that this is the only solution.

**Answer: the arcs listed above.**

prompt: Given a sphere, a *great circle* of the sphere is a circle on the sphere whose diameter is also a diameter of the sphere. For a given positive integer $n$, the surface of a sphere is divided into several regions by $n$ great circles, and each region is colored black or white. We say that a coloring is *good* if any two adjacent regions (that share an arc as boundary, not just a finite number of points) have different colors. Find, with proof, all positive integers $n$ such that in every good coloring with $n$ great circles, the sum of the areas of the black regions is equal to the sum of the areas of the white regions.
answer: Exactly the **odd** $n$. (For odd $n$ antipodal points always have opposite colors; for even $n$ take all circles through two poles with unequal alternating lune angles.)

solutions.title: Antipodal points
solutions.body:
**Odd $n$ works.** Let $P$ be any point not on the $n$ circles, and let $Q$ be its antipode. Choose a great circle $C$ through $P$ and $Q$ that avoids the finitely many points where two of the given circles meet. Each given great circle meets $C$ in two antipodal points, so exactly one of them lies on the open half of $C$ from $P$ to $Q$. Walking along that half from $P$ to $Q$, we therefore cross the given circles exactly $n$ times, each time through the interior of an arc, i.e. passing into an adjacent region. In a good coloring the color changes at every crossing, so after $n$ (odd) changes the color of $Q$ is opposite to that of $P$.

Hence the antipodal map $X \mapsto -X$ sends the black part of the sphere onto the white part (up to the circles themselves, which have zero area). Since this map preserves area, black and white areas are equal.

**Even $n$ fails.** Let all $n$ great circles pass through the north and south poles $N$, $S$. They cut the sphere into $2n$ lunes; adjacent lunes must have different colors, so the colors alternate around the axis. Choose the half-meridians bounding the lunes so that the lune angles, going around, are $a, b, a, b, \dots$ with $a \ne b$ and $n(a + b) = 2\pi$. Because $n$ is even, any $n$ consecutive angles add up to $\tfrac n2(a+b) = \pi$, so the half-meridian at each boundary and the one $n$ steps further are antipodal and together form a great circle — we really have $n$ great circles. The lunes of angle $a$ all get one color, and its area fraction is $\frac{na}{2\pi} \ne \frac12$.

For example, with $n = 2$ and the two circles at $30^\circ$ to each other, one color covers $\frac16$ of the sphere and the other $\frac56$.

**Answer: all odd positive integers $n$.** ∎

prompt:
Prove that there is a unique 1000-digit number $N$ in base 2022 with the following properties:

1. All of the digits of $N$ (in base 2022) are 1's or 2's, and
2. $N$ is a multiple of the base-10 number $2^{1000}$.

(Note that you must prove both that such a number exists and that there is not more than one such number. You do not have to write down the number! In fact, please don't!)
answer: Proof. Since $2022 = 2\cdot 1011$, two different digit strings of 1's and 2's whose lowest differing digit is in position $j$ differ by $2^j\cdot(\text{odd})$; so the $2^{1000}$ numbers have distinct residues mod $2^{1000}$ and exactly one is $\equiv 0$. (Equivalently: build $N$ digit by digit by induction.)

solutions.title: Induction on the number of digits
solutions.body:
We prove more generally: for every $k \ge 1$ there is exactly one $k$-digit base-2022 number with all digits in $\{1, 2\}$ that is divisible by $2^k$. For $k = 1$: $2$ is divisible by $2$ and $1$ is not.

Suppose the claim holds for $k - 1$, with unique number $M = m\cdot 2^{k-1}$. Put a digit $d \in \{1, 2\}$ in front:
$$N = d\cdot 2022^{k-1} + M = 2^{k-1}\left(d\cdot 1011^{k-1} + m\right).$$
Since $1011^{k-1}$ is odd, $d\cdot 1011^{k-1} + m$ is even for exactly one choice of $d$ ($d = 1$ if $m$ is odd, $d = 2$ if $m$ is even). So exactly one extension of $M$ is divisible by $2^k$: existence.

Uniqueness: if $N$ is any $k$-digit number of 1's and 2's divisible by $2^k$, with leading digit $d$, then $N' = N - d\cdot 2022^{k-1} = N - 2^{k-1}d\cdot 1011^{k-1}$ is a $(k-1)$-digit number of 1's and 2's divisible by $2^{k-1}$, so $N' = M$ by the induction hypothesis, and then $d$ is forced as shown. Taking $k = 1000$ proves the statement. ∎

solutions.title: Counting residues
solutions.body:
There are exactly $2^{1000}$ numbers $N = \sum_{i=0}^{999} d_i\, 2022^i$ with all $d_i \in \{1, 2\}$, and exactly $2^{1000}$ residues modulo $2^{1000}$. We show that two different such numbers are never congruent mod $2^{1000}$; then they hit every residue exactly once, in particular $0$ exactly once — which is the claim.

Take $N \ne N'$ and let $j$ be the lowest position where their digits differ (so $d_j - d'_j = \pm 1$). Then
$$N - N' = \pm 2022^j + \sum_{i > j}(d_i - d'_i)\,2022^i = 2^j\left(\pm 1011^j + 2\cdot(\text{integer})\right),$$
because $2022^i = 2^i\cdot 1011^i$ is divisible by $2^{j+1}$ for $i > j$. The bracket is odd, so $N - N'$ is divisible by $2^j$ but not by $2^{j+1}$; as $j \le 999$, it is not divisible by $2^{1000}$. ∎

prompt: Grogg and Winnie are playing a game using a deck of 50 cards numbered 1 through 50. They take turns with Grogg going first. On each turn a player chooses a card from the deck—this choice is made deliberately, not at random—and then adds it to one of two piles (both piles are empty at the start of the game). After all 50 cards are in the two piles, the values of the cards in each pile are summed, and Winnie wins the positive difference of the sums of the two piles, in dollars. (For instance, if the first pile has cards summing to 510 and the second pile has cards summing to 765, then Winnie wins \$255.) Winnie wants to win as much as possible, and Grogg wants Winnie to win as little as possible. If they both play with perfect strategy, find (with proof) the amount that Winnie wins.

solutions.title: Strategies for both players
solutions.body:
Call the current difference of the two pile sums the *score*.

**Winnie can guarantee at least \$75.** She pairs the cards as $\{49, 50\}$ and $\{2k - 1, 2k\}$ for $k = 1, \dots, 24$. Grogg always moves first in a fresh pair (Winnie only ever completes the pair Grogg just opened), so she can always answer immediately:
* when Grogg plays 49 or 50, she plays the other one **on the same pile**;
* when Grogg plays $2k-1$ or $2k$, she plays the other one **on the other pile**.

In the end, 49 and 50 contribute $99$ to one side, and each of the 24 small pairs contributes $\pm 1$ to the difference. So the final score is at least $99 - 24 = 75$.

**Grogg can hold Winnie to at most \$75.** On each of his turns Grogg plays the largest remaining card on the pile with the smaller sum (either pile if they are equal). Let $s_i$ be the score before Grogg's $i$-th turn ($s_1 = 0$) and $m_i$ the card he plays then.

* $m_i \le 51 - i$: by induction, before Grogg's $i$-th turn all cards larger than $51 - i$ are gone; he removes the largest remaining card, so afterwards all cards larger than $50 - i$ are gone.
* $s_{i+1} \le \max(s_i - 1,\ 2m_i - 1)$: every card Winnie can then play is smaller than $m_i$. If $s_i \ge m_i$, Grogg's card lowers the score to $s_i - m_i$ and Winnie's card $c \le m_i - 1$ raises it to at most $s_i - 1$. If $s_i < m_i$, the score after Grogg's move is $m_i - s_i \le m_i$, and after Winnie's at most $m_i + (m_i - 1) = 2m_i - 1$.

Hence $s_2 \le 99$, and if $s_i \le 101 - i$ then $s_{i+1} \le \max(100 - i,\ 101 - 2i) = 100 - i$. By induction the final score is $s_{26} \le 75$.

**Conclusion.** With perfect play Winnie wins exactly \$75. (For instance, with these strategies the piles can end as $\{1, 3, 5, \dots, 49, 50\}$ with sum 675 and $\{2, 4, \dots, 48\}$ with sum 600.)

**Answer: \$75**

solutions.title: Check on small decks
solutions.body:
The same two strategies work for a deck $1, \dots, 2m$: Winnie pairs $\{2m - 1, 2m\}$ on one pile and $m - 1$ small pairs on opposite piles, getting at least $(4m - 1) - (m - 1) = 3m$; Grogg's greedy strategy gives at most $3m$. A full game-tree search (minimax) for decks of $2, 4, \dots, 14$ cards gives values $3, 6, 9, \dots, 21$, i.e. exactly $3m$, confirming the pattern. For $50$ cards, $m = 25$ and the value is $3\cdot 25 = 75$.

**Answer: \$75**

prompt:
We call a positive integer $n$ *sixish* if $n = p(p+6)$, where $p$ and $p+6$ are prime numbers. For example, $187 = 11\cdot 17$ is sixish, but $475 = 19\cdot 25$ is not sixish.

Define a function $f$ on positive integers such that $f(n)$ is the sum of the squares of the positive divisors of $n$. For example, $f(10) = 1^2 + 2^2 + 5^2 + 10^2 = 130$.

(a) Find, with proof, an irreducible polynomial function $g(x)$ with integer coefficients such that $f(n) = g(n)$ for all sixish $n$. ("Irreducible" means that $g(x)$ cannot be factored as the product of two polynomials of smaller degree with integer coefficients.)

(b) We call a positive integer $n$ *pseudo-sixish* if $n$ is not sixish but nonetheless $f(n) = g(n)$, where $g(n)$ is the polynomial function that you found in part (a). Find, with proof, all pseudo-sixish positive integers.
answer: (a) $g(x) = x^2 + 2x + 37$. (b) The only pseudo-sixish number is $27$.

solutions.title: Pair up the divisors
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $n = p(p+6)$ with both factors prime, the divisors are $1, p, p+6, n$, so
$$f(n) = 1 + p^2 + (p+6)^2 + n^2 = n^2 + 2p(p+6) + 37 = n^2 + 2n + 37.$$
Take $g(x) = x^2 + 2x + 37$. Its discriminant $4 - 148 < 0$, so it has no rational roots and, being quadratic, is irreducible over the integers.

**(b)** We need all $n$ with $f(n) = n^2 + 2n + 37$, i.e.
$$\sum_{d \mid n,\ 1 < d < n} d^2 = 2n + 36. \qquad (*)$$
Pair each proper divisor $d$ with $n/d$. For a pair $d < n/d$:
$$d^2 + (n/d)^2 = (n/d - d)^2 + 2n \ge 2n + 1.$$

* $n = 1$: the left side of $(*)$ is $0 \ne 38$. $n$ prime: left side $0 \ne 2n + 36$.
* $n = p^2$: left side $p^2$, and $p^2 = 2p^2 + 36$ is impossible.
* **Exactly four divisors** ($n = pq$ with primes $p < q$, or $n = p^3$): one pair $r < s$ with $rs = n$, and $(*)$ becomes $(s - r)^2 + 2n = 2n + 36$, so $s - r = 6$. For $n = pq$ this is $q = p + 6$ — sixish, excluded. For $n = p^3$ it is $p^2 - p = 6$, so $p = 3$ and $n = 27$. Indeed $f(27) = 1 + 9 + 81 + 729 = 820 = 27^2 + 54 + 37$. ✓
* **Five divisors** ($n = p^4$): $p^2 + p^4 + p^6 = 2p^4 + 36$, i.e. $p^6 - p^4 + p^2 = 36$; for $p = 2$ the left side is $52$, and it is increasing in $p$. No solution.
* **At least six divisors**: there are at least two pairs, so the left side of $(*)$ is at least $2(2n + 1) = 4n + 2$, which exceeds $2n + 36$ once $n \ge 17$. The numbers below 17 with at least six divisors are $12$ (left side $4+9+16+36 = 65 \ne 60$). No solution.

Hence the only pseudo-sixish number is $27$. ∎

solutions.title: Official approach: $x_n = 36 - (s-r)^2$
solutions.body:
Let $h(n) = g(n) - f(n)$. One checks $h(1) = 39$, $h(p) = 2p + 36$ and $h(p^2) = p^2 + 36$, so pseudo-sixish numbers are not $1$, primes or prime squares. Otherwise write $n = rs$ with $1 < r < s$ (e.g. $r$ the smallest prime factor) and let $x_n$ be the sum of the squares of the divisors other than $1, r, s, n$. Then
$$0 = h(n) = 2rs + 36 - r^2 - s^2 - x_n \iff x_n = 36 - (s - r)^2.$$
If $x_n = 0$, the only divisors are $1, r, s, n$, so $n = pq$ (sixish when $s - r = 6$) or $n = r^3$ with $r^2 - r = 6$, i.e. $n = 27$. If $x_n > 0$ then $x_n \in \{11, 20, 27, 32, 35\}$ must be a sum of distinct squares of divisors larger than 1; only $20 = 2^2 + 4^2$ works, forcing the divisors $1, 2, 4, r, s, n$ — six divisors, so $n = 4q$ or $n = 32$, and neither fits $n = rs$ with the extra divisors exactly $2, 4$. So $27$ is the only one.

A computer check of all $n \le 10^6$ confirms: the solutions of $f(n) = n^2 + 2n + 37$ are $27$ and the sixish numbers $55, 91, 187, \dots$.

**Answer: (a) $g(x) = x^2 + 2x + 37$; (b) only $27$.** ∎

prompt:
Fill in the grid shown with the numbers 1 through 25, with each number used exactly once, subject to the following constraints:

1. Each shaded square contains an even number, and each unshaded square contains an odd number.
2. For any pair of squares that share a side, if $x$ and $y$ are the two numbers in those squares, then either $x \ge 2y$ or $y \ge 2x$.

Four numbers have been filled in already.

The grid is a diamond with rows of $1, 3, 5, 7, 5, 3, 1$ squares (centered). The given numbers are $16$ (top square), $25$ (first square of row 3), $13$ (center square) and $21$ (last square of row 5). The shaded squares are: the top square; the first two squares of row 2; the 2nd, 4th and 5th squares of row 3; the 1st and 5th squares of row 4; the 2nd and 4th squares of row 5; the 3rd square of row 6; and the bottom square.

There is a unique solution, but you do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible. You merely need to find an answer that satisfies the conditions of the problem.
answer:
The unique solution (even numbers are in the shaded squares):
$$\begin{array}{ccccccc} & & & 16 & & & \\ & & 24 & 6 & 17 & & \\ & 25 & 12 & 3 & 8 & 18 & \\ 22 & 11 & 5 & 13 & 4 & 9 & 19\\ & 23 & 2 & 1 & 10 & 21 & \\ & & 15 & 7 & 20 & & \\ & & & 14 & & & \end{array}$$

solutions.title: Place the extreme numbers first
solutions.body:
Two neighbours must differ by at least a factor of 2, so **large numbers can only sit next to small numbers**, and the numbers $13$–$25$ can never be adjacent to each other (the smaller would have to be at most half of the larger, i.e. at most 12). Similarly a number $x$ in $7$–$12$ can only touch numbers $\le x/2$ or $\ge 2x$.

* The center $13$ has four neighbours, all of which must be $\le 6$ (since $2\cdot 13 = 26 > 25$). Odd parity of three of them and even of one (from the shading) gives neighbours $5, 3, 1$ (odd) and $4$ (even, the shaded square right of center).
* $16$ (top) has a single neighbour, which must be even and $\le 8$; following the other forced placements it turns out to be $6$, whose other neighbours must then be $\le 3$ or $\ge 12$: $3$ below it and the large numbers $24$, $17$ beside it.
* $25$ needs neighbours $\le 12$: $12$ (right) and $11$ (below). $21$ needs neighbours $\le 10$: $10$ and $9$.
* The small numbers $1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7$ go around the center, and the remaining large numbers $14, 15, 18, 19, 20, 22, 23$ fill the tips and edges next to them.

Continuing in this way (each placement leaves only one option for some square) gives
$$\begin{array}{ccccccc} & & & 16 & & & \\ & & 24 & 6 & 17 & & \\ & 25 & 12 & 3 & 8 & 18 & \\ 22 & 11 & 5 & 13 & 4 & 9 & 19\\ & 23 & 2 & 1 & 10 & 21 & \\ & & 15 & 7 & 20 & & \\ & & & 14 & & & \end{array}$$

**Check.** All shaded squares hold the even numbers $2, 4, \dots, 24$, the unshaded squares hold the odd numbers, and every pair of side-neighbours, e.g. $13$ with $3, 5, 1, 4$; $25$ with $12, 11$; $21$ with $10, 9$; $22$ with $11$; $19$ with $9$; $14$ with $7$, satisfies $x \ge 2y$. A computer search confirms this is the only solution.

**Answer: the grid above.**

prompt:
Grogg's favorite positive integer is $n \ge 2$, and Grogg has a lucky coin that comes up heads with some fixed probability $p$, where $0 < p < 1$. Once each day, Grogg flips his coin, and if it comes up heads, he does two things:

1. He eats a cookie.
2. He then flips the coin $n$ more times. If the result of these $n$ flips is $n-1$ heads and 1 tail (in any order), he eats another cookie.

He never eats a cookie except as a result of his coin flips. Find all possible values of $n$ and $p$ such that the expected value of the number of cookies that Grogg eats each day is exactly 1.

solutions.title: Linearity of expectation
solutions.body:
The first cookie is eaten with probability $p$. The second cookie needs a first head (probability $p$) and then exactly $n-1$ heads among $n$ flips, which has probability $\binom{n}{n-1}p^{n-1}(1-p) = np^{n-1}(1-p)$. By linearity of expectation the expected number of cookies is
$$E = p + p\cdot np^{n-1}(1-p) = p + np^n - np^{n+1}.$$
Setting $E = 1$:
$$0 = p - 1 + np^n(1 - p) = (p - 1)(1 - np^n).$$
Since $p < 1$, we need $np^n = 1$, i.e. $p = n^{-1/n}$. For every $n \ge 2$ this value lies strictly between 0 and 1 (because $n > 1$), so it is admissible.

Check with $n = 4$: $p = 4^{-1/4} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, and $E = p + 4p^4(1-p) = p + (1 - p) = 1$. ✓

**Answer: every $n \ge 2$, with $p = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt[n]{n}}$.**

prompt: Let $n \ge 3$ be a positive integer. Alex and Lizzie play a game. Alex chooses $n$ positive integers (not necessarily distinct), writes them on a blackboard, and does nothing further. Then, Lizzie is allowed to pick some of the numbers—but not all of them—and replace them each by their average. For example, if $n = 7$ and the numbers Alex writes on the blackboard to start are $1, 2, 4, 5, 9, 4, 11$, then on her first turn Lizzie could pick $1, 4, 9$, erase them, and replace them each with the number $\frac{1+4+9}{3}$, leaving on the blackboard the numbers $\frac{14}{3}, 2, \frac{14}{3}, 5, \frac{14}{3}, 4, 11$. Lizzie can repeat this process of selecting and averaging some numbers as often as she wants. Lizzie wins the game if eventually all of the numbers written on the blackboard are equal. Find all positive integers $n \ge 3$ such that no matter what numbers Alex picks, Lizzie can win the game.
answer: Exactly the **composite** $n$. (Composite $n = rs$: average the rows, then the columns of an $r\times s$ array. Prime $n$: start with $1, \dots, 1, 2$; the final value would be $\frac{n+1}{n}$, but no denominator can ever contain the prime $n$.)

solutions.title: Rows and columns vs. denominators
solutions.body:
**Composite $n$: Lizzie wins.** Write $n = rs$ with $1 < r, s < n$ and arrange the numbers in an $r \times s$ array. First average each row (a set of $s < n$ numbers), one row per turn. Now every row consists of a single repeated value, so all columns are identical copies of one another. Then average each column ($r < n$ numbers). Each column becomes constant with value equal to the average of its entries, and since all columns were identical, all these averages are the same. Now all $n$ numbers are equal.

**Prime $n$: Alex wins.** Alex writes $n - 1$ ones and one $2$. Averaging a group does not change the total, so the sum is always $n + 1$; if all numbers became equal, each would be $\frac{n+1}{n}$, a fraction in lowest terms with denominator $n$ (as $\gcd(n+1, n) = 1$).

But we claim every number ever on the board is a fraction whose (reduced) denominator has only prime factors smaller than $n$. This holds at the start (integers). In a move, Lizzie picks $k < n$ numbers; their sum is a fraction whose denominator divides the product of their denominators, hence again has only prime factors $< n$, and dividing by $k < n$ introduces only primes $\le k < n$. So the claim persists. Since the prime $n$ never appears in a denominator, the board can never show $\frac{n+1}{n}$, and Lizzie cannot win.

**Answer: all composite $n \ge 4$.** ∎

prompt:
A *lattice point* of the coordinate plane is a point $(x, y)$ in which both $x$ and $y$ are integers. Let $k \ge 2$ be a positive integer. Find the smallest positive integer $c_k$ (which may depend on $k$) such that every lattice point can be colored with one of $c_k$ colors, subject to the following two conditions:

1. If $(x, y)$ and $(a, b)$ are two distinct neighboring points; that is, $|x-a| \le 1$ and $|y-b| \le 1$, then $(x, y)$ and $(a, b)$ must be different colors.
2. If $(x, y)$ and $(a, b)$ are two lattice points such that $x \equiv a \pmod k$ and $y \equiv b \pmod k$, then $(x, y)$ and $(a, b)$ must be the same color.
answer: $c_k = 4$ if $k$ is even, $c_3 = 9$, and $c_k = 5$ if $k \ge 5$ is odd.

solutions.title: Bounds and constructions
solutions.body:
Call two distinct lattice points *adjacent* if they are neighbours as in condition 1. The four points of any $2\times 2$ square are pairwise adjacent, so $c_k \ge 4$ always.

**$k$ even: 4 colors.** Color $(x, y)$ by the pair $(x \bmod 2,\ y \bmod 2)$. Adjacent points differ by $1$ in at least one coordinate, so they get different colors; and since $k$ is even, $x \equiv a \pmod k$ implies $x \equiv a \pmod 2$, so condition 2 holds.

**$k = 3$: 9 colors.** Any two different residue classes $(a, b) \ne (a', b')$ mod 3 contain adjacent points, because every residue mod 3 is $0$ or $\pm 1$: take $(a, b)$ and $(a + \delta, b + \varepsilon)$ with $\delta \equiv a' - a$, $\varepsilon \equiv b' - b$, $\delta, \varepsilon \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$. So the 9 classes need 9 different colors, and coloring by class works. $c_3 = 9$.

**$k \ge 5$ odd: 4 colors are not enough.** Suppose 4 colors suffice. Let $S_x$ be the set of the two colors of $(x, 0)$ and $(x, 1)$. The $2\times 2$ square with columns $x, x+1$ uses all four colors, so $S_{x+1}$ is the complement of $S_x$. Hence $S_0, S_1, S_2, \dots$ alternate between two disjoint sets, and as $k$ is odd, $S_k \ne S_0$. But condition 2 says $(k, 0), (k, 1)$ have the same colors as $(0, 0), (0, 1)$. Contradiction, so $c_k \ge 5$.

**$k \ge 5$ odd: 5 colors suffice.** Choose integers $u_0, \dots, u_{k-1}$ with
$$u = (0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 3, 4, \dots, 3, 4)$$
(after $0,1,2,3,4$ the pair $3, 4$ is repeated $\frac{k-5}{2}$ times). Consecutive terms differ by $\pm 1$, and also $u_0 - u_{k-1} = 0 - 4 \equiv 1 \pmod 5$, so cyclically consecutive terms differ by $\pm 1 \pmod 5$. Color $(x, y)$ with
$$c(x, y) = u_{x \bmod k} + 2u_{y \bmod k} \pmod 5.$$
Condition 2 holds by construction. For adjacent points the color difference is $\delta + 2\varepsilon \pmod 5$ with $\delta, \varepsilon \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ not both $0$, i.e. one of $\pm1, \pm2, \pm3$ — never $0 \bmod 5$. So the coloring is proper.

(The official solution gives an explicit $5\times 5$ pattern and extends it by repeating columns and rows with period 2; the idea is the same. A computer check of the chromatic numbers for $k = 2, \dots, 6$ gives $4, 9, 4, 5, 4$, and the 5-coloring above was checked by computer for all odd $k$ from 5 to 29.)

**Answer: $c_k = 4$ for even $k$, $c_3 = 9$, $c_k = 5$ for odd $k \ge 5$.** ∎

prompt: Let $r$ and $s$ be positive real numbers, and let $A = (0, 0)$, $B = (1, 0)$, $C = (r, s)$, and $D = (r + 1, s)$ be points on the coordinate plane. Find a point $P$, whose coordinates are expressed in terms of $r$ and $s$, with the following property: if $E$ is any point on the interior of line segment $AB$, and $F$ is the unique point other than $E$ that lies on the circumcircles of triangles $BCE$ and $ADE$, then $P$ lies on line $\overleftrightarrow{EF}$.

solutions.title: Radical axis in coordinates
solutions.body:
Line $EF$ is the radical axis of the two circles, i.e. the difference of their equations. Let $E = (e, 0)$ with $0 < e < 1$.

**Circle $ADE$.** It passes through $(0,0)$ and $(e, 0)$, so it has the form $x^2 + y^2 - ex + q_1 y = 0$. Plugging in $D = (r+1, s)$:
$$q_1 = \frac{e(r+1) - (r+1)^2 - s^2}{s}.$$

**Circle $BCE$.** It passes through $(1, 0)$ and $(e, 0)$, so it has the form $x^2 + y^2 - (1+e)x + e + q_2 y = 0$. Plugging in $C = (r, s)$:
$$q_2 = \frac{(1+e)r - e - r^2 - s^2}{s}.$$

**Radical axis.** Subtracting the equations gives the line through both intersection points $E$ and $F$:
$$x - e + (q_1 - q_2)\,y = 0, \qquad q_1 - q_2 = \frac{2e - 3r - 1}{s}.$$
Rearranged:
$$\left(x - \frac{(3r+1)\,y}{s}\right) + e\left(\frac{2y}{s} - 1\right) = 0.$$
This holds for **every** $e$ exactly when both brackets vanish: $y = \frac s2$ and $x = \frac{3r+1}{2}$. So every line $EF$ passes through
$$P = \left(\frac{3r+1}{2}, \frac s2\right).$$

**Answer: $P = \left(\frac{3r+1}{2}, \frac{s}{2}\right)$.**

solutions.title: Synthetic: an isosceles trapezoid (official idea)
solutions.body:
$ABDC$ is a parallelogram ($AB$ and $CD$ are parallel of length 1). Let $G = \left(\frac{r+1}{2}, \frac s2\right)$ be the intersection of its diagonals $AD$ and $BC$.

**Claim 1: $C, D, F, G$ are concyclic.** (In the configuration with $F$ on the same side of $CD$ as $E$; the other case is a similar angle chase.)
$$\angle DFC = \angle DFE - \angle CFE = (180^\circ - \angle DAE) - \angle CBE = \angle AGB = \angle DGC,$$
using that $AEFD$ and $CFBE$ are cyclic, the angle sum in triangle $ABG$, and vertical angles at $G$.

**Claim 2.** Let line $EF$ meet this circle again at $P$. Then
$$\angle DGP = 180^\circ - \angle DFP = \angle DAE = \angle CDG = \angle CPG,$$
using the cyclic quadrilaterals $DFPG$, $DFEA$, the parallel lines $AB \parallel CD$, and the circle $CDPG$. So $CDPG$ is an isosceles trapezoid with $GP \parallel CD$.

Thus $P$ lies on the horizontal line $y = \frac s2$ through $G$, and the trapezoid is symmetric about the perpendicular bisector $x = r + \frac12$ of $CD$. Reflecting $G$ in this line gives $P = \left(2r + 1 - \frac{r+1}{2}, \frac s2\right) = \left(\frac{3r+1}{2}, \frac s2\right)$, independent of $E$.

**Answer: $P = \left(\frac{3r+1}{2}, \frac{s}{2}\right)$.**

solutions.title: Start with the long lines of stars
solutions.body:
Number rows and columns $1$–$8$ from the top left. A marked square sees at most one label in each of the four directions (the first label it meets), and marked squares do not block the view.

* **Row 1** has stars in columns 3–7, so its X and Y lie in columns 1, 2 or 8. If both were on the left, each of these stars would see only one label in the row plus at most one below — fewer than 3. So one label is in column 8 and the other in column 1 or 2. Every row-1 star then sees one X and one Y in the row, so **the topmost label in each of columns 3–7 is an X**.
* **Column 8** has stars in rows 2–5 and a heart in row 6, so its two labels are in row 1 and in row 7 or 8. Each of the four stars sees both of them (one X, one Y), so **the rightmost label in each of rows 2–5 is an X**. The heart in row 6 also sees both, so **the rightmost label in row 6 is a Y**.
* The star in row 7, column 5 and the heart in row 4, column 2 then pin down the remaining positions.

Continuing these deductions gives
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline X & \phantom{X} & \star & \star & \star & \star & \star & Y\\\hline \phantom{X} & Y & X & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & Y & X & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \heartsuit & \phantom{X} & Y & \phantom{X} & X & \phantom{X} & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & Y & X & \star\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & X & \phantom{X} & Y & \heartsuit\\\hline Y & X & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \star & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X}\\\hline \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & Y & \phantom{X} & \phantom{X} & X\\\hline\end{array}$$

**Check.** Every row and column contains exactly one X and one Y, no marked square is labeled, each of the ten stars sees exactly two X's and one Y, and each of the two hearts sees exactly one X and two Y's. A computer search over all placements confirms the solution is unique.

**Answer: the grid above.**

prompt:
Let $\mathbb{Z}^+$ denote the set of positive integers. Determine, with proof, if there exists a function $f : \mathbb{Z}^+ \to \mathbb{Z}^+$ such that
$$f(f(f(f(f(n))))) = 2022n$$
for all positive integers $n$.
answer:
**Yes.** E.g. with a prime $p 
mid 2022$ (say $p = 5$) and $v = 
u_p(n)$: $f(n) = pn$ if $v 
ot\equiv 4 \pmod 5$, and $f(n) =  rac{2022\,n}{p^4}$ if $v \equiv 4 \pmod 5$.

solutions.title: Cycle the exponent of a spare prime
solutions.body:
Let $p$ be a prime not dividing $2022 = 2\cdot 3\cdot 337$, e.g. $p = 5$, and let $\nu_p(n)$ be the exponent of $p$ in $n$. Define
$$f(n) = \begin{cases} p\,n & \text{if } \nu_p(n) \not\equiv 4 \pmod 5,\\[2pt] \dfrac{2022\,n}{p^4} & \text{if } \nu_p(n) \equiv 4 \pmod 5.\end{cases}$$
In the second case $\nu_p(n) \ge 4$, so $f(n)$ is a positive integer.

**Effect on the exponent.** In the first case $\nu_p$ increases by 1; in the second case it decreases by 4 (since $p \nmid 2022$). In both cases the residue of $\nu_p$ modulo 5 increases by 1: $0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4 \to 0$.

**Five applications.** Starting from $n$, the residues of $\nu_p$ before each of the five applications run through all five classes mod 5, each exactly once. So exactly one of the five steps (the one starting in class 4) multiplies by $\frac{2022}{p^4}$, and the other four multiply by $p$. Multiplication commutes, so
$$f^{5}(n) = n\cdot p^4\cdot \frac{2022}{p^4} = 2022\,n.$$

So such a function exists. ∎ (Many other functions work too.)

prompt:
A positive integer $N$ is called *googolicious* if there are exactly $10^{100}$ positive integers $x$ that satisfy the equation
$$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{\left\lfloor \frac{N}{x} \right\rfloor} \right\rfloor = x,$$
where $\lfloor z \rfloor$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $z$. Find, with proof, all googolicious integers.

solutions.title: Count solutions via $m = \lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$
solutions.body:
Only $1 \le x \le N$ can work (for $x > N$ the inner floor is $0$). For such $x$ write $N = qx + r$ with $q = \lfloor N/x\rfloor \ge 1$ and $0 \le r < x$. Then
$$\left\lfloor \frac{N}{q}\right\rfloor = \left\lfloor x + \frac rq\right\rfloor = x + \left\lfloor \frac rq\right\rfloor,$$
so **$x$ is a solution iff $r < q$**, and then $\lfloor N/q\rfloor = x$.

Let $m = \lfloor\sqrt N\rfloor$, so $m^2 \le N < (m+1)^2$.

**Small solutions, $x \le m$.** Then $q = \lfloor N/x\rfloor \ge \lfloor N/m\rfloor \ge m \ge x > r$, so all $m$ values $x = 1, \dots, m$ are solutions.

**Large solutions, $x > m$.** Then $q \le N/x < (m+1)^2/(m+1) = m+1$, so $q \le m$, and $x = \lfloor N/q\rfloor$ is determined by $q$. Conversely, for each $q \in \{1, \dots, m\}$ put $x = \lfloor N/q\rfloor$, $N = qx + r'$ with $r' < q$. Since $x \ge \lfloor N/m\rfloor \ge m \ge q > r'$, we get $\lfloor N/x\rfloor = q$ and $\lfloor N/q\rfloor = x$: $x$ is a solution. So the large solutions correspond to those $q \le m$ with $\lfloor N/q\rfloor > m$. For $q \le m - 1$ we have $N/q \ge \frac{m^2}{m-1} > m + 1$, so these all count; for $q = m$, $\lfloor N/m\rfloor > m$ iff $N \ge m(m+1)$.

**Total.**
$$\#\text{solutions} = \begin{cases} 2m & \text{if } N \ge m(m+1),\\ 2m - 1 & \text{if } N < m(m+1).\end{cases}$$
(A computer check of all $N < 3000$ agrees.)

**Googolicious.** $10^{100}$ is even, so we need $m = 5\cdot 10^{99}$ and $N \ge m(m+1)$, together with $N < (m+1)^2$:
$$25\cdot 10^{198} + 5\cdot 10^{99} \le N \le 25\cdot 10^{198} + 10^{100}.$$
∎

prompt: Let $\omega$ be a circle with center $O$ and radius 10, and let $H$ be a point such that $OH = 6$. A point $P$ is called *snug* if, for all triangles $ABC$ with circumcircle $\omega$ and orthocenter $H$, we have that $P$ lies on $\triangle ABC$ or in the interior of $\triangle ABC$. Find the area of the region consisting of all snug points.

solutions.title: The ellipse with foci $O$ and $H$
solutions.body:
Let $\mathcal E$ be the closed region $\{X : OX + XH \le 10\}$, an ellipse with foci $O, H$ and major axis $10$. We show that the snug points are exactly $\mathcal E$.

**Lemma.** In a triangle $ABC$ with orthocenter $H$, the reflection $A'$ of $H$ in line $BC$ lies on the circumcircle. *Proof.* The triangles here are acute (from $\sin^2A + \sin^2B + \sin^2C = 2 + 2\cos A\cos B\cos C$ and $OH^2 = 9R^2 - (a^2+b^2+c^2)$, $OH < R$ forces $\cos A\cos B\cos C > 0$). With $H$ inside, $\angle BHC = 180^\circ - \angle A$ (in quadrilateral formed by $A$, the feet of two altitudes and $H$), so $\angle BA'C = \angle BHC = 180^\circ - \angle A$ and $A'$ (on the other side of $BC$) lies on the circle. $\square$

**Each side is tangent to $\mathcal E$.** For any point $X$ on line $BC$, $XH = XA'$, so
$$OX + XH = OX + XA' \ge OA' = 10,$$
with equality exactly where segment $OA'$ crosses $BC$. Hence line $BC$ touches $\mathcal E$ but does not enter its interior. Since $\mathcal E$ is convex and contains $O$ (as $0 + 6 < 10$), and $O$ is on the same side of $BC$ as $A$ (acute triangle), $\mathcal E$ lies in the closed half-plane of $BC$ containing $A$. The same holds for the other two sides, so $\mathcal E \subseteq \triangle ABC$ for every such triangle: **all points of $\mathcal E$ are snug**.

**Nothing else is snug.** Let $Q \notin \mathcal E$ and let ray $OQ$ meet the boundary of $\mathcal E$ at $T$. Let $t$ be the tangent line to $\mathcal E$ at $T$ and $A'$ the reflection of $H$ in $t$; by the reflection property of the ellipse, $O, T, A'$ are collinear and $OA' = OT + TH = 10$, so $A' \in \omega$. Line $t$ passes through $T$, which is inside $\omega$, so it meets $\omega$ at two points $B, C$; let line $A'H$ meet $\omega$ again at $A$. The altitude from $A$ is line $AA'$ (perpendicular to $t = BC$), and the orthocenter is the point on it whose reflection in $BC$ lies on $\omega$, namely $H$. So $ABC$ is an admissible triangle, its side $BC$ separates $O$ from $Q$ (the segment $OQ$ crosses $t$ at $T$ and $Q$ lies beyond it), and $Q$ is outside $\triangle ABC$: not snug.

**Area.** The ellipse has $2a = 10$, focal distance $2c = 6$, so $a = 5$, $c = 3$, $b = \sqrt{25 - 9} = 4$, and area $\pi ab = 20\pi$.

**Answer: $20\pi$**

prompt: A lattice point is a point on the coordinate plane with integer coordinates. Prove or disprove: there exists a finite set $S$ of lattice points such that for every line $\ell$ in the plane with slope $0$, $1$, $-1$, or undefined, either $\ell$ and $S$ intersect at exactly 2022 points, or they do not intersect.
answer: **True (such $S$ exists).** With $k = 2022$, take $S = \{(a + kb + 2k^2c,\ -a + kb + 2k^3d) : 0 \le a, b, c, d < k\}$; each of the four line directions fixes three of $a, b, c, d$ and leaves the fourth free.

solutions.title: A four-parameter construction
solutions.body:
Let $k = 2022$ (any $k \ge 1$ works) and
$$S = \{(a + kb + 2k^2c,\ \ -a + kb + 2k^3d) : a, b, c, d \in \{0, 1, \dots, k-1\}\}.$$

**Two facts.** (i) The numbers $a + kb$ take each value in $[0, k^2)$ exactly once (base-$k$ digits). (ii) The numbers $kb - a$ take each value in $[-(k-1), k^2 - k]$ exactly once — $k^2$ consecutive integers — so they are distinct modulo $k^2$.

**The points are distinct.** Since $x = (a + kb) + 2k^2c$ with $0 \le a + kb < k^2$, the value of $x$ determines $c$ (quotient by $2k^2$) and $a + kb$ (remainder), hence $(a, b, c)$ by fact (i); then $y$ determines $d$. So $|S| = k^4$.

For each line, we show the intersection points are obtained by fixing three of the parameters uniquely and letting the fourth run freely over its $k$ values; hence each line meets $S$ in $0$ or exactly $k$ points.

* **Vertical, $x = n$:** $(a + kb) + 2k^2 c = n$ determines $(a, b, c)$ (if a solution exists); $d$ is free.
* **Horizontal, $y = n$:** $(kb - a) + 2k^3 d = n$. Modulo $k^2$ this fixes $kb - a$ by fact (ii), hence $(a, b)$, and then $d$; $c$ is free.
* **Slope 1, $x - y = n$:** $x - y = 2(a + k^2 c - k^3 d)$. The number $a + k^2c$ lies in $[0, k^3)$ and is determined by $n/2 \bmod k^3$; it determines $(a, c)$ (digits), and then $d$. $b$ is free.
* **Slope $-1$, $x + y = n$:** $x + y = 2k(b + kc + k^2 d)$, and $b + kc + k^2d$ determines $(b, c, d)$ (base-$k$ digits). $a$ is free.

So every such line meets $S$ in either no points or exactly $k = 2022$ points. (A computer check confirms the construction for $k = 3, 4, 5$.) ∎

prompt:
Fill each unshaded cell of the grid with a number that is either 1, 3, or 5. For each cell, exactly one of the touching cells must contain the same number. Here touching includes cells that only share a point, i.e. touch diagonally.

The grid is shown in the picture; below, shaded cells are drawn as $\blacksquare$:
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline 1 & \phantom{0} & 1 & \phantom{0} & 3 & \phantom{0} & 5\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & 1 & 1 & 3 & 5 & \phantom{0}\\\hline \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \blacksquare\\\hline \phantom{0} & \blacksquare & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline 5 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & 5 & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0} & \phantom{0}\\\hline\end{array}$$

There is a unique solution, but you do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible. You merely need to find an answer that satisfies the conditions of the problem.

solutions.title: Pairs of equal numbers
solutions.body:
The rule says that the cells with the same number come in **touching pairs**: every cell has exactly one touching cell with its own number, so equal numbers form "dominoes" (possibly diagonal) that do not touch any other cell with that number.

Number rows $1$–$7$ from the top and columns $1$–$7$ from the left.

* The given $1, 1$ in row 4 (columns 3, 4) touch each other, so they are a complete pair: **no other cell touching them can be a 1**. This rules out 1 in row 3, columns 2, 3, 5 in row 5, columns 2–4, and in row 4, column 2.
* The cells in row 2, column 2 and row 1, column 2 touch both given 1's of row 2, so they cannot be 1 (they would see two 1's). Hence the 1 in row 2, column 1 must pair with row 1, column 1 or row 3, column 1, and the 1 in row 2, column 3 with row 1, column 3 or 4, or row 2, column 4.
* Similarly the given $3$ and $5$ in rows 2 and 4 each need exactly one partner, and the two $5$'s in row 7 each need one; a cell that touches two equal given numbers can never take that number.

Repeating these partner arguments (every cell has at most 8 neighbours, and each completed pair removes options from all cells around it) leads to
$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline 5 & 3 & 3 & 5 & 5 & 3 & 5\\\hline 1 & 5 & 1 & 1 & 3 & 1 & 5\\\hline 1 & 3 & 3 & \blacksquare & 5 & 1 & 3\\\hline \blacksquare & 5 & 1 & 1 & 3 & 5 & 3\\\hline 3 & 3 & 5 & 3 & \blacksquare & 1 & \blacksquare\\\hline 5 & \blacksquare & 1 & 1 & 5 & 1 & 5\\\hline 5 & 3 & 3 & 5 & 3 & 3 & 5\\\hline\end{array}$$

**Check.** Each of the 44 unshaded cells has exactly one touching cell (including diagonals) with the same number; for example the top-left $5$ has neighbours $3$, $1$, $5$ — exactly one 5. A computer search over all fillings confirms the solution is unique.

**Answer: the grid above.**

prompt:
Suppose that the 101 positive integers
$$2024,\ 2025,\ 2026,\ \dots,\ 2124$$
are concatenated in some order to form a 404-digit number. Can this number be prime?
answer: **No.** Since $10^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{9999}$, the number is $\equiv 2024 + 2025 + \dots + 2124 = 101\cdot 2074 \pmod{9999}$, and $101 \mid 9999$, so the number is a multiple of $101$.

solutions.title: Work modulo 101
solutions.body:
Each of the numbers has 4 digits, so the concatenation is
$$N = a_{100}\cdot 10^{400} + a_{99}\cdot 10^{396} + \dots + a_1\cdot 10^4 + a_0,$$
where $a_0, \dots, a_{100}$ is some ordering of $2024, \dots, 2124$.

Since $10^2 = 100 \equiv -1 \pmod{101}$, we have $10^4 \equiv 1 \pmod{101}$, and therefore
$$N \equiv a_{100} + a_{99} + \dots + a_0 = 2024 + 2025 + \dots + 2124 \pmod{101}.$$
This sum has 101 terms with average $\frac{2024 + 2124}{2} = 2074$, so it equals $101\cdot 2074$, a multiple of 101. (Equivalently, work modulo $9999 = 99\cdot 101$, where $10^4 \equiv 1$ as well.)

Hence $101 \mid N$ for every ordering, and since $N > 101$, $N$ is never prime.

**Answer: No.** ∎

prompt: Let $n \ge 2$ be a positive integer, and suppose buildings of height $1, 2, \dots, n$ are built in a row on a street. Two distinct buildings are said to be *roof-friendly* if every building between the two is shorter than both buildings in the pair.
