$$\frac{a_1}{k^2 + 1} + \frac{a_2}{k^2 + 2} + \frac{a_3}{k^2 + 3} + \frac{a_4}{k^2 + 4} + \frac{a_5}{k^2 + 5} = \frac{1}{k^2} \quad \text{for } k = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.$$
Find the value of $\dfrac{a_1}{37} + \dfrac{a_2}{38} + \dfrac{a_3}{39} + \dfrac{a_4}{40} + \dfrac{a_5}{41}$. (Express the value in a single fraction.)

solutions.title: A polynomial with known roots
solutions.body:
Let $R(x)=\sum_{i=1}^5\frac{a_i}{x^2+i}$; we want $R(6)$. The hypothesis says $R(k)=\frac1{k^2}$ for $k=\pm1,\dots,\pm5$.

Let $P(x)=\prod_{i=1}^5(x^2+i)$ and $Q(x)=R(x)P(x)$, a polynomial of degree at most $8$. Then $P(x)-x^2Q(x)$ is a polynomial of degree at most $10$ that vanishes at the ten numbers $x=\pm1,\pm2,\dots,\pm5$ (there $x^2Q(x)=x^2R(x)P(x)=P(x)$). Hence
$$P(x)-x^2Q(x)=A\,(x^2-1)(x^2-4)(x^2-9)(x^2-16)(x^2-25)$$
for a constant $A$. At $x=0$: $P(0)=120$ and $(-1)(-4)(-9)(-16)(-25)=-14400$, so $A=-\frac{1}{120}$. Dividing by $P(x)$:
$$1-x^2R(x)=-\frac1{120}\cdot\frac{(x^2-1)(x^2-4)(x^2-9)(x^2-16)(x^2-25)}{(x^2+1)(x^2+2)(x^2+3)(x^2+4)(x^2+5)} .$$
At $x=6$:
$$1-36R(6)=-\frac{35\cdot32\cdot27\cdot20\cdot11}{120\cdot37\cdot38\cdot39\cdot40\cdot41}=-\frac{231}{374699},$$
because $\frac{35\cdot32\cdot27\cdot20\cdot11}{120\cdot40}=\frac{6652800}{4800}=1386$ and $37\cdot38\cdot39\cdot41=2248194$, and $\frac{1386}{2248194}=\frac{231}{374699}$ (divide by $6$; $374699=13\cdot19\cdot37\cdot41$).

Hence $36R(6)=1+\frac{231}{374699}=\frac{374930}{374699}$ and
$$R(6)=\frac{374930}{36\cdot374699}=\frac{187465}{6744582}.$$

**Answer:** $\dfrac{187465}{6744582}$.

solutions.title: Solve the system (check)
solutions.body:
Solving the $5\times5$ linear system directly (tedious but mechanical) gives
$$a_1=\frac{1105}{72},\quad a_2=-\frac{2673}{40},\quad a_3=\frac{1862}{15},\quad a_4=-\frac{1885}{18},\quad a_5=\frac{1323}{40},$$
and then $\frac{a_1}{37}+\frac{a_2}{38}+\frac{a_3}{39}+\frac{a_4}{40}+\frac{a_5}{41}=\frac{187465}{6744582}$, confirming the first method.

prompt: Let three circles $\Gamma_1, \Gamma_2, \Gamma_3$, which are non-overlapping and mutually external, be given in the plane. For each point $P$ in the plane, outside the three circles, construct six points $A_1, B_1, A_2, B_2, A_3, B_3$ as follows: For each $i = 1, 2, 3$, $A_i, B_i$ are distinct points on the circle $\Gamma_i$ such that the lines $PA_i$ and $PB_i$ are both tangents to $\Gamma_i$. Call the point $P$ *exceptional* if, from the construction, three lines $A_1B_1, A_2B_2, A_3B_3$ are concurrent. Show that every exceptional point of the plane, if exists, lies on the same circle.
answer: Proof: if the chords of contact meet at $Q$, the circle on diameter $PQ$ passes through the feet $X_i$ on $PO_i$ and $O_iX_i\cdot O_iP=r_i^2$, so it is orthogonal to all three circles; its centre is therefore the radical centre $O$ and its radius $\sqrt{\text{pow}(O)}$ — the same circle for every exceptional $P$.

solutions.title: The circle on diameter $PQ$ is orthogonal to all three circles
solutions.body:
Let $O_i$ and $r_i$ be the centre and radius of $\Gamma_i$. Let $P$ be exceptional and let the lines $A_iB_i$ meet at $Q$.

**The feet $X_i$.** By symmetry in line $PO_i$, the chord $A_iB_i$ is perpendicular to $PO_i$; let $X_i$ be their intersection. Triangle $PA_iO_i$ has a right angle at $A_i$ and $A_iX_i$ is its altitude, so
$$O_iX_i\cdot O_iP=O_iA_i^2=r_i^2 .$$
In particular $O_iX_i<r_i<O_iP$: $X_i$ lies strictly between $O_i$ and $P$. So $P$ is not on line $A_iB_i$, and $Q\ne P$. Let $\Gamma$ be the circle with diameter $PQ$, centre $O$, radius $\rho$. Since $Q\in A_iB_i$ and $PX_i\perp A_iB_i$, we have $\angle PX_iQ=90^\circ$ (or $X_i=Q$), so $X_i\in\Gamma$.

**Power of $O_i$.** The line $O_iP$ meets $\Gamma$ at $X_i$ and $P$, both on the same side of $O_i$, so the power of $O_i$ with respect to $\Gamma$ is
$$OO_i^2-\rho^2=O_iX_i\cdot O_iP=r_i^2 .$$
Hence $\rho^2=OO_i^2-r_i^2$, which is the power of $O$ with respect to $\Gamma_i$, for $i=1,2,3$.

**$O$ is a fixed point.** So $O$ has equal power with respect to the three circles. The set of such points is the intersection of the radical axes. If the centres $O_1,O_2,O_3$ are not collinear, the radical axes meet in a single point, the radical centre $Z$; then $O=Z$ and $\rho^2=\text{pow}_{\Gamma_1}(Z)$, both independent of $P$. So every exceptional point $P$ lies on the one circle with centre $Z$ and radius $\sqrt{\text{pow}_{\Gamma_1}(Z)}$.

If the centres are collinear, the radical axes are all perpendicular to the line of centres; if they are distinct parallel lines there is no point with equal powers, hence no exceptional point. They cannot all coincide: put the centres at $(c_i,0)$ and the common radical axis at $x=0$; then $c_i^2-r_i^2=\kappa$ is the same for all $i$. If $\kappa\le0$ every disc contains the origin, so the discs overlap. If $\kappa>0$, then $|c_i|>r_i$ and two of the three centres, say $0<c_i<c_j$ (or the mirror image), are on the same side; then
$$c_j-r_j=\frac{\kappa}{c_j+r_j}\le\sqrt\kappa\le c_i+r_i$$
(because $c+\sqrt{c^2-\kappa}\ge\sqrt\kappa$ for $c\ge\sqrt\kappa$), so these two discs overlap — contradicting the hypothesis.

Hence all exceptional points, if any, lie on one circle (the circle centred at the radical centre and orthogonal to $\Gamma_1,\Gamma_2,\Gamma_3$). ∎

prompt:
Prove that for any positive integer $k$, there exists an arithmetic sequence
$$\frac{a_1}{b_1},\ \frac{a_2}{b_2},\ \ldots,\ \frac{a_k}{b_k}$$
of rational numbers, where $a_i, b_i$ are relatively prime positive integers for each $i = 1, 2, \ldots, k$, such that the positive integers $a_1, b_1, a_2, b_2, \ldots, a_k, b_k$ are all distinct.
answer: Proof: take $\frac{(k!)^2+i}{k!}$, $i=1,\dots,k$ (difference $\frac1{k!}$); since $\gcd(k!,(k!)^2+i)=i$, the reduced forms are $a_i=\frac{(k!)^2}{i}+1$, $b_i=\frac{k!}{i}$, all distinct because $a_1>\dots>a_k>k!\ge b_1>\dots>b_k$.

solutions.title: Fractions with denominator $k!$
solutions.body:
For $k=1$ take $\frac21$. Let $k\ge2$ and $N=k!$. Consider
$$\frac{N^2+1}{N},\ \frac{N^2+2}{N},\ \dots,\ \frac{N^2+k}{N},$$
an arithmetic sequence with common difference $\frac1N$.

**Reduced forms.** For $1\le i\le k$ we have $i\mid N$, so $\gcd(N,N^2+i)=\gcd(N,i)=i$. Dividing numerator and denominator by $i$ gives the fraction in lowest terms:
$$a_i=\frac{N^2+i}{i}=\frac{N^2}{i}+1,\qquad b_i=\frac Ni,\qquad\gcd(a_i,b_i)=1 .$$

**Distinctness.** Both $a_i$ and $b_i$ are strictly decreasing in $i$, so the $a$'s are distinct and the $b$'s are distinct. Moreover for all $i,j$:
$$a_i\ge\frac{N^2}{k}+1=N\cdot(k-1)!+1>N\ge b_j .$$
So no $a_i$ equals any $b_j$, and all $2k$ numbers are distinct. ∎

prompt:
Larry and Rob are two robots travelling in one car from Argovia to Zillis. Both robots have control over the steering and steer according to the following algorithm: Larry makes a $90^\circ$ left turn after every $\ell$ kilometer driving from start; Rob makes a $90^\circ$ right turn after every $r$ kilometer driving from start, where $\ell$ and $r$ are relatively prime positive integers. In the event of both turns occurring simultaneously, the car will keep going without changing direction. Assume that the ground is flat and the car can move in any direction.

Let the car start from Argovia facing towards Zillis. For which choices of the pair $(\ell, r)$ is the car guaranteed to reach Zillis, regardless of how far it is from Argovia?
answer: Exactly when $\ell\equiv r\pmod 4$, i.e. $\ell\equiv r\equiv1$ or $\ell\equiv r\equiv3\pmod4$. Then every stretch of $\ell r$ km moves the car exactly $1$ km straight ahead; otherwise its path is closed and bounded.

solutions.title: Look at blocks of $\ell r$ kilometres
solutions.body:
Put Argovia at $0$ and Zillis at the point $d>0$ of the complex plane, so the car starts facing the direction $1$ (east). Turns happen only at integer distances, so the $(k+1)$-st kilometre ($k=0,1,2,\dots$) is driven in a constant direction $m_k\in\{1,i,-1,-i\}$, and a left turn multiplies the direction by $i$, a right turn by $-i$.

**Blocks.** Split the trip into blocks of $\ell r$ km. Turns occur at multiples of $\ell$ and of $r$, a pattern with period $\ell r$, and at the end of every block both robots turn simultaneously (no change). Inside a block, Larry turns at the $r-1$ multiples of $\ell$ in $(0,\ell r)$ and Rob at the $\ell-1$ multiples of $r$, and no two coincide ($\gcd(\ell,r)=1$). So all blocks are driven identically up to the starting direction, and each block rotates the car by $\ell-r$ quarter-turns to the right. Let $w=\sum_{k=0}^{\ell r-1}m_k$ be the displacement during the first block.

**Case $\ell-r\equiv2\pmod4$.** After one block the car has turned $180^\circ$, so the second block's displacement is $-w$; after two blocks the car is back at Argovia facing east, and the motion repeats. The path is closed of length $2\ell r$, so the car never gets farther than $\ell r$ from Argovia: it misses a Zillis farther away.

**Case $\ell-r\equiv\pm1\pmod4$.** The block displacements are $w,\ \mp iw,\ -w,\ \pm iw$, summing to $0$; after four blocks the car is back in its initial state. The path is closed of length $4\ell r$, so it stays within $2\ell r$ of Argovia: again Zillis may be missed.

**Case $\ell\equiv r\pmod4$.** Then $\ell,r$ are both odd (they are coprime), and $\ell\equiv r\equiv\varepsilon\in\{1,3\}\pmod4$, $\varepsilon^2\equiv1$. Before the $(k+1)$-st kilometre there have been $\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor$ left and $\lfloor k/r\rfloor$ right turns, so $m_k=i^{\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor}(-i)^{\lfloor k/r\rfloor}$. Let $\alpha_k$, $\beta_k$ be the remainders of $k$ mod $\ell$ and mod $r$. From $\ell\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor=k-\alpha_k$ we get $\lfloor k/\ell\rfloor\equiv\varepsilon(k-\alpha_k)\pmod4$, and similarly $\lfloor k/r\rfloor\equiv\varepsilon(k-\beta_k)$. With $\omega=i^{-\varepsilon}$ (so $(-i)^{-\varepsilon}=\bar\omega$) and $i\cdot(-i)=1$:
$$m_k=i^{\varepsilon k}(-i)^{\varepsilon k}\,i^{-\varepsilon\alpha_k}(-i)^{-\varepsilon\beta_k}=\omega^{\alpha_k}\,\bar\omega^{\beta_k}.$$
By the Chinese remainder theorem, $k\mapsto(\alpha_k,\beta_k)$ is a bijection from $\{0,\dots,\ell r-1\}$ onto $\{0,\dots,\ell-1\}\times\{0,\dots,r-1\}$. Therefore
$$w=\Big(\sum_{\alpha=0}^{\ell-1}\omega^{\alpha}\Big)\Big(\sum_{\beta=0}^{r-1}\bar\omega^{\beta}\Big).$$
Four consecutive powers of the primitive fourth root $\omega$ sum to $0$, so the first sum equals $1$ if $\varepsilon=1$ and $1+\omega+\omega^2=\omega$ if $\varepsilon=3$; likewise the second is $1$ or $\bar\omega$. In both cases $w=1$ (as $\omega\bar\omega=1$).

So each block ends $1$ km further east, facing east again. The first kilometre of every block is driven facing east (no turn occurs before $\min(\ell,r)\ge1$ km into the block), so block number $j$ starts by driving along the segment from $j-1$ to $j$. Hence the car passes through every point of the ray towards Zillis and reaches it, whatever $d$ is.

**Answer:** exactly the coprime pairs with $\ell\equiv r\pmod4$, i.e. $\ell\equiv r\equiv1\pmod4$ or $\ell\equiv r\equiv3\pmod4$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $\angle BAC \ne 90^\circ$. Let $O$ be the circumcenter of the triangle $ABC$ and let $\Gamma$ be the circumcircle of the triangle $BOC$. Suppose that $\Gamma$ intersects the line segment $AB$ at $P$ different from $B$, and the line segment $AC$ at $Q$ different from $C$. Let $ON$ be a diameter of the circle $\Gamma$. Prove that the quadrilateral $APNQ$ is a parallelogram.
answer: Proof: $\angle OBN=\angle OCN=90^\circ$, so $NB$, $NC$ are the tangents to the circumcircle at $B$, $C$; then $\angle(QN,QC)=\angle(BN,BC)=\angle(AB,AC)$ gives $QN\parallel AB$, and likewise $PN\parallel AC$.

solutions.title: $N$ is the pole of $BC$
solutions.body:
We use directed angles between lines, mod $180^\circ$. Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle of $ABC$.

**$NB$ and $NC$ are tangent to $\omega$.** Since $ON$ is a diameter of $\Gamma$ and $B\in\Gamma$, $\angle OBN=90^\circ$, i.e. $NB\perp OB$. So $NB$ is the tangent to $\omega$ at $B$; similarly $NC$ is the tangent at $C$. (Because $\angle A\ne90^\circ$, $O\notin BC$, so $\Gamma$ exists, and the two tangents are not parallel.) In particular $N$ lies outside $\omega$, while $P$, $Q$ lie on the sides, so $N\ne P,Q$.

**$QN\parallel AB$.** The points $Q,B,N,C$ lie on $\Gamma$, so
$$\angle(QN,QC)=\angle(BN,BC).$$
By the tangent–chord angle in $\omega$, $\angle(BN,BC)=\angle(AB,AC)$. Since line $QC$ is line $AC$, this says $\angle(QN,AC)=\angle(AB,AC)$, hence $QN\parallel AB$.

**$PN\parallel AC$.** In the same way, $\angle(PN,PB)=\angle(CN,CB)=\angle(AC,AB)$ and $PB$ is line $AB$, so $PN\parallel AC$.

Thus in quadrilateral $APNQ$ the side $AP$ (on line $AB$) is parallel to $QN$ and the side $AQ$ (on line $AC$) is parallel to $PN$; a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel is a parallelogram. ∎

prompt: For a positive integer $k$, call an integer a *pure $k$-th power* if it can be represented as $m^k$ for some integer $m$. Show that for every positive integer $n$ there exist $n$ distinct positive integers such that their sum is a pure $2009$-th power, and their product is a pure $2010$-th power.
answer: Proof: with $k=2009$, take $b_i=i^{k+1}$ (product $t^{k+1}$), $s=\sum b_i$, and $a_i=b_is^{k^2-1}$: then $\sum a_i=s^{k^2}=(s^k)^{2009}$ and $\prod a_i=\big(s^{n(k-1)}t\big)^{2010}$ since $k^2-1=(k-1)(k+1)$.

solutions.title: Scale a good product by a power of the sum
solutions.body:
Let $k=2009$, so $k+1=2010$. Put $b_i=i^{k+1}$ for $i=1,\dots,n$; these are distinct positive integers with
$$b_1b_2\cdots b_n=(n!)^{k+1}=t^{k+1},\qquad t=n!.$$
Let $s=b_1+\dots+b_n$ and define
$$a_i=b_i\,s^{k^2-1}\qquad(i=1,\dots,n).$$
The $a_i$ are distinct positive integers (the $b_i$ are distinct and we multiply by the same positive number).

- Sum: $a_1+\dots+a_n=s^{k^2-1}\cdot s=s^{k^2}=\left(s^{k}\right)^{2009}$, a pure $2009$-th power.
- Product: since $k^2-1=(k-1)(k+1)$,
$$a_1\cdots a_n=s^{n(k^2-1)}\,t^{k+1}=\left(s^{n(k-1)}\,t\right)^{k+1}=\left(s^{n(k-1)}\,t\right)^{2010},$$
a pure $2010$-th power. ∎

*Where the exponent comes from:* we need an exponent $x$ with $x+1\equiv0\pmod{2009}$ (for the sum) and $x\equiv0\pmod{2010}$ (for the product); $x=k^2-1$ works.

prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer. $n$ people take part in a certain party. For any pair of the participants, either the two are acquainted with each other or they are not. What is the maximum possible number of the pairs for which the two are not acquainted but have a common acquaintance among the participants?
answer: $\dfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}{2}=\binom{n-1}{2}$ (a star: one person knows everybody; upper bound since a connected group of $c$ people has at least $c-1$ acquainted pairs).

solutions.title: Count inside connected groups
solutions.body:
Form the acquaintance graph: people are vertices, acquainted pairs are edges. A pair is *counted* if it is not an edge but the two have a common neighbour; in particular both lie in the same connected component.

**Example.** If one person knows everybody and nobody else is acquainted, every pair of the other $n-1$ people is counted: $\binom{n-1}2$ pairs.

**Upper bound.** *Lemma:* a connected graph on $c$ vertices has at least $c-1$ edges. (Delete the edges one by one; each deletion increases the number of components by at most $1$, and at the end there are $c$ components, so there were at least $c-1$ edges.)

Let the components have $c_1,\dots,c_m$ vertices ($\sum c_j=n$, $m\ge1$). Counted pairs are non-edges inside a component, so their number is at most
$$\sum_{j=1}^m\left[\binom{c_j}2-(c_j-1)\right]=\sum_{j=1}^m\binom{c_j-1}2 .$$
For non-negative integers $\binom x2+\binom y2\le\binom{x+y}2$ (the difference is $xy\ge0$), so
$$\sum_j\binom{c_j-1}2\le\binom{\sum_j(c_j-1)}2=\binom{n-m}2\le\binom{n-1}2 .$$

**Answer:** the maximum is $\binom{n-1}2=\dfrac{(n-1)(n-2)}2$.

solutions.title: Count around one person

prompt: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle satisfying the condition $AB > BC$ and $AC > BC$. Denote by $O$ and $H$ the circumcenter and the orthocenter, respectively, of the triangle $ABC$. Suppose that the circumcircle of the triangle $AHC$ intersects the line $AB$ at $M$ different from $A$, and that the circumcircle of the triangle $AHB$ intersects the line $AC$ at $N$ different from $A$. Prove that the circumcenter of the triangle $MNH$ lies on the line $OH$.
answer: Proof: $M$, $N$ are the reflections of $B$, $C$ in lines $CH$, $BH$, so $HBM'M$ and $HCN'N$ (with $M'$, $N'$ the reflections of $H$ in $AB$, $AC$, which lie on the circumcircle) are rhombi exchanged by a similarity centred at $H$; it maps the feet of the perpendiculars from $O$ onto $HM$, $HN$ to each other and the midpoints of $HM$, $HN$ to each other, so a homothety at $H$ sends $O$ to the circumcentre of $MNH$.

solutions.title: Two similar rhombi and a homothety at $H$
solutions.body:
Let $\alpha=\angle BAC$. From $AB>BC$ and $AC>BC$, $\alpha$ is the smallest angle, so $\alpha<60^\circ$ and the triangle is not equilateral ($O\ne H$). Let $\omega$ be the circumcircle, $\rho_\ell$ the reflection in a line $\ell$, and use directed angles mod $180^\circ$.

**Step 1: $M=\rho_{CH}(B)$ and $N=\rho_{BH}(C)$.** Let $M_0=\rho_{CH}(B)$. As $CH\perp AB$, $M_0$ lies on line $AB$, and $M_0\ne A$ because $CA\ne CB$. A reflection reverses directed angles and fixes lines $AB$ and $CH$, so $\angle(M_0A,M_0C)=-\angle(BA,BC)=\angle(BC,BA)$. Also $HA\perp BC$ and $HC\perp BA$, so $\angle(HA,HC)=\angle(BC,BA)$. Hence $A,C,H,M_0$ are concyclic, so $M_0$ is the second intersection of circle $AHC$ with line $AB$: $M_0=M$. Similarly $N=\rho_{BH}(C)$. Consequently $HM=HB$ and $HN=HC$.

**Step 2: two rhombi.** Let $M'$, $N'$ be the reflections of $H$ in $AB$, $AC$; it is well known that they lie on $\omega$. The segments $HM'$ (along line $CH$) and $BM$ (along line $AB$) are perpendicular and bisect each other at the foot of the altitude from $C$, so $HBM'M$ is a rhombus and $M'=B+M-H$ (as vectors). Likewise $HCN'N$ is a rhombus and $N'=C+N-H$.

**Step 3: a similarity.** Let $\sigma$ be the reflection in the bisector of angle $BHC$ and $h$ the homothety with centre $H$ and ratio $\frac{HC}{HB}$; put $\varphi=h\circ\sigma$, a similarity fixing $H$. Then $\varphi(B)=C$. Since $\sigma\rho_{HC}\sigma=\rho_{HB}$ and $h$ commutes with $\rho_{HB}$,
$$\varphi(M)=h\sigma\rho_{HC}(B)=h\rho_{HB}\sigma(B)=\rho_{HB}(h\sigma(B))=\rho_{HB}(C)=N .$$
As $\varphi$ is affine, $\varphi(M')=\varphi(B)+\varphi(M)-H=N'$. Hence $\varphi$ maps line $HM$ to line $HN$, the midpoint $P$ of $HM$ to the midpoint $Q$ of $HN$, and the perpendicular bisector of $BM'$ to that of $CN'$.

**Step 4: the feet of the perpendiculars from $O$.** Let $R$, $S$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $O$ to lines $HM$, $HN$. Since $O$ is on the perpendicular bisector of the chord $BM'$ of $\omega$, and $BM'\parallel HM$, that bisector is the line through $O$ perpendicular to $HM$; so $R$ is its intersection with $HM$. Likewise $S$ is the intersection of $HN$ with the perpendicular bisector of $CN'$. By Step 3, $\varphi(R)=S$.

**Step 5: the homothety.** Lines $HM$ and $HN$ are distinct: they are the images of line $HB$ under rotation by $2\theta$ and $-\theta$, where $\theta=\angle(HB,HC)\equiv\pm\alpha$, and $3\alpha\not\equiv0\pmod{180^\circ}$ because $0<\alpha<60^\circ$. (So $MNH$ is a genuine triangle; let $O'$ be its circumcentre.) If $R=H$ then $S=\varphi(R)=H$, and $O$ would project to $H$ on two distinct lines through $H$, i.e. $O=H$ — impossible. So $R\ne H$ and $\vec{HP}=\lambda\,\vec{HR}$ for some real $\lambda$. The linear part of $\varphi$ then gives $\vec{HQ}=\lambda\,\vec{HS}$.

The homothety $\eta$ with centre $H$ and ratio $\lambda$ maps $R\mapsto P$ and $S\mapsto Q$, hence maps the perpendicular to $HM$ at $R$ onto the perpendicular to $HM$ at $P$, and the perpendicular to $HN$ at $S$ onto the perpendicular to $HN$ at $Q$. The first two lines meet at $O$; the last two are the perpendicular bisectors of $HM$ and $HN$, which meet at $O'$. Therefore $O'=\eta(O)$ lies on line $HO$. ∎

prompt:
Find all functions $f$ from the set $\mathbb{R}$ of real numbers into $\mathbb{R}$ which satisfy for all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}$ the identity
$$f(f(x) + f(y) + f(z)) = f(f(x) - f(y)) + f(2xy + f(z)) + 2f(xz - yz).$$
answer: $f(x)=0$ for all $x$, and $f(x)=x^2$ for all $x$ (show a non-constant solution is even, then that $f(u)=f(v)$ forces $u=\pm v$, then $f(0)=0$, and finally $x=y$ gives $f(x)=x^2$).

solutions.title: Even, then almost injective
solutions.body:
Write $E(x,y,z)$ for the identity. A constant $f\equiv c$ gives $c=4c$, so $c=0$; and $f\equiv0$ works. From now on let $f$ be non-constant.

**1. $f(f(t)-f(0))=f(f(0)-f(t))$.** Compare $E(t,0,0)$ and $E(0,t,0)$: both left sides are $f(f(t)+2f(0))$, and the right sides are $f(f(t)-f(0))+f(f(0))+2f(0)$ and $f(f(0)-f(t))+f(f(0))+2f(0)$.

**2. Key lemma: if $f(u_1)=f(u_2)$ then $f(su_1)=f(su_2)$ for all $s$.** Compare $E(s,0,u_1)$ and $E(s,0,u_2)$: $f(f(s)+f(0)+f(u))=f(f(s)-f(0))+f(f(u))+2f(su)$, and everything except the last term is the same for $u=u_1,u_2$.

**3. $f$ is even.** Pick $s_0$ with $f(s_0)\ne f(0)$ and let $u=f(s_0)-f(0)\ne0$. By 1, $f(u)=f(-u)$, so by 2, $f(su)=f(-su)$ for all $s$, i.e. $f(x)=f(-x)$ for all $x$.

**4. $f(s)\ne f(0)$ for $s\ne0$.** If $f(u)=f(0)$ with $u\ne0$, step 2 gives $f(su)=f(0)$ for all $s$, so $f$ is constant.

**5. $f(x)=f(y)\Rightarrow x=\pm y$.** Suppose $f(x_0)=f(y_0)$ with $x_0\ne\pm y_0$. By 4, $x_0,y_0\ne0$; replacing $y_0$ by $-y_0$ (step 3) we may assume they have the same sign, so $r=y_0/x_0>0$, $r\ne1$. Step 2 with $s=x/x_0$ gives $f(x)=f(rx)$ for all $x$. Now compare $E(rx,ry,z)$ and $E(r^2x,y,z)$:
$$\begin{aligned}f(f(rx)+f(ry)+f(z))&=f(f(rx)-f(ry))+f(2r^2xy+f(z))+2f(r(x-y)z),\\ f(f(r^2x)+f(y)+f(z))&=f(f(r^2x)-f(y))+f(2r^2xy+f(z))+2f((r^2x-y)z).\end{aligned}$$
Since $f(rx)=f(r^2x)=f(x)$ and $f(ry)=f(y)$, all terms but the last agree, so $f(r(x-y)z)=f((r^2x-y)z)$, and with $f(rt)=f(t)$: $f((x-y)z)=f((r^2x-y)z)$. Given arbitrary $u,v$, take $z=1$, $x=\frac{v-u}{r^2-1}$, $y=x-u$; then $x-y=u$, $r^2x-y=v$, so $f(u)=f(v)$: $f$ is constant, a contradiction.

**6. $f(0)=0$.** Compare $E(x,y,0)$ with $E(x,-y,0)$; by evenness everything agrees except $f(2xy+f(0))$ versus $f(-2xy+f(0))$, so these are equal for all $x,y$. Take $x,y$ with $t=2xy\ne0$: by 5, $t+f(0)=\pm(-t+f(0))$; the plus sign gives $t=0$, so the minus sign holds: $f(0)=0$.

**7. $f(x)=x^2$.** $E(x,x,z)$ with $f(0)=0$ gives $f(2f(x)+f(z))=f(2x^2+f(z))$, so by 5, for all $x,z$:
$$2f(x)+f(z)=2x^2+f(z)\quad\text{or}\quad 2f(x)+f(z)=-2x^2-f(z).$$
If $f(x_0)\ne x_0^2$ for some $x_0$, the first option fails for $x=x_0$ and every $z$, so $f(z)=-f(x_0)-x_0^2$ for all $z$ — constant, a contradiction. Hence $f(x)=x^2$.

**Check.** For $f(x)=x^2$ the right side is $(x^2-y^2)^2+(2xy+z^2)^2+2(x-y)^2z^2=x^4+y^4+z^4+2x^2y^2+2y^2z^2+2z^2x^2=(x^2+y^2+z^2)^2$, the left side.

**Answer:** $f\equiv0$ and $f(x)=x^2$.

prompt: Let $a$, $b$, $c$ be positive integers. Prove that it is impossible to have all of the three numbers $a^2 + b + c$, $b^2 + c + a$, $c^2 + a + b$ to be perfect squares.
answer: Proof: if $a$ is the largest, then $a^2<a^2+b+c\le a^2+2a<(a+1)^2$, so $a^2+b+c$ is not a square.

solutions.title: Squeeze between consecutive squares
solutions.body:
By symmetry assume $a\ge b$ and $a\ge c$. Then
$$a^2<a^2+b+c\le a^2+2a<a^2+2a+1=(a+1)^2 .$$
So $a^2+b+c$ lies strictly between two consecutive squares and is not a perfect square. Hence the three numbers cannot all be squares. ∎

solutions.title: Add three inequalities
solutions.body: Suppose all three are squares. $a^2+b+c$ is a square larger than $a^2$, so it is at least $(a+1)^2$, i.e. $b+c\ge2a+1$. Similarly $c+a\ge2b+1$ and $a+b\ge2c+1$. Adding: $2(a+b+c)\ge2(a+b+c)+3$, a contradiction. ∎

prompt: Five points $A_1, A_2, A_3, A_4, A_5$ lie on a plane in such a way that no three among them lie on a same straight line. Determine the maximum possible value that the minimum value for the angles $\angle A_iA_jA_k$ can take where $i, j, k$ are distinct integers between $1$ and $5$.

solutions.title: Regular pentagon and the convex hull
solutions.body:
**$36^\circ$ is achievable.** For the vertices of a regular pentagon, every angle $\angle A_iA_jA_k$ is an inscribed angle in the circumcircle standing on an arc that is a multiple of $72^\circ$, so it is a positive multiple of $36^\circ$. The minimum is $36^\circ$.

**The minimum is always at most $36^\circ$.** Take the convex hull of the five points; it is a convex polygon with $3$, $4$ or $5$ vertices chosen among the points. A convex $k$-gon has angle sum $(k-2)\cdot180^\circ$, so some interior angle is at most $\frac{(k-2)180^\circ}{k}\le108^\circ$ (for $k\le5$). Say this angle is $\angle A_1A_2A_3$, at hull vertex $A_2$ with hull neighbours $A_1$, $A_3$.

All five points lie in the hull, hence in the angular region of $\angle A_1A_2A_3$; $A_4$ and $A_5$ do not lie on the rays $A_2A_1$, $A_2A_3$ (no three points collinear). So the four rays from $A_2$ to $A_1,A_4,A_5,A_3$ divide $\angle A_1A_2A_3$ into three angles of the form $\angle A_iA_2A_j$ whose sum is at most $108^\circ$. One of them is at most $36^\circ$.

**Answer:** $36^\circ$.

prompt: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with $\angle BAC = 30^\circ$. The internal and external angle bisectors of $\angle ABC$ meet the line $AC$ at $B_1$ and $B_2$, respectively, and the internal and external angle bisectors of $\angle ACB$ meet the line $AB$ at $C_1$ and $C_2$, respectively. Suppose that the circles with diameters $B_1B_2$ and $C_1C_2$ meet inside the triangle $ABC$ at point $P$. Prove that $\angle BPC = 90^\circ$.
answer: Proof: the two circles are Apollonius circles, so $PA:PC=BA:BC$ and $PA:PB=CA:CB$, i.e. $PA\sin A=PB\sin B=PC\sin C$; these are the sides of the pedal triangle $DEF$ of $P$, which is therefore equilateral, and then $\angle BPC=360^\circ-150^\circ-(180^\circ-60^\circ)=90^\circ$.

solutions.title: Apollonius circles and an equilateral pedal triangle
solutions.body:
Write $A,B,C$ also for the angles of the triangle; $A=30^\circ$.

**Apollonius circles.** $B_1$ and $B_2$ divide $AC$ internally and externally in the ratio $BA:BC$ (angle bisector theorems; $B_2$ exists, so $BA\ne BC$). The locus $\{X:XA:XC=BA:BC\}$ is a circle (the Apollonius circle); it is symmetric about line $AC$ and meets that line exactly at $B_1$ and $B_2$, so $B_1B_2$ is its diameter. Thus the circle with diameter $B_1B_2$ is this Apollonius circle. As $P$ lies on it, using the law of sines,
$$\frac{PA}{PC}=\frac{BA}{BC}=\frac{\sin C}{\sin A},\quad\text{so}\quad PA\sin A=PC\sin C .$$
In the same way the circle with diameter $C_1C_2$ gives $\frac{PA}{PB}=\frac{CA}{CB}=\frac{\sin B}{\sin A}$, so $PA\sin A=PB\sin B$.

**The pedal triangle is equilateral.** Let $D,E,F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to $BC,CA,AB$. Since $P$ is inside the acute triangle, the angles $\angle PBC<\angle B<90^\circ$ etc., so the feet lie inside the sides. $E$ and $F$ lie on the circle with diameter $PA$, so by the extended law of sines in that circle, $EF=PA\sin\angle EAF=PA\sin A$. Similarly $FD=PB\sin B$ and $DE=PC\sin C$. Hence $DE=EF=FD$ and $\angle EDF=60^\circ$.

**The angle.** Quadrilateral $PDCE$ has right angles at $D$ and $E$, so it is inscribed in the circle with diameter $PC$; $P$ and $D$ lie on the same side of line $CE=AC$ (both on $B$'s side), so $\angle CPE=\angle CDE$. Similarly $\angle FPB=\angle FDB$. Since $D$ lies on segment $BC$ with $F$ on $AB$ and $E$ on $AC$, the rays $DB,DF,DE,DC$ occur in this order and
$$\angle CDE+\angle FDB=180^\circ-\angle EDF=120^\circ .$$
In quadrilateral $AFPE$ (right angles at $E$, $F$), $\angle EPF=180^\circ-A=150^\circ$. Around the interior point $P$ the rays to $B,D,C,E,A,F$ occur in this cyclic order, so
$$\angle BPC=360^\circ-\angle CPE-\angle EPF-\angle FPB=360^\circ-150^\circ-120^\circ=90^\circ .\ ∎$$

prompt:
Let $n$ be a fixed positive odd integer. Take $m + 2$ **distinct** points $P_0, P_1, \ldots, P_{m+1}$ (where $m$ is a non-negative integer) on the coordinate plane in such a way that the following $3$ conditions are satisfied:

(1) $P_0 = (0, 1)$, $P_{m+1} = (n + 1, n)$, and for each integer $i$, $1 \le i \le m$, both $x$- and $y$-coordinates of $P_i$ are integers lying in between $1$ and $n$ ($1$ and $n$ inclusive).

(2) For each integer $i$, $0 \le i \le m$, $P_iP_{i+1}$ is parallel to the $x$-axis if $i$ is even, and is parallel to the $y$-axis if $i$ is odd.

(3) For each pair $i, j$ with $0 \le i < j \le m$, line segments $P_iP_{i+1}$ and $P_jP_{j+1}$ share at most $1$ point.

Determine the maximum possible value that $m$ can take.
answer: $m_{\max}=n(n-1)$: the vertical segments pair up the points $P_1,\dots,P_m$ inside each column, so each column holds an even number $\le n-1$ of them; a recursive construction (an outer frame of width $2$ around a solution for $n-4$) attains $n(n-1)$.

solutions.title: Column parity bound and a frame construction
solutions.body:
Call $P_1,\dots,P_m$ the *turning points*; they are distinct lattice points of the square $[1,n]^2$.

**Upper bound.** $m$ is even: if $m$ were odd, $P_mP_{m+1}$ would be vertical, but $P_{m+1}$ has $x$-coordinate $n+1$ while $P_m$ (as $m\ge1$) has $x$-coordinate $\le n$. Hence the vertical segments are exactly $P_1P_2,\ P_3P_4,\ \dots,\ P_{m-1}P_m$, and they split the turning points into pairs with equal $x$-coordinate. So each column $x=k$ ($1\le k\le n$) contains an even number of turning points; as it has only $n$ lattice points and $n$ is odd, at most $n-1$. Therefore $m\le n(n-1)$.

**Construction with $m=n(n-1)$**, by induction from $n-4$ to $n$. Throughout, the conditions to check are: the points are distinct, segments alternate horizontal/vertical starting with a horizontal one, and two horizontal segments on the same row (or two vertical ones in the same column) overlap in at most one point — a horizontal and a vertical segment always share at most one point.

*$n=1$:* $P_0=(0,1)$, $P_1=(2,1)$, $m=0$.

*$n=3$:* $(0,1),(1,1),(1,3),(2,3),(2,1),(3,1),(3,3),(4,3)$, $m=6$.

*$n\ge5$.* Let $\rho(x,y)=(n+1-x,\,n+1-y)$ (half-turn about the centre; it swaps $(0,1)$ and $(n+1,n)$). Define the path $\mathcal A$ from $(0,1)$ to $(n-1,n-2)$:
- $(0,1)\to(1,1)\to(1,2)\to(2,2)\to(2,1)\to(3,1)\to(3,2)\to\cdots\to(n-2,1)\to(n-2,2)$ — a zigzag through rows $1,2$ of columns $1,\dots,n-2$ (odd columns are climbed, even columns descended);
- then $\to(n,2)\to(n,1)\to(n-1,1)\to(n-1,3)$;
- then for $j=3,5,\dots,n-4$: $(n-1,j)\to(n,j)\to(n,j+1)\to(n-1,j+1)\to(n-1,j+2)$, ending at $(n-1,n-2)$ (for $n=5$ this part is empty).

Next take a valid path for $n-4$, shift it by $(2,2)$ and traverse it backwards: it runs from $(n-1,n-2)$ to $(2,3)$ with all turning points in $[3,n-2]^2$ and all its segments inside the strip $2\le x\le n-1$, $3\le y\le n-2$. Finally traverse $\rho(\mathcal A)$ backwards, from $\rho(n-1,n-2)=(2,3)$ to $\rho(0,1)=(n+1,n)$.

*Alternation.* Inside each piece segments alternate; $\mathcal A$ starts horizontally and its last segment $(n-1,n-3)\to(n-1,n-2)$ is vertical; the inner path starts and ends with horizontal segments; $\rho(\mathcal A)$ reversed starts with a vertical segment and ends with a horizontal one.

*Distinctness.* $\mathcal A$ uses rows $1,2$ of all columns, plus columns $n-1,n$ of rows $3,\dots,n-3$ and the point $(n-1,n-2)$; $\rho(\mathcal A)$ uses the mirror region (rows $n-1,n$; columns $1,2$ of rows $4,\dots,n-2$; the point $(2,3)$); the inner path uses $[3,n-2]^2$. These regions are disjoint.

*No overlaps.* Rows: row $1$ carries the intervals $[0,1],[2,3],\dots,[n-3,n-2],[n-1,n]$; row $2$ carries $[1,2],[3,4],\dots,[n-4,n-3],[n-2,n]$ — disjoint. Rows $3,\dots,n-2$ carry $[n-1,n]$ (from $\mathcal A$), $[1,2]$ (from $\rho(\mathcal A)$), and inner intervals inside $[2,n-1]$, which can touch the others only at an endpoint. Columns: columns $k\le n-2$ carry $[1,2]$ from $\mathcal A$, columns $n-1$ and $n$ carry $[1,3],[4,5],\dots,[n-3,n-2]$ and $[1,2],[3,4],\dots,[n-4,n-3]$; the inner path's vertical segments lie in columns $3..n-2$ within rows $[3,n-2]$; and $\rho$ gives the mirror picture. All disjoint. Rows $n-1,n$ and the remaining columns follow by the symmetry $\rho$.

*Count.* $\mathcal A$ has $2(n-2)+3+2(n-5)+1=4n-10$ turning points, so does $\rho(\mathcal A)$, and the inner path has $(n-4)(n-5)$. Total $(n-4)(n-5)+8n-20=n^2-n$.

Since every odd $n\ge5$ reduces to $n-4$, starting from $n=1$ and $n=3$ the construction exists for all odd $n$. (For $n=5$ it is $(0,1),(1,1),(1,2),(2,2),(2,1),(3,1),(3,2),(5,2),(5,1),(4,1),(4,3),(2,3),(2,5),(1,5),(1,4),(3,4),(3,5),(4,5),(4,4),(5,4),(5,5),(6,5)$ with $m=20$.)

**Answer:** the maximum is $m=n(n-1)$.

prompt:
Determine all functions $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, where $\mathbb{R}$ is the set of all real numbers, satisfying the following $2$ conditions:

(1) There exists a real number $M$ such that for every real number $x$, $f(x) < M$ is satisfied.

(2) For every pair of real numbers $x$ and $y$,
$$f(xf(y)) + yf(x) = xf(y) + f(xy)$$
is satisfied.
answer: $f\equiv0$, and $f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\ge0\\2x,&x<0\end{cases}$ (show $f(1)=0$, $f(f(y))=2f(y)$ so $f\le0$, then $yf(x)\ge f(xy)$ gives $f=0$ on $[0,\infty)$, and $y=c=f(b)<0$ gives $f(x)=2x$ for $x<0$).

solutions.title: Doubling, sign, then the negative half-line
solutions.body:
Write $E(x,y)$ for the identity in (2).

**$f(1)=0$.** $E(1,1)$: $f(f(1))+f(1)=f(1)+f(1)$, so $f(f(1))=f(1)$. $E(1,f(1))$: $f(f(f(1)))+f(1)^2=f(f(1))+f(f(1))$, i.e. $f(1)+f(1)^2=2f(1)$, so $f(1)\in\{0,1\}$. If $f(1)=1$, then $E(x,1)$ reads $f(x)+f(x)=x+f(x)$, so $f(x)=x$, which is unbounded above — contradicting (1). So $f(1)=0$.

**$f\le0$.** $E(1,y)$: $f(f(y))+0=f(y)+f(y)$, so $f(f(y))=2f(y)$. Thus if $t$ is a value of $f$, so is $2t$, and hence $2^kt$ for all $k\ge0$. A positive value would make $f$ unbounded above. So $f(x)\le0$ for all $x$.

**$f(xy)\le yf(x)$.** $E\!\left(\frac x2,f(y)\right)$ together with $f(f(y))=2f(y)$ gives
$$f(xf(y))+f(y)f\!\left(\tfrac x2\right)=xf(y)+f\!\left(\tfrac x2f(y)\right),$$
so $xf(y)-f(xf(y))=f(y)f\!\left(\frac x2\right)-f\!\left(\frac x2f(y)\right)\ge0$, as $f(y)f(\frac x2)\ge0$ (product of two non-positive numbers) and $-f(\cdot)\ge0$. By $E(x,y)$, $f(xy)-yf(x)=f(xf(y))-xf(y)\le0$.

**$f=0$ on $[0,\infty)$.** For $x>0$ take $y=\frac1x$: $0=f(1)\le\frac{f(x)}x$, so $f(x)\ge0$, hence $f(x)=0$. Also $f(0)=f(f(1))=2f(1)=0$.

**Negative arguments.** If $f\not\equiv0$, there is $b<0$ with $c=f(b)<0$, and $f(c)=f(f(b))=2c$. For $x<0$ we have $cx>0$ and $2cx>0$, so $f(cx)=f(2cx)=0$. Then $E(x,c)$ gives
$$f(2cx)+cf(x)=2cx+f(cx)\ \Longrightarrow\ cf(x)=2cx\ \Longrightarrow\ f(x)=2x .$$

**Check** for $f(x)=0$ ($x\ge0$), $f(x)=2x$ ($x<0$); it is bounded above by $1$.
- $x\ge0,\ y\ge0$: both sides are $0$.
- $x\ge0,\ y<0$: $xf(y)=2xy\le0$ and $xy\le0$; both sides equal $4xy$.
- $x<0,\ y\ge0$: $f(y)=0$, $xy\le0$; both sides equal $2xy$.
- $x<0,\ y<0$: $xf(y)=2xy>0$, $xy>0$; both sides equal $2xy$.

$f\equiv0$ clearly works too.

**Answer:** $f\equiv0$ and $f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&x\ge0,\\2x,&x<0.\end{cases}$

prompt: Let $P$ be a point in the interior of a triangle $ABC$, and let $D$, $E$, $F$ be the point of intersection of the line $AP$ and the side $BC$ of the triangle, of the line $BP$ and the side $CA$, and of the line $CP$ and the side $AB$, respectively. Prove that the area of the triangle $ABC$ must be $6$ if the area of each of the triangles $PFA$, $PDB$ and $PEC$ is $1$.
answer: Proof: with $x=[PAB]$, $y=[PBC]$, $z=[PCA]$, ratio arguments give $y=z(x-1)$, $z=x(y-1)$, $x=y(z-1)$, so $x(z+1)=y(x+1)=z(y+1)$; taking $x$ largest forces $x=y=z=2$, and the area is $6$.

solutions.title: Area ratios along the cevians
solutions.body:
Write $[\,\cdot\,]$ for area and let $x=[PAB]$, $y=[PBC]$, $z=[PCA]$, so $[ABC]=x+y+z$.

Since $F$ lies on $AB$, $[PFB]=x-[PFA]=x-1$. Triangles $BCP$ and $ACP$ share the side $CP$, so the ratio of their areas is the ratio of the distances of $B$ and $A$ from line $CF$, which is $BF:FA$; and triangles $BPF$, $APF$ with common apex $P$ also have area ratio $BF:FA$. Hence
$$\frac yz=\frac{BF}{FA}=\frac{x-1}{1},\qquad y=z(x-1).$$
In the same way ($D$ on $BC$, $E$ on $CA$): $z=x(y-1)$ and $x=y(z-1)$.

From $y=zx-z$ we get $x+y+z=x+zx=x(z+1)$; similarly $x+y+z=y(x+1)=z(y+1)$. So
$$x(z+1)=y(x+1)=z(y+1).$$
By cyclic symmetry assume $x\ge y$ and $x\ge z$. From $x(z+1)=z(y+1)$:
$$z(x-y)+(x-z)=0 .$$
Both terms are $\ge0$ ($z>0$), so $x=y$ and $x=z$. Then $y=z(x-1)$ gives $1=x-1$, so $x=y=z=2$ and $[ABC]=6$. ∎

prompt: Into each box of a $2012 \times 2012$ square grid, a real number greater than or equal to $0$ and less than or equal to $1$ is inserted. Consider splitting the grid into $2$ non-empty rectangles consisting of boxes of the grid by drawing a line parallel either to the horizontal or the vertical side of the grid. Suppose that for at least one of the resulting rectangles the sum of the numbers in the boxes within the rectangle is less than or equal to $1$, no matter how the grid is split into $2$ such rectangles. Determine the maximum possible value for the sum of all the $2012 \times 2012$ numbers inserted into the boxes.

solutions.title: A plus sign, and a central row and column
solutions.body:
Let $n=2012$.

**Example with sum $5$.** Put $1$ in some box $(i,j)$ with $2\le i,j\le n-1$ and in its four neighbours $(i\pm1,j)$, $(i,j\pm1)$, and $0$ elsewhere (a plus sign). Cut horizontally between rows $k$ and $k+1$: if $k\le i-2$ the upper part has sum $0$; if $k=i-1$ it has sum $1$; if $k=i$ the lower part has sum $1$; if $k\ge i+1$ the lower part has sum $0$. Vertical cuts are the same. So the condition holds and the total is $5$.

**Upper bound.** Let $R(x,y)$ be the sum of rows $x$ through $y$ (and $0$ if $x>y$). Let $a$ be the largest integer in $[1,n]$ with $R(1,a-1)\le1$ (it exists since $R(1,0)=0$), and $c$ the smallest integer in $[a,n]$ with $R(c+1,n)\le1$ (exists since $R(n+1,n)=0$). If $a<c$, then $a<n$, so by maximality of $a$, $R(1,a)>1$; and by minimality of $c$, $R(a+1,n)>1$. Then the cut between rows $a$ and $a+1$ leaves two rectangles with sums $>1$, contradicting the hypothesis. So $a=c$:
$$R(1,a-1)\le1,\qquad R(a+1,n)\le1 .$$
In the same way, with column sums $C(x,y)$, there is a column $b$ with $C(1,b-1)\le1$ and $C(b+1,n)\le1$.

The entries of row $a$ lie in columns $<b$, in columns $>b$, or in box $(a,b)$; all entries are non-negative, so the sum of row $a$ is at most $C(1,b-1)+C(b+1,n)+r$, where $r\le1$ is the entry in box $(a,b)$. Therefore the total is
$$R(1,a-1)+R(a+1,n)+(\text{row }a)\le1+1+1+1+1=5 .$$

**Answer:** $5$.

prompt: Determine all the pairs $(p, n)$ of a prime number $p$ and a positive integer $n$ for which $\dfrac{n^p + 1}{p^n + 1}$ is an integer.
answer: $(p,n)=(p,p)$ for every prime $p$, and $(2,4)$ (need $p^n\le n^p$; for odd $p$ this gives $n\le p$, and the order of $n$ modulo $p+1$ is $2$, so $p+1\mid n+1$).

solutions.title: Size, then the order of $n$ modulo $p+1$
solutions.body:
If the quotient is an integer, it is positive, so $p^n+1\le n^p+1$, i.e. $p^n\le n^p$.

**$p=2$.** We need $2^n\le n^2$. For $n\ge5$, $2^n>n^2$ (true at $n=5$; and $2^{n+1}>2n^2\ge(n+1)^2$ for $n\ge3$). So $n\le4$: $n=1$ gives $\frac25$, $n=2$ gives $\frac55=1$, $n=3$ gives $\frac{3^2+1}{2^3+1}=\frac{10}9$, not an integer, and $n=4$ gives $\frac{17}{17}=1$. So $(2,2)$ and $(2,4)$.

**$p\ge3$: first $n\le p$.** The function $g(t)=\frac{\ln t}t$ has $g'(t)=\frac{1-\ln t}{t^2}<0$ for $t>e$, so it is decreasing on $[3,\infty)$. If $n>p\ge3$, then $\frac{\ln n}n<\frac{\ln p}p$, i.e. $n^p<p^n$, which is excluded. So $n\le p$.

**$n$ is odd.** $p^n+1$ is even, so $n^p+1$ is even and $n$ is odd. Hence $p\equiv-1\pmod{p+1}$ gives $p^n\equiv-1$, i.e. $p+1\mid p^n+1\mid n^p+1$:
$$n^p\equiv-1\pmod{p+1}.$$
In particular $\gcd(n,p+1)=1$ and $n^{2p}\equiv1$. Let $e$ be the order of $n$ modulo $p+1$; then $e\mid2p$, so $e\in\{1,2,p,2p\}$.
- $e=1$ or $e=p$ would give $n^p\equiv1$, so $1\equiv-1$, i.e. $p+1\mid2$ — false.
- $e=2p$ is impossible since $e\mid\varphi(p+1)$ and $\varphi(p+1)\le p<2p$.

So $e=2$, $n^2\equiv1$, and $-1\equiv n^p=n\cdot(n^2)^{(p-1)/2}\equiv n\pmod{p+1}$. Thus $p+1\mid n+1$, so $n\ge p$. Together with $n\le p$: $n=p$.

**Check:** $(p,p)$ gives quotient $1$, and $(2,4)$ gives $1$.

**Answer:** all pairs $(p,p)$ with $p$ prime, and $(2,4)$.

prompt:
Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle. Denote by $D$ the foot of the perpendicular line drawn from the point $A$ to the side $BC$, by $M$ the midpoint of $BC$, and by $H$ the orthocenter of $ABC$. Let $E$ be the point of intersection of the circumcircle $\Gamma$ of the triangle $ABC$ and the half line $MH$, and $F$ be the point of intersection (other than $E$) of the line $ED$ and the circle $\Gamma$. Prove that $\dfrac{BF}{CF} = \dfrac{AB}{AC}$ must hold.

Here we denote by $XY$ the length of the line segment $XY$.
answer: Proof: with $K$ the antipode of $A$, $BHCK$ is a parallelogram, so $E$ lies on line $MK$ and $\angle AEM=90^\circ=\angle ADM$; hence $A,E,D,M$ are concyclic, which makes $\triangle BMA\sim\triangle FCA$ and $\triangle CMA\sim\triangle FBA$; with $BM=CM$ this gives $\frac{AC}{FC}=\frac{AB}{FB}$.

solutions.title: The antipode of $A$ and two similar pairs
solutions.body:
If $AB=AC$, then $D=M$, the line $MH$ is the axis of symmetry, $E$ and $F$ are the two ends of the diameter through $A$, and $BF=CF$; the claim holds. Assume $AB\ne AC$, so $D\ne M$. Use directed angles mod $180^\circ$.

**$E$ sees $AM$ at a right angle.** Let $K$ be the antipode of $A$ on $\Gamma$. Then $KB\perp AB$ and $CH\perp AB$, so $KB\parallel CH$; likewise $KC\parallel BH$. Hence $BHCK$ is a parallelogram and its diagonals bisect each other: $M$ is the midpoint of $HK$. Since $M$ is inside $\Gamma$, the line $HK$ meets $\Gamma$ at $K$ and at a second point on the other side of $M$, i.e. on the half-line $MH$; that point is $E$. So $E,M,K$ are collinear and $\angle AEM=\angle AEK=90^\circ$ ($AK$ is a diameter). As also $\angle ADM=90^\circ$, the points $A,E,D,M$ lie on the circle with diameter $AM$.

**Two pairs of similar triangles.** Using that circle, then $\Gamma$ (and $E,D,F$ collinear):
$$\angle(MA,MB)=\angle(MA,MD)=\angle(EA,ED)=\angle(EA,EF)=\angle(CA,CF),$$
and on $\Gamma$, $\angle(BA,BM)=\angle(BA,BC)=\angle(FA,FC)$. Two directed angles agree, so triangles $BMA$ and $FCA$ are directly similar, and
$$\frac{AM}{BM}=\frac{AC}{FC}.$$
Similarly $\angle(MA,MC)=\angle(EA,EF)=\angle(BA,BF)$ and $\angle(CA,CM)=\angle(CA,CB)=\angle(FA,FB)$, so triangles $CMA$ and $FBA$ are directly similar and
$$\frac{AM}{CM}=\frac{AB}{FB}.$$
Since $BM=CM$, $\frac{AC}{FC}=\frac{AB}{FB}$, i.e. $\dfrac{BF}{CF}=\dfrac{AB}{AC}$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ be an integer greater than or equal to $2$. Prove that if the real numbers $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ satisfy $a_1^2 + a_2^2 + \cdots + a_n^2 = n$, then
$$\sum_{1 \le i < j \le n} \frac{1}{n - a_ia_j} \le \frac{n}{2}$$
must hold.
answer: Proof: reduce to $a_i\ge0$ and to $\sum_{i<j}\frac{a_ia_j}{n-a_ia_j}\le\frac n2$; bound each term by $\frac12\cdot\frac{(a_i+a_j)^2}{(n-a_i^2)+(n-a_j^2)}\le\frac12\left(\frac{a_j^2}{n-a_i^2}+\frac{a_i^2}{n-a_j^2}\right)$ (Cauchy–Schwarz), and the sum of the right sides is exactly $\frac n2$.

solutions.title: Reduce, then Cauchy–Schwarz
solutions.body:
**Denominators are positive.** For $i\ne j$, $a_ia_j\le\frac{a_i^2+a_j^2}2\le\frac n2$, so $n-a_ia_j\ge\frac n2>0$.

**Reduction to $a_i\ge0$.** With $b_i=|a_i|$ we still have $\sum b_i^2=n$, and $a_ia_j\le b_ib_j$ gives $\frac1{n-a_ia_j}\le\frac1{n-b_ib_j}$. So it suffices to treat non-negative $a_i$.

**Reformulation.** $\frac{n}{n-a_ia_j}=1+\frac{a_ia_j}{n-a_ia_j}$. Multiplying the claim by $n$ and subtracting $\binom n2$, it becomes
$$\sum_{i<j}\frac{a_ia_j}{n-a_ia_j}\le\frac{n^2}2-\frac{n(n-1)}2=\frac n2 .\tag{$*$}$$
If some $a_i^2=n$, all other $a_j$ are $0$ and the left side of $(*)$ is $0$. So assume $a_i^2<n$ for all $i$.

**One term.** Since $0\le a_ia_j\le\left(\frac{a_i+a_j}2\right)^2\le\frac{a_i^2+a_j^2}2$, increasing the numerator and decreasing the (positive) denominator,
$$\frac{a_ia_j}{n-a_ia_j}\le\frac{\left(\frac{a_i+a_j}2\right)^2}{n-\frac{a_i^2+a_j^2}2}=\frac12\cdot\frac{(a_i+a_j)^2}{(n-a_i^2)+(n-a_j^2)} .$$
By Cauchy–Schwarz (Engel form), with positive $n-a_i^2$, $n-a_j^2$:
$$\frac{(a_j+a_i)^2}{(n-a_i^2)+(n-a_j^2)}\le\frac{a_j^2}{n-a_i^2}+\frac{a_i^2}{n-a_j^2}.$$

**Summing.**
$$\sum_{i<j}\frac{a_ia_j}{n-a_ia_j}\le\frac12\sum_{i<j}\left(\frac{a_j^2}{n-a_i^2}+\frac{a_i^2}{n-a_j^2}\right)=\frac12\sum_{i}\frac{\sum_{j\ne i}a_j^2}{n-a_i^2}=\frac12\sum_i\frac{n-a_i^2}{n-a_i^2}=\frac n2 .$$
This is $(*)$, and the inequality is proved. ∎

prompt: Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle with altitudes $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$, and let $O$ be the center of its circumcircle. Show that the segments $OA$, $OF$, $OB$, $OD$, $OC$, $OE$ dissect the triangle $ABC$ into three pairs of triangles that have equal areas.
answer: Proof: $[OBD]=[OAE]$, $[OCD]=[OAF]$, $[OCE]=[OBF]$; e.g. with $M,N$ the midpoints of $BC,CA$, the similar right triangles $OMC\sim AEB$ and $ONA\sim BDA$ give $BD\cdot OM=AE\cdot ON$.

solutions.title: Similar right triangles
solutions.body:
Since the triangle is acute, $O$ lies inside it and $D,E,F$ lie inside the sides $BC,CA,AB$, so the six segments cut $ABC$ into the triangles $OBD, ODC, OCE, OEA, OAF, OFB$. Write $[\,\cdot\,]$ for area and $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ for the angles at $A,B,C$. We show $[OBD]=[OAE]$; the other two equalities $[OCD]=[OAF]$ and $[OCE]=[OBF]$ follow in the same way by permuting the letters.

Let $M$ and $N$ be the midpoints of $BC$ and $CA$. Then $OM\perp BC$ and $ON\perp CA$, so $OM$ and $ON$ are the heights of triangles $OBD$ (base $BD$ on line $BC$) and $OAE$ (base $AE$ on line $CA$):
$$[OBD]=\tfrac12\,BD\cdot OM,\qquad [OAE]=\tfrac12\,AE\cdot ON .$$

* Triangles $OMC$ and $AEB$: $\angle OMC=90^\circ=\angle AEB$, and $\angle MOC=\tfrac12\angle BOC=\alpha=\angle EAB$ (central angle; $O$ is inside the acute triangle). So they are similar and $\dfrac{OM}{AE}=\dfrac{OC}{AB}$.
* Triangles $ONA$ and $BDA$: $\angle ONA=90^\circ=\angle BDA$ and $\angle NOA=\tfrac12\angle COA=\beta=\angle DBA$. So $\dfrac{ON}{BD}=\dfrac{OA}{BA}$.

Since $OA=OC$, the two ratios are equal: $\dfrac{OM}{AE}=\dfrac{ON}{BD}$, i.e. $BD\cdot OM=AE\cdot ON$. Hence $[OBD]=[OAE]$. ∎

solutions.title: Trigonometry
solutions.body:
Let $R$ be the circumradius, $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ the angles and $b=CA$. In triangle $OCD$ we have $OC=R$, $CD=b\cos\gamma$ (from the right triangle $ADC$), and since triangle $OBC$ is isosceles with $\angle BOC=2\alpha$, $\angle OCD=\angle OCB=90^\circ-\alpha$. Hence
$$[OCD]=\tfrac12\,R\cdot b\cos\gamma\cdot\sin(90^\circ-\alpha)=\tfrac12 Rb\cos\alpha\cos\gamma .$$
Similarly $OA=R$, $AF=b\cos\alpha$ (right triangle $AFC$) and $\angle OAF=\angle OAB=90^\circ-\gamma$, so
$$[OAF]=\tfrac12\,R\cdot b\cos\alpha\cdot\sin(90^\circ-\gamma)=\tfrac12 Rb\cos\alpha\cos\gamma=[OCD].$$
(All these angles are acute and $D,F$ lie on the sides because the triangle is acute.) Exactly the same computation gives $[OBD]=[OAE]$ and $[OCE]=[OBF]$. ∎

prompt: Determine all positive integers $n$ for which $\dfrac{n^2+1}{[\sqrt{n}]^2+2}$ is an integer. Here $[r]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $r$.
answer: There are no such $n$: with $m=[\sqrt n]$, $n=m^2+a$ ($0\le a\le 2m$) the condition becomes $m^2+2\mid (a-2)^2+1$, which forces $(a-2)^2+1=k(m^2+2)$ with $k\in\{1,2,3\}$, and each case is impossible.

solutions.title: Reduce modulo $m^2+2$
solutions.body:
Let $m=[\sqrt n]\ge 1$ and $a=n-m^2$. Since $m^2\le n<(m+1)^2$, we have $0\le a\le 2m$.

Modulo $m^2+2$ we have $m^2\equiv-2$, so $n=m^2+a\equiv a-2$ and
$$n^2+1\equiv (a-2)^2+1\pmod{m^2+2}.$$
Thus the fraction is an integer exactly when $m^2+2$ divides $(a-2)^2+1$.

**Size.** Because $0\le a\le 2m$, $|a-2|\le\max(2,\,2m-2)\le 2m$ (as $m\ge1$). Hence
$$0<(a-2)^2+1\le 4m^2+1<4(m^2+2),$$
so $(a-2)^2+1=k(m^2+2)$ with $k\in\{1,2,3\}$.

* $k=1$: $(a-2)^2-m^2=1$, i.e. $(|a-2|-m)(|a-2|+m)=1$. Both factors are integers and the second is positive, so both equal $1$, giving $m=0$ — impossible.
* $k=2$: $(a-2)^2+1=2m^2+4$. Squares are $0,1,4\pmod 8$, so the left side is $1,2$ or $5\pmod 8$, while $2m^2\in\{0,2\}\pmod 8$ makes the right side $4$ or $6\pmod 8$. Impossible.
* $k=3$: the right side is divisible by $3$, but squares are $0,1\pmod 3$, so the left side is $1$ or $2\pmod 3$. Impossible.

Therefore no positive integer $n$ works. ∎

prompt:
For $2k$ real numbers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_k, b_1, b_2, \dots, b_k$ define the sequence of numbers $X_n$ by
$$X_n=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\,[a_in+b_i]\qquad (n=1,2,\dots).$$
If the sequence $X_n$ forms an arithmetic progression, show that $\sum_{i=1}^k a_i$ must be an integer. Here $[r]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $r$.
answer: Proof: with $A=\sum a_i$, $B=\sum b_i$ we have $An+B-k<X_n\le An+B$, so $X_n-An$ is bounded; for an arithmetic progression $X_n=X_1+(n-1)d$ this forces $d=A$, and $d$ is an integer because the $X_n$ are integers.

solutions.title: Compare growth rates
solutions.body:
Let $A=\sum_{i=1}^k a_i$ and $B=\sum_{i=1}^k b_i$. From $r-1<[r]\le r$ applied to each $r=a_in+b_i$ and summing over $i$,
$$An+B-k<X_n\le An+B\qquad\text{for all }n\ge1. \tag{1}$$
So the numbers $X_n-An$ all lie in the bounded interval $(B-k,\,B]$.

Suppose $X_n=X_1+(n-1)d$ for all $n$. Then
$$X_n-An=(d-A)(n-1)+(X_1-A).$$
If $d\ne A$, the right side is unbounded as $n\to\infty$, contradicting (1). Hence $d=A$.

Finally, every $X_n$ is an integer (a sum of integer parts), so $d=X_2-X_1$ is an integer. Therefore $A=\sum a_i=d$ is an integer. ∎

prompt:
Let $a$ and $b$ be positive integers, and let $A$ and $B$ be finite sets of integers satisfying:

(i) $A$ and $B$ are disjoint;

(ii) if an integer $i$ belongs either to $A$ or to $B$, then $i+a$ belongs to $A$ or $i-b$ belongs to $B$.

Prove that $a|A| = b|B|$. (Here $|X|$ denotes the number of elements in the set $X$.)
answer: Proof: with $A^*=A-a$ and $B^*=B+b$, condition (ii) gives $A\cup B\subseteq A^*\cup B^*$; comparing sizes forces equality and $A^*\cap B^*=\varnothing$, and then comparing the sums of the elements gives $a|A|=b|B|$.

solutions.title: Shifted sets and sums
solutions.body:
Let $A^*=\{x-a: x\in A\}$ and $B^*=\{x+b: x\in B\}$. Condition (ii) says: every $i\in A\cup B$ satisfies $i+a\in A$ (i.e. $i\in A^*$) or $i-b\in B$ (i.e. $i\in B^*$). So
$$A\cup B\subseteq A^*\cup B^*.$$
Using (i),
$$|A|+|B|=|A\cup B|\le|A^*\cup B^*|\le|A^*|+|B^*|=|A|+|B| .$$
Hence equality holds throughout: $A\cup B=A^*\cup B^*$ and $A^*\cap B^*=\varnothing$.

For a finite set $X$ let $\Sigma(X)$ be the sum of its elements. Since $A\cup B$ and $A^*\cup B^*$ are the same set and both unions are disjoint,
$$\Sigma(A)+\Sigma(B)=\Sigma(A^*)+\Sigma(B^*)=\big(\Sigma(A)-a|A|\big)+\big(\Sigma(B)+b|B|\big).$$
Therefore $a|A|=b|B|$. ∎

solutions.title: Cycles in a graph
solutions.body:
Draw a directed graph on the vertex set $A\cup B$: put an arrow $i\to j$ when $j\in A$ and $j=i+a$, or $j\in B$ and $j=i-b$. By (ii) every vertex has out-degree at least $1$. A vertex $j$ can be entered only from $j-a$ (if $j\in A$) or from $j+b$ (if $j\in B$), and by (i) only one of these applies, so every in-degree is at most $1$. As the total in-degree equals the total out-degree, all in- and out-degrees equal $1$, and the graph is a disjoint union of directed cycles.

Along a cycle, each step into an element of $A$ adds $a$ and each step into an element of $B$ subtracts $b$. Going once around a cycle containing $p$ elements of $A$ and $q$ elements of $B$ returns to the start, so $pa-qb=0$. Every element of $A\cup B$ lies on exactly one cycle, so summing over the cycles gives $a|A|=b|B|$. ∎

prompt: Let $ABCD$ be a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle $\omega$, and let $P$ be a point on the extension of $AC$ such that $PB$ and $PD$ are tangent to $\omega$. The tangent at $C$ intersects $PD$ at $Q$ and the line $AD$ at $R$. Let $E$ be the second point of intersection between $AQ$ and $\omega$. Prove that $B$, $E$, $R$ are collinear.
answer: Proof: let $R'=BE\cap AD$. Harmonic quadrilaterals $ABCD$ and $ACED$ plus Ptolemy give $\frac{DB}{AB}=\frac{2DC}{CA}$ and $\frac{ED}{AE}=\frac{DC}{2CA}$; then $\frac{RD}{RA}=\big(\frac{DC}{CA}\big)^2=\frac{R'D}{R'A}$ with $R,R'$ both outside segment $AD$, so $R=R'$.

solutions.title: Compare the ratios in which $R$ and $BE$ divide $AD$
solutions.body:
**Two harmonic quadrilaterals.** $P$ lies outside $\omega$ on line $AC$, with tangents $PB=PD$. Triangles $PAD$ and $PDC$ share the angle at $P$ and $\angle PDC=\angle PAD$ (tangent–chord angle), so they are similar and $\frac{AD}{DC}=\frac{PA}{PD}$. In the same way $\frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{PA}{PB}$. As $PB=PD$,
$$AB\cdot CD=BC\cdot AD. \tag{1}$$
The same argument for the point $Q$ (tangents $QC=QD$, secant $QEA$) gives
$$AC\cdot DE=CE\cdot AD. \tag{2}$$

**Order of the points.** $ABCD$ is inscribed in this order. The line $AQ$ through the intersection of the tangents at $C$ and $D$ is the $A$-symmedian of triangle $ACD$, so it runs inside angle $CAD$ and $E$ lies on arc $CD$ not containing $A$ (and hence not containing $B$). So the cyclic order is $A,B,C,E,D$.

**Ptolemy.** In $ABCD$: $AC\cdot BD=AB\cdot CD+BC\cdot AD=2\,AB\cdot CD$ by (1). In $ACED$: $AE\cdot CD=AC\cdot ED+CE\cdot AD=2\,AC\cdot ED$ by (2). Hence
$$\frac{DB}{AB}=\frac{2\,DC}{CA},\qquad \frac{ED}{AE}=\frac{DC}{2\,CA}. \tag{3}$$
Multiplying, $\dfrac{ED\cdot DB}{AE\cdot AB}=\Big(\dfrac{DC}{CA}\Big)^2$.

**The point $R$.** $R$ lies on the tangent at $C$ and on line $AD$, so $RC^2=RD\cdot RA$ and $R$ is outside segment $AD$. Triangles $RDC$ and $RCA$ share the angle at $R$ and $RD/RC=RC/RA$, so they are similar with $\frac{RD}{RC}=\frac{RC}{RA}=\frac{DC}{CA}$. Therefore
$$\frac{RD}{RA}=\frac{RD}{RC}\cdot\frac{RC}{RA}=\Big(\frac{DC}{CA}\Big)^2 .$$
Since $R$ exists, $DC\ne CA$ (otherwise the tangent at $C$ would be parallel to $AD$), so this ratio is not $1$.

**The line $BE$.** If $BE\parallel AD$, then $ABED$ would be an isosceles trapezoid with $AB=ED$ and $DB=AE$, making $\frac{ED\cdot DB}{AE\cdot AB}=1$, which we just excluded. So $BE$ meets line $AD$ at a point $R'$. Because $B$ and $E$ lie on the same arc $AD$ (order $A,B,C,E,D$), the chords $BE$ and $AD$ do not cross, and $R'$ is outside segment $AD$. From the power of the point, $R'A\cdot R'D=R'B\cdot R'E$, so triangles $R'AB\sim R'ED$ and $R'DB\sim R'EA$ (common angle at $R'$, proportional sides), giving $\frac{R'D}{R'B}=\frac{ED}{AB}$ and $\frac{R'B}{R'A}=\frac{DB}{EA}$. Hence
$$\frac{R'D}{R'A}=\frac{ED\cdot DB}{AB\cdot EA}=\Big(\frac{DC}{CA}\Big)^2=\frac{RD}{RA}.$$

**Conclusion.** On line $AD$ outside the segment $AD$, the ratio $XD/XA$ takes every value in $(0,1)$ exactly once (beyond $D$) and every value in $(1,\infty)$ exactly once (beyond $A$). So $R'=R$, which means $R$ lies on line $BE$. ∎

prompt:
For a positive integer $m$ denote by $S(m)$ and $P(m)$ the sum and product, respectively, of the digits of $m$. Show that for each positive integer $n$, there exist positive integers $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$ satisfying the following conditions:
$$S(a_1)<S(a_2)<\cdots<S(a_n)\quad\text{and}\quad S(a_i)=P(a_{i+1})\quad(i=1,2,\dots,n).$$
(We let $a_{n+1}=a_1$.)
answer: Construction: for large $k$ take $a_i$ ($2\le i\le n$) with $k+i-2$ digits $2$ and $2^{k+i-1}-2(k+i-2)$ digits $1$, and $a_1$ with $k+n-1$ digits $2$ and $2^k-2(k+n-1)$ digits $1$; then $S(a_i)=2^{k+i-1}$ and the products match.

solutions.title: Digits $1$ and $2$ only
solutions.body:
A number whose digits are $x$ twos and $y$ ones (and nothing else) has digit sum $2x+y$ and digit product $2^x$. We aim for
$$S(a_i)=2^{k+i-1}\quad(i=1,\dots,n),$$
which is strictly increasing. The conditions $S(a_i)=P(a_{i+1})$ then require $P(a_i)=2^{k+i-2}$ for $2\le i\le n$ and $P(a_1)=S(a_n)=2^{k+n-1}$.

Choose an integer $k$ so large that $2^k\ge 2(k+n-1)$ (possible since $2^k$ grows faster than $2k$).

* For $2\le i\le n$ let $a_i$ consist of $k+i-2$ digits $2$ and $2^{k+i-1}-2(k+i-2)$ digits $1$. This count is non-negative because $2^{k+i-1}\ge 2^k\ge 2(k+n-1)\ge 2(k+i-2)$. Then $S(a_i)=2^{k+i-1}$ and $P(a_i)=2^{k+i-2}$.
* Let $a_1$ consist of $k+n-1$ digits $2$ and $2^k-2(k+n-1)\ge0$ digits $1$. Then $S(a_1)=2^k$ and $P(a_1)=2^{k+n-1}$.

Now $S(a_1)<S(a_2)<\dots<S(a_n)$, $S(a_i)=2^{k+i-1}=P(a_{i+1})$ for $1\le i\le n-1$, and $S(a_n)=2^{k+n-1}=P(a_1)$. (For $n=1$ the single number $a_1$ has $S(a_1)=2^k=P(a_1)$.) ∎

prompt: Let $S=\{1,2,\dots,2014\}$. For each non-empty subset $T\subseteq S$, one of its members is chosen as its representative. Find the number of ways to assign representatives to all non-empty subsets of $S$ so that if a subset $D\subseteq S$ is a disjoint union of non-empty subsets $A, B, C\subseteq S$, then the representative of $D$ is also the representative of at least one of $A$, $B$, $C$.

solutions.title: Peel off one element at a time
solutions.body:
Write $r(X)$ for the representative of $X$, and call an assignment on the subsets of a finite set $T$ *good* if it satisfies the condition for all $D\subseteq T$. Let $N(t)$ be the number of good assignments on a $t$-element set.

**Key fact.** If $|T|\ge5$ and $x=r(T)$, then $r(X)=x$ for every $X\subseteq T$ containing $x$.

*Proof.* If $|X|\le|T|-2$, split $T\setminus X$ into two non-empty sets $Y,Z$. Then $T=X\sqcup Y\sqcup Z$, so $x\in\{r(X),r(Y),r(Z)\}$; since $x\notin Y\cup Z$, $r(X)=x$. If $X=T$ there is nothing to prove. If $|X|=|T|-1\ge4$, take any $y\in X$, $y\ne x$, and split $X\setminus\{x,y\}$ (at least $2$ elements) into non-empty $Y,Z$. Then $X=\{x,y\}\sqcup Y\sqcup Z$; by the first case $r(\{x,y\})=x$, and $r(Y),r(Z)\in Y\cup Z$, so $r(X)\in\{x\}\cup Y\cup Z$, i.e. $r(X)\ne y$. As $y$ was arbitrary, $r(X)=x$. $\square$

**Recursion.** Let $|T|=t\ge5$. Choose $x=r(T)$ ($t$ ways); by the key fact all subsets containing $x$ get representative $x$. Conversely, with this choice every condition for a set $D\ni x$ holds automatically ($r(D)=x$ and the part containing $x$ also has representative $x$), and conditions for $D\not\ni x$ only involve subsets of $T\setminus\{x\}$. So the remaining choices are exactly the good assignments on $T\setminus\{x\}$, and $N(t)=t\,N(t-1)$ for $t\ge5$. Hence
$$N(2014)=2014\cdot2013\cdots5\cdot N(4)=\frac{2014!}{24}\,N(4).$$

**Four elements.** Let $T=\{y_1,y_2,y_3,y_4\}$. Singletons are forced. A $3$-element set is only a union of three singletons, so its condition holds automatically. The only $4$-element set is $T$, and its decompositions into three parts are a pair plus two singletons. If $r(T)=y$, the condition fails exactly for a decomposition $\{y,z\}\sqcup\{u\}\sqcup\{w\}$ with $r(\{y,z\})\ne y$. So the condition is: $r(\{y,z\})=y$ for the three pairs containing $y$. Everything else is free: $4$ three-element sets ($3$ choices each) and the $3$ pairs not containing $y$ ($2$ choices each). Thus
$$N(4)=4\cdot3^4\cdot2^3=2592 .$$

**Answer.** $N(2014)=\dfrac{2014!}{24}\cdot2592=108\cdot2014!$. ∎

prompt: Find all positive integers $n$ such that for any integer $k$ there exists an integer $a$ for which $a^3+a-k$ is divisible by $n$.
answer: $n=3^b$ ($b\ge0$): $a\mapsto a^3+a$ is injective mod $3^b$ because $a^2+ab+b^2+1\not\equiv0\pmod 3$; it is not surjective mod $2$ or mod any prime $p>3$, hence not mod any multiple of these.

solutions.title: Bijectivity modulo $n$
solutions.body:
The condition says that $f(a)=a^3+a$ takes every residue modulo $n$. Since $f(a)\bmod n$ depends only on $a\bmod n$, this means $f$ is a bijection of $\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z$, i.e. it is injective there.

**Powers of $3$ work.** ($n=1$ is trivial.) Suppose $a^3+a\equiv b^3+b\pmod{3^j}$. Then $(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2+1)\equiv0\pmod{3^j}$. If $a\equiv b\pmod 3$ then $a^2+ab+b^2+1\equiv3a^2+1\equiv1$; otherwise $a^2+ab+b^2=(a-b)^2+3ab\equiv1$, so $a^2+ab+b^2+1\equiv2\pmod 3$. Either way the second factor is prime to $3$, so $3^j\mid a-b$. Thus $f$ is injective mod $3^j$.

**Reduction.** If some residue $k$ is missed modulo $m$, it is also missed modulo every multiple $n$ of $m$ (if $n\mid a^3+a-k$ then $m\mid a^3+a-k$). So it suffices to show that $f$ fails for $m=2$ and for every prime $p>3$; then the only possible $n$ are powers of $3$.

* $m=2$: $a^3+a=a(a^2+1)$ is always even, so $k=1$ is missed.
* $p\equiv1\pmod 4$: there is $b$ with $b^2\equiv-1$, so $f(b)=b(b^2+1)\equiv0=f(0)$ with $b\not\equiv0$.
* $p\equiv3\pmod 4$, $p>3$. It suffices to find $a\not\equiv b$ with $a^2+ab+b^2\equiv-1$, since then $f(a)-f(b)=(a-b)(a^2+ab+b^2+1)\equiv0$.

  *Step 1: $x^2+x+1$ takes some non-residue value.* We have $x^2+x+1\equiv y^2+y+1$ iff $p\mid(x-y)(x+y+1)$, so as $x$ runs over $\mathbb Z/p$ the polynomial takes exactly $\frac{p+1}{2}$ values. Let $C$ be the set consisting of $0$ and the quadratic residues; $|C|=\frac{p+1}2$. If all values were in $C$, the values would be all of $C$. Then for $y=z^2\in C$, writing $z=2w+1$, we get $y+3=4(w^2+w+1)\in 4C=C$. So $C+3\subseteq C$; starting from $0$ this gives all multiples of $3$, i.e. all of $\mathbb Z/p$ (as $p\ne3$), contradicting $|C|<p$.

  *Step 2.* Take $x$ with $x^2+x+1=N$ a non-residue. Since $p\equiv3\pmod4$, $-1$ is a non-residue, so $-N$ is a non-zero quadratic residue, i.e. $N\equiv-c^2$ for some $c\not\equiv0$. Put $b\equiv c^{-1}$ and $a\equiv xb$. Then $a^2+ab+b^2=b^2(x^2+x+1)\equiv c^{-2}\cdot(-c^2)=-1$.

  *Step 3.* If it happens that $a\equiv b$, then $3a^2\equiv-1$, and the pair $(2a,-a)$ works instead: $(2a)^2+(2a)(-a)+a^2=3a^2\equiv-1$ and $2a\not\equiv-a$ because $3a\not\equiv0$.

So for every prime $p>3$ the map is not injective, hence not surjective. The answer is: all $n=3^b$ with $b\ge0$. ∎

prompt:
Let $n$ and $b$ be positive integers. We say $n$ is *$b$-discerning* if there exists a set consisting of $n$ different positive integers less than $b$ that has no two different subsets $U$ and $V$ such that the sum of all elements in $U$ equals the sum of all elements in $V$.

(a) Prove that $8$ is $100$-discerning.

(b) Prove that $9$ is not $100$-discerning.
answer: (a) $\{3,6,12,24,48,95,96,97\}$ works (look at sums mod $3$). (b) Pigeonhole on the subsets of size $3$–$6$ and on the subsets with $2$–$4$ of the six largest elements gives $s_6+s_7+s_8+s_9\ge409>96+97+98+99$.

solutions.title: Explicit set; double pigeonhole
solutions.body:
**(a)** Take $S=\{3,6,12,24,48,96\}\cup\{95,97\}$. A subset $U$ has sum $3t+95\varepsilon_1+97\varepsilon_2$, where $3t$ is the sum of $U\cap\{3,\dots,96\}$ and $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\in\{0,1\}$ record whether $95,97\in U$. By binary representation, $t\in\{0,\dots,63\}$ determines $U\cap\{3,6,\dots,96\}$ uniquely. Modulo $3$ the sum is $0,2,1,0$ for $(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)=(0,0),(1,0),(0,1),(1,1)$. Suppose two subsets have equal sums. If the common residue is $1$ or $2$, the pair $(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2)$ is the same for both. If it is $0$, note that sums with $(0,0)$ are at most $3\cdot63=189$, while sums with $(1,1)$ are at least $192$; so again the pairs agree. Then the values of $t$ agree, so the subsets are equal. Hence all subset sums are distinct and $8$ is $100$-discerning.

**(b)** Suppose $s_1<s_2<\dots<s_9<100$ are positive integers with all subset sums distinct.

*First count.* There are $\binom93+\binom94+\binom95+\binom96=84+126+126+84=420$ subsets with $3$ to $6$ elements. Each has sum at least $s_1+s_2+s_3$ and at most $s_4+\dots+s_9$. These $420$ distinct integers lie in an interval containing $(s_4+\dots+s_9)-(s_1+s_2+s_3)+1$ integers, so
$$(s_4+\dots+s_9)-(s_1+s_2+s_3)\ge419. \tag{1}$$

*Second count.* Consider the subsets containing exactly $2$, $3$ or $4$ of the six elements $s_4,\dots,s_9$ (and any subset of $\{s_1,s_2,s_3\}$). There are $8\left(\binom62+\binom63+\binom64\right)=8\cdot50=400$ of them. Each has sum at least $s_4+s_5$ and at most $s_1+s_2+s_3+s_6+s_7+s_8+s_9$. As before,
$$(s_1+s_2+s_3+s_6+s_7+s_8+s_9)-(s_4+s_5)\ge399. \tag{2}$$

Adding (1) and (2) gives $2(s_6+s_7+s_8+s_9)\ge818$, so $s_6+s_7+s_8+s_9\ge409$. But these are distinct integers below $100$, so their sum is at most $96+97+98+99=390$. Contradiction; $9$ is not $100$-discerning. ∎

prompt: Circles $\omega$ and $\Omega$ meet at points $A$ and $B$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of the arc $AB$ of circle $\omega$ ($M$ lies inside $\Omega$). A chord $MP$ of circle $\omega$ intersects $\Omega$ at $Q$ ($Q$ lies inside $\omega$). Let $\ell_P$ be the tangent line to $\omega$ at $P$, and let $\ell_Q$ be the tangent line to $\Omega$ at $Q$. Prove that the circumcircle of the triangle formed by the lines $\ell_P$, $\ell_Q$, and $AB$ is tangent to $\Omega$.
answer: Proof: with $R$ the second point of $PQ$ on $\Omega$, $S,T\in\Omega$ with $RS\parallel AB$, $RT\parallel\ell_P$, triangle $RST$ (inscribed in $\Omega$) has sides parallel to those of $XYZ$; the homothety between them has its centre $D=XR\cap\Omega$ on $\Omega$, so the two circumcircles are tangent at $D$.

solutions.title: A homothety centred on $\Omega$
solutions.body:
We use directed angles between lines, $\angle(\ell,m)$, taken modulo $180^\circ$. Let $X=AB\cap\ell_P$, $Y=AB\cap\ell_Q$, $Z=\ell_P\cap\ell_Q$ (the triangle is assumed non-degenerate) and $F=MP\cap AB$.

**Step 1: $\angle(AB,MP)=\angle(MP,\ell_P)$, so $XF=XP$.** The tangent $\ell_M$ to $\omega$ at $M$ is parallel to $AB$, since $M$ is the midpoint of arc $AB$. The tangents at the two ends of the chord $MP$ are symmetric in the perpendicular bisector of $MP$, so $\angle(\ell_M,MP)=\angle(MP,\ell_P)$, which gives the claim. In triangle $XFP$ this says $\angle(FX,FP)=\angle(PF,PX)$, i.e. equal base angles, so $XF=XP$.

**Step 2: a triangle in $\Omega$ with sides parallel to $XYZ$.** Let $R$ be the second intersection of line $MP$ with $\Omega$, and let $S,T$ be the points of $\Omega$ with $RS\parallel AB$ and $RT\parallel\ell_P$. Then, by Step 1,
$$\angle(RS,RQ)=\angle(AB,MP)=\angle(MP,\ell_P)=\angle(RQ,RT).$$
These are inscribed angles of $\Omega$ on the chords $SQ$ and $QT$, so $QS=QT$. Hence $Q$ lies on the perpendicular bisector of $ST$, which passes through the centre of $\Omega$, and therefore the tangent $\ell_Q$ at $Q$ is parallel to $ST$. So $RS\parallel XY$, $RT\parallel XZ$, $ST\parallel YZ$, and there is a homothety $h$ with $h(R)=X$, $h(S)=Y$, $h(T)=Z$. It maps $\Omega$, the circumcircle of $RST$, to the circumcircle of $XYZ$.

**Step 3: the centre of $h$ is on $\Omega$.** Let $D$ be the second intersection of line $XR$ with $\Omega$. By Step 1 and the power of $X$ with respect to $\omega$ and $\Omega$,
$$XF^2=XP^2=XA\cdot XB=XD\cdot XR .$$
So $XF/XD=XR/XF$, and triangles $XDF$ and $XFR$ (common angle at $X$) are similar with opposite orientation. Hence
$$\angle(FX,FD)=\angle(RF,RX)=\angle(RQ,RD)=\angle(QY,QD),$$
the last step being the tangent–chord angle in $\Omega$ ($QY=\ell_Q$). As $FX$ is the line $AB$, which passes through $Y$, this reads $\angle(FY,FD)=\angle(QY,QD)$, so $F,Q,Y,D$ are concyclic. Then
$$\angle(DY,DQ)=\angle(FY,FQ)=\angle(AB,MP)=\angle(RS,RQ)=\angle(DS,DQ),$$
using the circle $FQYD$, then $RS\parallel AB$, then the circle $\Omega$. Hence the lines $DY$ and $DS$ coincide: $D$ lies on $SY$ as well as on $RX$.

The centre of $h$ lies on every line joining a point to its image, so it is $XR\cap YS=D$, a point of $\Omega$. The homothety fixes $D$, so $D$ is on both $\Omega$ and $h(\Omega)$, and their centres $O$ and $h(O)$ are collinear with $D$. Two circles through a common point $D$ whose centres are collinear with $D$ are tangent at $D$. Therefore the circumcircle of $XYZ$ is tangent to $\Omega$. ∎

prompt: Let $ABC$ be a triangle, and let $D$ be a point on side $BC$. A line through $D$ intersects side $AB$ at $X$ and ray $AC$ at $Y$. The circumcircle of triangle $BXD$ intersects the circumcircle $\omega$ of triangle $ABC$ again at point $Z\neq B$. The lines $ZD$ and $ZY$ intersect $\omega$ again at $V$ and $W$, respectively. Prove that $AB=VW$.
answer: Proof: angle chasing gives that $Z,D,C,Y$ are concyclic; then the inscribed angle $\angle VZW$ equals (or is supplementary to) $\angle BCA$, so the chords $VW$ and $AB$ of $\omega$ are equal.

solutions.title: Directed angle chase
solutions.body:
We use directed angles between lines, $\angle(\ell,m)$, modulo $180^\circ$; this makes the argument independent of the configuration.

**Step 1: $Z,D,C,Y$ are concyclic.** Using that $X,D,Y$ are collinear, that $B,X,D,Z$ are concyclic, that $X$ lies on $AB$, that $A,B,Z,C$ lie on $\omega$, and that $Y$ lies on $AC$:
$$\angle(DZ,DY)=\angle(DZ,DX)=\angle(BZ,BX)=\angle(BZ,BA)=\angle(CZ,CA)=\angle(CZ,CY).$$
Hence $Z,D,C,Y$ lie on a circle.

**Step 2: compare inscribed angles in $\omega$.** Since $W$ is on line $ZY$, $V$ on line $ZD$, then by Step 1, and since $Y\in AC$, $D\in BC$:
$$\angle(ZW,ZV)=\angle(ZY,ZD)=\angle(CY,CD)=\angle(CA,CB).$$
In a circle of radius $r$, a chord seen from a point of the circle under the directed angle $\varphi$ has length $2r|\sin\varphi|$. The chord $VW$ is seen from $Z$ under $\angle(ZW,ZV)$ and the chord $AB$ is seen from $C$ under $\angle(CA,CB)$. These angles are equal, so $VW=AB$. ∎

prompt:
Let $S=\{2,3,4,\dots\}$ denote the set of integers that are greater than or equal to $2$. Does there exist a function $f\colon S\to S$ such that
$$f(a)f(b)=f(a^2b^2)\quad\text{for all } a,b\in S \text{ with } a\neq b\,?$$
answer: No. Comparing two evaluations of $f(a^4b^4c^4)$ ($c$ large) gives $f(a^2)=kf(a)$ for a constant $k$, then $f(ab)=f(a)f(b)/k$ for $a\ne b$; computing $f(a^6)$ two ways forces $f\equiv k$, and then $k^2=k$ gives $k=1\notin S$.

solutions.title: Show $f$ would have to be constant
solutions.body:
Suppose such an $f$ exists.

**Step 1: $f(a^2)/f(a)$ is constant.** Take $a,b\in S$ and choose $c\in S$ larger than both. Apply the equation to the pair $a^2\ne b^2c^2$ (distinct because $bc>a$) and then to the pair $b\ne c$:
$$f(a^4b^4c^4)=f(a^2)f(b^2c^2)=f(a^2)f(b)f(c).$$
Exchanging the roles of $a$ and $b$ (now $ac>b$ and $c\ne a$):
$$f(a^4b^4c^4)=f(b^2)f(a^2c^2)=f(b^2)f(a)f(c).$$
So $f(a^2)f(b)=f(b^2)f(a)$, i.e. $\dfrac{f(a^2)}{f(a)}=\dfrac{f(b^2)}{f(b)}$ for all $a,b$. Hence there is a constant $k>0$ with
$$f(a^2)=k\,f(a)\quad\text{for all }a\in S. \tag{1}$$

**Step 2.** For $a\ne b$: $f(a)f(b)=f\big((ab)^2\big)=k\,f(ab)$, so
$$f(ab)=\frac{f(a)f(b)}{k}\quad(a\ne b). \tag{2}$$

**Step 3: $f$ is constant.** Fix $a\in S$; since $a\ge2$, the numbers $a^2,a^4,a^5$ all differ from $a$. The equation for the pair $a\ne a^2$ gives $f(a)f(a^2)=f(a^6)$. On the other hand, by (2) twice and (1),
$$f(a^6)=f(a\cdot a^5)=\frac{f(a)f(a^5)}{k}=\frac{f(a)}{k}\cdot\frac{f(a)f(a^4)}{k}=\frac{f(a)^2\,k\,f(a^2)}{k^2}=\frac{f(a)^2f(a^2)}{k}.$$
Comparing, $f(a)f(a^2)=f(a)^2f(a^2)/k$, so $f(a)=k$ for every $a$.

**Step 4.** Then the equation with $a=2,b=3$ reads $k\cdot k=k$, so $k=1$. But $1\notin S$. Contradiction — no such function exists. ∎

prompt:
A sequence of real numbers $a_0, a_1, \dots$ is said to be *good* if the following three conditions hold.

(i) The value of $a_0$ is a positive integer.

(ii) For each non-negative integer $i$ we have $a_{i+1}=2a_i+1$ or $a_{i+1}=\dfrac{a_i}{a_i+2}$.

(iii) There exists a positive integer $k$ such that $a_k=2014$.

Find the smallest positive integer $n$ such that there exists a good sequence $a_0, a_1, \dots$ of real numbers with the property that $a_n=2014$.

solutions.title: Substitute $u_i=1/(a_i+1)$
solutions.body:
All terms are positive. Put $u_i=\dfrac{1}{a_i+1}\in(0,1)$. The two moves become
$$a_{i+1}=2a_i+1\iff a_{i+1}+1=2(a_i+1)\iff u_{i+1}=\tfrac12u_i,$$
$$a_{i+1}=\frac{a_i}{a_i+2}\iff a_{i+1}+1=\frac{2(a_i+1)}{a_i+2}\iff u_{i+1}=\frac{a_i+2}{2(a_i+1)}=\tfrac12u_i+\tfrac12 .$$
So $u_{i+1}=\frac12(u_i+\varepsilon_{i+1})$ with $\varepsilon_{i+1}\in\{0,1\}$, and by induction
$$2^n u_n=u_0+E,\qquad E=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\varepsilon_i2^{i-1}\in\{0,1,\dots,2^n-1\}.$$

**Necessity.** If $a_n=2014$, then $u_n=\frac1{2015}$ and
$$\frac{2^n}{2015}=\frac{1}{a_0+1}+E\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2^n=d+2015E,\qquad d=\frac{2015}{a_0+1}.$$
So $d=2^n-2015E$ is an integer, hence a divisor of $2015$; then $d$ divides $2^n$ as well, and since $2015$ is odd, $d=1$. Thus $a_0=2014$ and $2015\mid 2^n-1$.

Now $2015=5\cdot13\cdot31$, and the multiplicative order of $2$ is $4$ modulo $5$, $12$ modulo $13$ (as $2^6\equiv-1$) and $5$ modulo $31$ (as $2^5=32$). So $2015\mid2^n-1$ iff $\operatorname{lcm}(4,12,5)=60$ divides $n$. Hence $n\ge60$.

**Sufficiency.** Let $n=60$, $a_0=2014$, and let $\varepsilon_1,\dots,\varepsilon_{60}$ be the binary digits of $E=\frac{2^{60}-1}{2015}$, an integer with $0\le E\le2^{60}-1$. Define the sequence by choosing at step $i$ the move given by $\varepsilon_i$ (and, say, always $a_{i+1}=2a_i+1$ after step $60$). All terms are positive reals, and
$$u_{60}=\frac{u_0+E}{2^{60}}=\frac{\frac1{2015}+\frac{2^{60}-1}{2015}}{2^{60}}=\frac1{2015},$$
so $a_{60}=2014$. This sequence is good (with $k=60$).

**Answer: $60$.** ∎

solutions.title: Run the sequence backwards
solutions.body: Each move is invertible on positive numbers: from $a_{i+1}$ we recover $a_i=\frac{a_{i+1}-1}{2}$ if $a_{i+1}>1$ (only the first move gives values above $1$) and $a_i=\frac{2a_{i+1}}{1-a_{i+1}}$ if $a_{i+1}<1$. So starting from $2014$ the sequence backwards is forced. Write the terms as fractions $m_i/n_i$, starting from $2014/1$; the inverse moves are $(m,n)\mapsto(m-n,2n)$ if $m>n$ and $(2m,n-m)$ if $m<n$. By induction $m_i+n_i=2015$, $\gcd(m_i,n_i)=1$ and $n_i\equiv2^i\pmod{2015}$. A positive integer is reached exactly when $n_i=1$, i.e. when $2^i\equiv1\pmod{2015}$ (as $1\le n_i\le2014$). The least such $i$ is $60$ (the order of $2$ modulo $2015$), so the answer is $60$.

prompt: Let $n$ be a positive integer. Consider $2n$ distinct lines on the plane, no two of which are parallel. Of the $2n$ lines, $n$ are colored blue, the other $n$ are colored red. Let $\mathcal B$ be the set of all points on the plane that lie on at least one blue line, and $\mathcal R$ the set of all points on the plane that lie on at least one red line. Prove that there exists a circle that intersects $\mathcal B$ in exactly $2n-1$ points, and also intersects $\mathcal R$ in exactly $2n-1$ points.
answer: Proof: order the lines by direction and pick two consecutive ones $\ell,\ell'$ of different colours; a large circle tangent to $\ell$ and $\ell'$ in the angle whose directions contain all other lines' directions meets each other line twice and avoids all intersection points.

solutions.title: Two directionally adjacent lines of different colours
solutions.body:
**Choosing two lines.** Measure the direction of each line by an angle in $[0^\circ,180^\circ)$; the $2n$ directions are distinct. List the lines as $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_{2n}$ in increasing order of direction. Both colours occur, so some consecutive pair $\ell_k,\ell_{k+1}$ has different colours. No other line has a direction strictly between those of $\ell_k$ and $\ell_{k+1}$.

**The angle.** Let $O=\ell_k\cap\ell_{k+1}$. The two lines divide the plane into two pairs of vertical angles. The rays from $O$ in one pair have directions (mod $180^\circ$) strictly between those of $\ell_k$ and $\ell_{k+1}$; the rays in the other pair have all the remaining directions. Let $W$ be one angle of the second pair. Every other line $\ell$ is parallel to a line $\ell^0$ through $O$ that passes through the interior of $W$.

**The circle.** Let $C_1$ be a circle inscribed in $W$ (tangent to both sides), with centre $o_1$ and radius $\rho_1$, and for $t>0$ let $C_t$ be its image under the homothety with centre $O$ and ratio $t$ (centre $to_1$, radius $t\rho_1$); $C_t$ is also tangent to $\ell_k$ and $\ell_{k+1}$. The tangents from $O$ to $C_1$ are the two sides of $W$, so every line through $O$ entering the interior of $W$ cuts $C_1$ in two points: $\operatorname{dist}(o_1,\ell^0)<\rho_1$. For the parallel line $\ell$,
$$\operatorname{dist}(to_1,\ell)\le t\operatorname{dist}(o_1,\ell^0)+\operatorname{dist}(\ell^0,\ell)<t\rho_1$$
for all large $t$. Also the finitely many intersection points of pairs of lines lie in some disc around $O$, while the distance from $O$ to $C_t$ is $t(|Oo_1|-\rho_1)\to\infty$ (note $|Oo_1|>\rho_1$). Fix $t$ so large that both hold for all $2n-2$ other lines.

**Counting.** Then $C_t$ is tangent to $\ell_k$ and $\ell_{k+1}$ (one point each), meets each of the other $2n-2$ lines in exactly two points, and no point of $C_t$ lies on two lines (for $\ell_k,\ell_{k+1}$ these meet only at $O\notin C_t$). Say $\ell_k$ is blue and $\ell_{k+1}$ red. Then $C_t\cap\mathcal B$ consists of $1$ point on $\ell_k$ and $2$ points on each of the other $n-1$ blue lines, all distinct: $1+2(n-1)=2n-1$ points. The same count holds for $\mathcal R$. ∎

solutions.title: Recurrence, bounds, then divisibility
solutions.body:
**A recurrence.** Write (ii) as $s_{n+1}=(n+1)a_n+h_n$ with $h_n=\pm1$ ($n\ge1$). Since $s_{n+1}+s_n=a_{n+1}$, for $n\ge2$
$$a_{n+1}=(n+1)a_n+na_{n-1}+\delta_n,\qquad \delta_n=h_n+h_{n-1}\in\{-2,0,2\}. \tag{1}$$

**All terms are large.** For $n=1$, $s_2=a_2-a_1+a_0$ and $|s_2-2a_1|=1$ give $a_0=3a_1-a_2\pm1\le3a_1$, so $a_1\ge\frac{2015}3$, i.e. $a_1\ge672$. By (1), $a_3=3a_2+2a_1+\delta_2$, and $a_1\mid a_3$ by (i), so $a_1\mid 3a_2+\delta_2>0$; thus $3a_2+2\ge672$ and $a_2\ge224$. From (1), $a_{n+1}\ge(n+1)a_n-2>a_n$ for $n\ge2$. Hence $a_n\ge 223$ for all $n\ge0$.

**Two inequalities.** For $n\ge3$, (1) at index $n-1$ gives
$$a_n=na_{n-1}+(n-1)a_{n-2}+\delta_{n-1}>na_{n-1}+3, \tag{2}$$
and for $n\ge4$, using (2) at $n-1$, i.e. $(n-1)a_{n-2}<a_{n-1}-3$,
$$a_n<na_{n-1}+a_{n-1}-3+2<(n+1)a_{n-1}. \tag{3}$$

**Lemma 1.** For $n\ge4$, $a_{n+2}=(n+1)(n+4)a_n$.

Applying (1) at $n+1$ and then at $n$:
$$a_{n+2}=(n+1)(n+3)a_n+n(n+2)a_{n-1}+(n+2)\delta_n+\delta_{n+1}.$$
Upper bound: by (2), $na_{n-1}<a_n-3$, so $n(n+2)a_{n-1}<(n+2)a_n-3(n+2)$, and $(n+2)\delta_n+\delta_{n+1}\le2n+6$; hence $a_{n+2}<(n^2+5n+5)a_n$. Lower bound: by (3), $a_{n-1}>\frac{a_n}{n+1}$, so $n(n+2)a_{n-1}>\big(n+1-\frac1{n+1}\big)a_n\ge na_n+\frac45a_n$, and $\frac45a_n>\frac45\cdot223n>2n+6\ge-\big((n+2)\delta_n+\delta_{n+1}\big)$ (using $a_n>na_{n-1}\ge223n$). Hence $a_{n+2}>(n^2+5n+3)a_n$. Since $a_n\mid a_{n+2}$, the only possibility is $a_{n+2}=(n^2+5n+4)a_n=(n+1)(n+4)a_n$. $\square$

**Lemma 2.** For $n\ge4$, $(n+2)a_{n+1}=(n+1)(n+3)a_n$.

By (1) at $n+2$, $a_{n+3}=(n+3)a_{n+2}+(n+2)a_{n+1}+\delta_{n+2}$. Substituting $a_{n+3}=(n+2)(n+5)a_{n+1}$ and $a_{n+2}=(n+1)(n+4)a_n$ (Lemma 1 at $n+1$ and $n$):
$$(n+2)(n+4)a_{n+1}=(n+1)(n+3)(n+4)a_n+\delta_{n+2}.$$
So $n+4\mid\delta_{n+2}$; as $|\delta_{n+2}|\le2<n+4$, $\delta_{n+2}=0$ and the claim follows. $\square$

**The relation also holds for $n=1,2,3$.** Suppose not, and let $m\in\{1,2,3\}$ be the largest index with $(m+2)a_{m+1}\ne(m+1)(m+3)a_m$. Then $(m+3)a_{m+2}=(m+2)(m+4)a_{m+1}$; as $\gcd(m+3,(m+2)(m+4))=1$, write $a_{m+1}=(m+3)k$, $a_{m+2}=(m+2)(m+4)k$. By (1) at $m+1\ge2$,
$$(m+1)a_m+\delta_{m+1}=a_{m+2}-(m+2)a_{m+1}=(m+2)k.$$
If $\delta_{m+1}=0$ this gives $(m+2)a_{m+1}=(m+1)(m+3)a_m$, against the choice of $m$; so $\delta_{m+1}=\pm2$. Now $a_m$ divides $(m+2)k-\delta_{m+1}$ and also $a_{m+2}=(m+2)(m+4)k$ (by (i)), hence it divides $(m+4)\big((m+2)k-\delta_{m+1}\big)-(m+2)(m+4)k=-(m+4)\delta_{m+1}$. So $a_m\le2(m+4)\le14$, contradicting $a_m\ge223$.

**Solving.** So $(n+2)a_{n+1}=(n+1)(n+3)a_n$ for all $n\ge1$. For $n=1$: $3a_2=8a_1$, so $3\mid a_1$; write $a_1=3c$. By induction $a_n=c(n+2)\,n!$ for $n\ge1$ (indeed $a_{n+1}=\frac{(n+1)(n+3)}{n+2}c(n+2)n!=c(n+3)(n+1)!$). From $|s_2-2a_1|=1$: $s_2=8c-3c+a_0$, so $|a_0-c|=1$, i.e. $a_0=c\pm1$.
